title: LOOK: Ja'Marr Chase makes absurd TD catch that could be best grab you'll see all season
summary: The Bengals wideout adjusted in mid-air against former LSU teammate Derek Stingley Jr. and dragged his toes in bounds to break a scoreless tie in Houston
full_text:
The first half of Cincinnati Bengals at Houston Texans was defined by defense. Yards were seemingly at a premium, as both offenses struggled to move the ball.
We were scoreless late into the second quarter before Cincy's dynamic duo of Joe Burrow and Ja'Marr Chase finally showed up and coordinated on what will go down as one of the best plays of the year.
On a first-and-10 from the Texans' 32-yard line, Burrow identified Chase deep downfield one-on-one with cornerback Derek Stingley Jr . Stingley is one of the best defensive backs in the league, but Burrow decided to roll the dice. It proved to be the correct decision, as Chase readjusted mid-air and made an incredible grab for the first touchdown of the game.
Check out what happened here:
WHAT A CATCH BY JA'MARR CHASE FOR THE TD pic.twitter.com/M1vbRIiESS
Look at it again: Chase had to adjust to the ball, swing his body around, keep his feet in bounds with a couple toe drags — and oh yeah, actually catch the football.
Ja'Marr holy pic.twitter.com/pEmKtXJm6K
After the game, Chase told CBS Sports' Melanie Collins that "it was just a go-ball," and he adjusted well at the end of the play.
"It was just a go-ball. Joe just threw it up, gave me an opportunity. Man, Stingley fighting to hold possession of where the ball was at and I adjusted really well at the end." Ja'Marr Chase breaks down his highlight reel TD catch with @Melanie_Collins pic.twitter.com/Z0w8oHQruX
If you recall, Chase and Stingley were actually college teammates on that famed 2019 LSU team. They have faced off against each other just once before, back in Week 10 of the 2023 season. In that game, Chase exploded for 124 yards and a touchdown.
Plays like this are why Chase is arguably the best wide receiver in the National Football League. He joined Randy Moss as the only two players to record 1,000 yards receiving and at least seven touchdowns in each of a player's first five seasons. He has averaged the third-most receiving yards per game in NFL history with 86.7. Not only is Chase a home-run hitter capable of scoring on any touch he gets, but he's remarkable when it comes to reeling in those catches that not many athletes can. This one will be included in the NFL's 2026 highlight reel.
author: Jordan Dajani

title: Bears QB Caleb Williams exits vs. Vikings after suffering non-contact hamstring injury
summary: The Bears quarterback went down untouched while rolling to his left and appeared to be in significant pain as trainers helped him off the field
full_text:
Caleb Williams left the Chicago Bears ' 9-3 loss to the Minnesota Vikings in Week 2 after he suffered a non-contact injury. The team ruled him out with a hamstring issue, which occurred on a rollout as Williams attempted to keep a play alive deep in Minnesota territory.
While in search of a go-ahead touchdown in the fourth quarter, Williams pulled up during a run to the left of the pocket and fell to the ground. He held one of his legs and let out an audible yell before trainers assisted him off the field.
Chicago's medical staff briefly attended to Williams in the sideline medical tent and promptly carted him into the locker room for further evaluation.
Caleb Williams gives a thumbs up as he's carted off the field. 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/omeGyES2s5
Coach Ben Johnson said after the game that the team does not yet know the severity of Williams' injury but will have more information on Monday. He noted that Williams is in "good spirits" despite the ailment and the loss.
"I'm actually happy it's nothing with the knee," Johnson said. "That was my first inclination. But a hamstring could be pretty damaging, as well. So we'll see how bad it is tomorrow and we'll go from there. But it's quick; you gotta turn the page, particularly when you're right there. We needed points desperately at that point. Shame."
Soggy field conditions could have contributed to the non-contact nature of the injury. Consistent rain in Chicago turned the NFC East showdown into a defensive battle and undoubtedly made for a slippery playing surface.
Tyson Bagent entered the game for the Bears, who trailed 6-3 at the time of Williams' injury. A promising drive stalled in the red zone when Williams departed from action, and the Bears settled for a field goal attempt. The Vikings blocked that potential game-tying kick.
Chicago's uncharacteristic offensive struggles against Minnesota came as Williams slogged through an inefficient afternoon. The star signal-caller completed 15 of 26 passes for 138 yards before he left the contest, and he tossed one interception and took three sacks. Williams' escapability contributed to his injury, but before the fateful play, it also helped him accumulate 42 rushing yards on five carries.
author: Carter Bahns

title: Saints left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. suffers ankle injury: New Orleans loses 2025 No. 9 overall pick
summary: Banks went down awkwardly after a sack
full_text:
Saints standout left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr . was carted off with an ankle injury during Sunday's game at Baltimore and ruled out shortly thereafter. Banks got rolled up on awkwardly after a Mike Green sack.
#KelvinBanksJr LT @Saints Carted off with likely high ankle sprain pic.twitter.com/eRHL4DNTZ9
Banks was emerging as a stalwart for New Orleans, and his injury is a big one. The Saints had to go to Asim Richards , a fourth-year pro who has just five career starts, to protect Tyler Shough's blind side. With Richards in, the Saints used an extra running back or tight end to chip in pass protection
The No. 9 pick in 2025 out of Texas, Banks started all 17 games last season and was showing real strides late in the season. Across the final five weeks of the year, he was Pro Football Focus' 12th-rated offensive tackle.
Banks is part of a talented young offensive core for New Orleans, a group that includes Shough, wide receiver Chris Olave and right tackle Taliese Fuaga . Wide receiver Jordyn Tyson , the No. 8 overall pick in 2025, is yet to make his NFL debut due to a hamstring injury, but when he's healthy, he oozes potential, too.
Should Banks miss significant time, the Saints could look into finding outside help. The only other tackle on the roster after Banks, Fuaga and Richards is Mason Murphy , a 2026 undrafted free agent.
author: Zachary Pereles

title: Eagles' Saquon Barkley (stinger) returns after halftime vs. Titans, Dallas Goedert questionable
summary: Tank Bigsby took over as Philadelphia's top running back after Barkley suffered a stinger on the first offensive play
full_text:
After suffering a stinger on his first run of the day, Saquon Barkley returned to the Eagles ' Week 2 game against the Titans in the second half. Here's a look at the injury:
#SaquonBarkley to locker room after this play No official word yet Hopefully to return after equipment for L shoulder pic.twitter.com/s9aJQmMRNH
Tank Bigsby took over as the top running back following Barkley's departure. The Eagles drove down the field before Jalen Hurts threw an interception, and Tennessee capitalized with a touchdown a few plays later. Bigsby scored a touchdown on the ensuing drive. Will Shipley is also seeing some action in the backfield, mostly in passing situations.
Dallas Goedert is questionable to return for Philadelphia due to a knee injury. The veteran tight end, who had two touchdown catches in Week 1, took a hard hit to his right leg.
Both players returned to the sideline before the end of the first half. Barkley was sporting a neck roll on top of his shoulder pads.
Barkley, 29, had 15 carries for 83 yards in the Eagles' Week 1 win over the Commanders , though 42 of those yards came on one run. The three-time Pro Bowler is coming off another stellar season with 1,413 yards from scrimmage and nine touchdowns. It was a far cry from his 2024 season, when he led the NFL with 2,283 yards from scrimmage (on an NFL-high 378 touches), but he remains the engine of Philadelphia's offense.
It's worth noting that the Eagles shuffled their offensive line this week with left guard Landon Dickerson going on IR. Philadelphia moved Cam Jurgens from center to left guard and inserted Drew Kendall at center; Barkley's injury happened while running behind those two players.
Bigsby is the clear top option behind Barkley -- he had 10 carries and two catches across the Eagles' first three drives -- but the rushing duties will be more spread out. Shipley had seven carries on the first three drives, and the designed quarterback run game could become more of a factor, too.
Hurts also started making some impressive downfield throws (except for the interception) with Barkley not playing. He was 14 for 17 for 141 yards and a touchdown across the Eagles' first three drives.
Floating it to 6️⃣ for 6️⃣ pic.twitter.com/0yR7DgLNE1
DeVonta Smith was already up to five catches for 66 yards and a score across the first three possessions; Dontayvion Wicks had four catches for 54 yards.
Bigsby, 26, started his career as a 2023 third-round pick of the Jaguars . He had a difficult rookie year, averaging just 2.6 yards per carry in limited action, but he had a strong second season: 766 rushing yards and seven touchdowns while splitting time with Travis Etienne Jr.
Even though he appeared to be trending upward in Jacksonville, Bigsby got traded just one game into last season. As Barkley's backup last year, Bigsby averaged 5.9 yards per carry. He received just one carry for three yards last week.

title: Arizona Cardinals need offensive stars to breakout
summary: Through two games the high flying, wheeling and dealing offense has been. Not great. Yes they scored 26 points against the Los Angeles Chargers, but they settled for five field goals, making four and really never looking in sync for the entirety of the game. Then game two happened and it was one of the […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - SEPTEMBER 20: Head coach Mike LaFleur of the Arizona Cardinals looks on during the fourth quarter of the game against the Seattle Seahawks at State Farm Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Through two games the high flying, wheeling and dealing offense has been. Not great. Yes they scored 26 points against the Los Angeles Chargers, but they settled for five field goals, making four and really never looking in sync for the entirety of the game. Then game two happened and it was one of the most listless performances on offense I can remember. If you take out Bam Knight’s 24 rushing yards at the end of the game, the team had 127 yards of offense. Even with Knight’s 24 yards, the 151 total yards is the low water mark for the franchise since 2023 when rookie Clayton Tune was a sacrificial lamb to the best defense in the league, the Cleveland Browns. On that day, no one expected much and the 58 yards was embarrassing, but not exactly out of left field. Outside of that one, you’d have to go back to 2018 to be sub 151 yards of total offense. Maybe more than the lack of offensive output is the fact that outside of the second highest paid tight end in the NFL, this group looks devoid of talent. And it’s not because they lack talent, they just don’t seem to be interested in utilizing the talent. Look at these numbers through two games: Jeremiyah Love – 20 carries 70 yards one touchdown, five receptions 25 yards 25 touches for 95 yards for the third overall pick. Michael Wilson – 7 receptions 74 yards on 14 targets Marvin Harrison Jr – 1 reception 33 yards on four targets Eight receptions for 107 yards on 18 targets for the former fourth overall pick and the newly paid receiver. Even Trey McBride’s numbers today looked more like a running back than a tight end with eight receptions for 41 yards and one touchdown. Look, no one is expecting the greatest show on turf by week two, but with the talent we believe this team has, you can’t put up a game that takes you back to Steve Wilks, Mike McCoy and Sam Bradford era. Of course that team had David Johnson, Larry Fitzgerald and Christian Kirk… ok, maybe the names were nice, but DJ was coming off his career altering injury, Fitz was 35 and Kirk was a rookie in game two of his career, so saying that is equal is disingenuous, but this wasn’t fun to watch in the least.

full_text: The Arizona Cardinals are getting ready for their first home game of the year against division foe Seattle Seahawks this Sunday, September 20, with a 3:25 (Eastern) kickoff. A lot of time and work has been put into this year’s roster to bring forth a new offense. The game, to be played at State Farm Stadium, has some new food items this year. RELATED: 3 TAKES ON THE 2026 CARDINALS SCHEDULE The stadium food and beverage menu guide has identified several new items available for home games throughout the 2026 season. This year, the Cardinals will play nine home games. The kitchen’s creations are from Craft Culinary Concepts, which means the stadium’s food menu is available from chefs instead of just cooks. Whereas hot dogs, soft pretzels, cheeseburgers, and popcorn remain steady sellers, this menu will offer different dining experiences presented by Executive Chef Sean Kavanaugh. Among these new creations are a variety of gluten-free, vegan, and vegetarian options. Something new for 2026: Beef Birria Machete This is a two-foot-long birria machete quesadilla, filled with savory beef birria. Whoever orders this will need larger plates and more napkins. This creation feeds four or five people. Available in Sections 210 and 240. Chopped Cheese Machete Quesadilla This is also pretty massive and is about two feet long. It is griddled ground beef with melted cheese inside an extra-large, elongated tortilla, then topped with adobo seasoning and diced onions. Again, it will serve several fans in one outing so come hungry. Available in Sections 210 and 240. BBQ Brisket Burger Part of the “Rivalry Items” for 2026. This brisket burger features homemade roasted garlic and Sriracha BBQ sauce and comes with jalapeno candy. Available in Sections 129, 235, and 420. Sonoran Style Seattle Dog Another “Rivalry Item,” debuting when the Seahawks are in town in Week 2. This is a fat all-beef hot dog wrapped in bacon, then topped with whipped cream cheese, griddled onions, roasted jalapeño sauce, and yellow mustard, all on a fresh brioche bun. Available in Sections 129, 235, and 420. Milk Toast Sandwiches This creation is an inspiration from Uptown Phoenix restaurant “Let’s Toast.” It’s made in Korean style with Japanese-style milk bread, which is soft and fluffy. Several different varieties are offered, including the trendy mozzarella grilled cheese, and are served with homemade kettle chips. This is an exclusive offering in the Club Level. Chicken and Waffle Wings These are crispy chicken wings tossed in a sweet maple-bourbon glaze and then coated in waffle dust. This is a fun take on the traditional “chicken and waffles” without the mess and the process of continually making waffles all game long. Available in Sections 107, 129, 247, 408, and 420. Arizona Chiltepin Honey Hot Chicken Breast Sandwich Chef Kavanaugh offers a fried chicken breast and tops it with sweet-and-spicy chiltepin chiles and hot honey, lettuce, tomato, pickles, ranch sauce, and presents it on a brioche bun. Available in Section 124 only. Big Red Turkey Wrap This item comes on a big red tortilla with shaved smoked turkey breast, grilled flank steak, slaw, a smashed cucumber salad, and a seed-based crunch. Available in Sections 103, 119, 125, 220, 406, 434, 437, 450, and 452. Spicy Super Protein Salad Not your typical salad. It starts with Little Gem lettuce, Chile Pequin grilled flank steak, hard-boiled egg, roasted vegetables, Ancho Chimichurri dressing, and a superfood crunch combination of chia seeds, pepitas, and toasted hemp seeds. Available in Sections 103, 125, 220, and 229. Indian Frybread Dog A different spin on the traditional hot dog. It begins with a Big City Reds hot dog, topped with chili, diced tomatoes, shredded lettuce, crema, roasted jalapeño sauce, and all topped with shredded cheese. Comes on a puffy, traditional Indian frybread. Available in Sections 107, 129, 235, 247, 408, and 420. Walkin Taco-Fritos Layered seasoned beef, warm nacho cheese sauce, street corn, and Tostitos Vegetarian Chile are spread over either Fritos or Nacho Cheese Flavored Doritos. Served right inside the snack-size chip bag. Available in Sections 126 and 434. Soppressata Pizza Comes on a crisp crust with thinly-sliced, crispy Soppressata dry-cured salami, classic marinara sauce, and melted mozzarella cheese. Available in Sections 209, 240, and at Tarbell’s Pizza on the Club Level.

title: Falcons vs. Panthers recap: A famine for the eyes
summary: Every NFL season begins with a glimmer of hope, a flickering candle in the darkness that seems to show an open door. If you’re a good team, that light burns brighter and longer, and your confident steps forward carry you toward a destination you desire. If you’re a bad team, that light is quickly snuffed […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Chuba Hubbard #30 of the Carolina Panthers runs the ball against the Atlanta Falcons during the second quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Butch Dill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Every NFL season begins with a glimmer of hope, a flickering candle in the darkness that seems to show an open door. If you’re a good team, that light burns brighter and longer, and your confident steps forward carry you toward a destination you desire. If you’re a bad team, that light is quickly snuffed and you are plunged into umbra, and months are spent fumbling in the darkness looking for a latch that may not even exist. The Atlanta Falcons saw their light snuffed on Sunday. I know that it’s a long season, and the struggling Green Bay Packers are up next on a short week with Michael Penix Jr. potentially returning, and that the state of the NFC South means Atlanta is not out of it two weeks into the year. But I also know that 0-2 is a tough hole to climb out of, and that this Falcons team has to look like a completely different squad with a change at quarterback to see a reasonable way to climb to a winning season. They are already at the fumbling in the darkness stage, because things are bleak and I have not seen enough from this coaching staff or roster to assume they’re going to be able to clean up this mess quickly. And it is a mess. The defense is game and clearly the best unit on the field, but they also allowed Xavier Legette to get behind them for a 55 yard gain, got eviscerated by Bryce Young to the tune of 287 yards and three touchdowns, and let Chuba Hubbard have a solid day on the ground. Special teams looks mediocre in terms of returns and coverage and alarming in terms of the kicking game, now that Nick Folk has missed three field goals in two weeks. And the offense is abysmal, with playmakers looking forlorn on the sideline as Cooper Rush and Jack Strand combined for five turnovers and three points, with Bijan and Brian Robinson doing as much as they could (123 yards on 27 carries, five catches for 25 yards) and London trying his damndest as the only real bright lights on a tough day. An improvement in quarterbacking play will lift this offense to competence, but the pass protection, the miscues, and the penalties suggest it’s going to take a lot of growth to make them better than that. Bad luck and unimaginative planning got the Falcons to their current state at quarterback—you never sign a third quarterback expecting he’ll have to start the first two games of the season, but Penix and Tua were your top two options—but the rest can be hung on game plan and execution. The Falcons can’t (and won’t even try) to attack defenses deep, do not have a good plan for getting the ball to playmakers with those limitations, and are not getting the blocking to just run teams over. I would say the plan to keep Bryce Young in check was a good one—he was pressured at a very high rate, for example—but he repeatedly found open options because the secondary slipped up. And so on. This does not look like a team that has easy answers to adversity, to say the least. What can the Falcons do? Keep going, obviously, because there’s no choice but to do so. But they also need to figure out quickly how to put together a coherent offense that can get them more than 16 points in two games, no matter who ends up being under center in a given week, and how to clamp down on the miscues that have led to defensive and special teams woes that cost them further. The team that just lost by 30-plus points to the Panthers for the second time in two seasons does not look any better under a new regime than it looked under the old one, and while I’ll grant you it takes time and the team’s true goal for contention seems very likely to be 2027, they did want to be fun and competent this year lest they completely lose a fanbase early on that has endured way too many losing seasons. I don’t know what it will look like if the Falcons figure things out starting on Thursday Night Football against the Packers, but I do know that it won’t look anything like this. What I do know is that 0-3 with Atlanta’s schedule and Carolina and New Orleans actually looking like competent football teams probably will mean the lights are out on the 2026 season. On to the full recap. The Good Bijan Robinson looked awfully glum on the sidelines at the end of the game, and it’s difficult to blame him. He’s the player Atlanta counts on to make this thing go, and right now that job is too big for any one man to do. Still, Bijan averaged 4.5 yards on 16 carries and rushed for over 70 yards, doing his part despite being stymied regularly early for minimal gains thanks to subpar blocking. Brian Robinson Jr. is proving to be a nice second fiddle for Bijan, too. He looked decisive and powerful as a runner in this one, putting up 51 yards on 11 carries and doing his best work late when the game was out of hand. Atlanta’s likely to try to keep Bijan fresh when things go awry like this, but I’d trust Brian Robinson in short yardage and goal line situations…if the Falcons ever get into them. Drake London is relentless. Rush missed him badly at least once in the first half, but every catch he got was either a first down or a first down and a major gain. He easily finished as the team’s leading receiver with 51 yards on four grabs, but looked incredibly frustrated on the sideline at the end of the game (again, with justification) and simply isn’t getting enough from his quarterbacks to put up the monster lines he did last year. He needs Penix back in action. Za’Darius Smith is a playmaker. He split a sack in this one with Cameron Thomas—who also had a nice game, I should note—and also hit Bryce Young’s arm on a key third down to force an incompletion. Through two games, he’s been an impactful signing, something I expect to continue. Samson Ebukam and Gervon Dexter came up with a terrific second quarter sack of Bryce Young to decisively end a drive. On second and long, Young went backwards in an attempt to escape but Ebukam got his arm around him and he and Dexter drilled the quarterback to the ground to make it 3rd and 21. Carolina would try a short run and then punt. On a shakier day for the secondary, I thought Xavier Watts mostly played quite well. He forced a fumble, led the team in tackles, and more than once basically crossed the entire field to make a stop. It’s been a quiet start for Watts and Jessie Bates, who are expected to turn up some turnovers for Atlanta, but Watts is still having an impact. I wouldn’t say Jack Strand was good , but after the Falcons pulled some starters alongside Cooper Rush and he threw an unfortunate pick six that was tipped into the air, he looked more competent than I would’ve expected given that he was being thrust into game action in an impossible situation. He threw multiple balls too hard but did deliver some nice quick passes along the way, and as a runner he was very effective, picking up multiple first downs. I don’t want to see him again this season because it would imply we are firmly in football hell and because he’s not remotely ready to play extended action against good football teams, but there’s very obviously a backup quarterback worth developing here. The game did end! At varying points I was afraid it would not. The Ugly Cooper Rush went for it on the very first offensive play of the game, scrambling away on play action for nine yards…but then put the ball on the ground at the end of the play and gave it right to Carolina. Rush had no need to dive for the first down, especially since he was short of the marker, and it was just another ill-advised decision from a quarterback who is very clearly over his head. He followed that up by hesitating for way too long on third down on the next drive, throwing it late and seeing the ball tipped and then picked off. The icing on the cake was an…

title: Week 2 Snap Reactions: Falcons continue to flail
summary: The Atlanta Falcons lost in embarrassing fashion. The Carolina Panthers have now won four straight against the dirty birds, making Bryce Young a minority owner. Here are the Week 2 snap reactions: Tommy Rees’ questionable play-calling continues  A Drake London end around on 4th and 1? The Falcons have $100M tied up in the interior, […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Jack Strand #18 of the Atlanta Falcons runs the ball for a first down against the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Butch Dill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons lost in embarrassing fashion. The Carolina Panthers have now won four straight against the dirty birds, making Bryce Young a minority owner. Here are the Week 2 snap reactions: Tommy Rees’ questionable play-calling continues A Drake London end around on 4th and 1? The Falcons have $100M tied up in the interior, but you’d never know it from calls like that. Cooper Rush isn’t making it easy, but neither is the young coordinator Stefanski brought with him. Things didn’t get much better when Strand came in. Most route concepts were static and all within 5 yards. I understand wanting to build confidence, but you can’t neglect areas of the field and make things easier for the defense to cover. Rees is still struggling to get multiple skill players involved. For some reason, Zachariah Branch has been locked in a cage. It’s only been two games, but the Falcons offensive scheme looks worse than the product Zac Robinson put on the field. The Atlanta Falcons are on pace to have the SECOND WORST offensive start to the season since 2022. pic.twitter.com/bReVVEAbtU — Sam Bruchhaus (@sambruchhaus) September 20, 2026 Not so special teams Aukerman and Blackburn aren’t beating the allegations. They had some of the worst units in 2025, and their new operation looks sloppy out of the gate. This unit needed to be competent and not put the team in unfavorable field position, but they can’t get out of their own way. To make matters worse, Nick Folk looks washed. He hasn’t missed three field goals in a season since 2022 but has hit that mark in just 2 games. This side of the ball isn’t dealing with injuries or other major issues; they have everything they need, but the product is still not up to par. Special teams continues to be a thorn in the Falcons wings. Defense is being stretched thin Ulbrich’s defense started strong, but offensive turnovers kept putting them against the wall. To make matters worse, AJ Terrell left early in the 1st quarter and didn’t return. Without complementary play from offense or special teams, it doesn’t matter how good the defense starts. They were gashed on the final drive of the first half, and that carried over to the first drive of the second half. While the other sides of the ball haven’t done their job, this secondary was lauded as the team’s strength, especially the safety duo of Jessie Bates III and Xaiver Watts, but they haven’t looked like it. Hopefully Terrell is ready for Green Bay, because his absence became increasingly noticeable as the game progressed. Darren Waller with his SECOND TD of the game 😤 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/7l0FAG8guo — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) September 20, 2026 Jack Strand (not his fault) Strand threaded the needle on his first pass with a laser to Dotson, who couldn’t hold on to the ball, leading to a pick-six. You can’t make this stuff up. He ended his day with an untouched fumble while trying to throw the ball. All that being said, this offense still would’ve been more viable with him from the start than Cooper Rush. He offered more with his legs and arm than the veteran, and you can live with turnovers from your UDFA rookie. In a perfect world, Strand would’ve been allowed to sit as long as possible, but we don’t live in that world. With a quick turnaround heading into Thursday Night Football, it’s possible Strand could be seen again if Penix and Tua remain unavailable. This is a miserable product. I haven’t heard boos this loud through the broadcast in a long time, but don’t worry, your Falcons play in 4 days. Surely that’s enough time to fix this mess.

title: Falcons – Panthers Week 2 instant recap: Brutalized in the Benz
summary: We came into this game knowing it had the potential to be ugly. Bryce Young usually kills the Falcons, Cooper Rush was starting at quarterback, and that alone seemed like it could go awry. It did go awry, and it did get ugly. Rush fumbled on the first play of the game. Rush threw an […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers passes the ball against the Atlanta Falcons during the first quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Butch Dill/Getty Images) | Getty Images We came into this game knowing it had the potential to be ugly. Bryce Young usually kills the Falcons, Cooper Rush was starting at quarterback, and that alone seemed like it could go awry. It did go awry, and it did get ugly. Rush fumbled on the first play of the game. Rush threw an interception. He threw another interception. Jack Strand got in the game and saw his first NFL pass tipped into the air, intercepted, and returned for a touchdown. Strand later fumbled it to end the game by having the ball slip out of his hand for a Carolina recovery. The Falcons allowed Xavier Legette to get wide open on a 55 yard strike downfield and let Darren Waller casually make a couple of nice touchdown grabs. Bryce Young made very few mistakes and killed Atlanta through the air, as he does. And special teams miscues, penalties, and a lack of high-end blocking for Bijan Robinson essentially sealed this one. Early in the third quarter, Atlanta was down 27-3, and even if the Falcons get their starting quarterback(s) back, it’s difficult to imagine them climbing out of an 0-2 hole and finding something that works well enough to keep this from being yet another lost season. It’s way too early to say that, but even the dejected faces of the Falcons on the sideline told you it’s going to take time to repair the damage done by this caliber of miserable effort. Here’s a drive-by-drive recap of the game you just watched. I’m sorry you had to. 1st Quarter The opening kickoff went into the end zone, bringing Cooper Rush and company on the field. Rush rolled out on play action and ran the football, nearly picking up a first down, but the ball came out at the end of the play and it was ruled a fumble after review. Carolina ball. Bryce Young hit the running back with a quick swing pass under pressure for eight yards. Carolina then got a first down before a false start backed them up a bit. A checkdown to Jalen Coker went for a couple of yards. The second down pass was tipped by Kendal Daniels, but the pass was slapped down by Carolina. A roughing the passer call on Gervon Dexter Sr. at the same time as Tet McMillan got wide open downfield put Carolina around the two yard line. The first down slant to McMillan was slapped away, but A.J. Terrell was down on the play. The Panthers were then called for another false start. Chuba Hubbard then took the toss up the middle for about four yards. Young tried to run away from pressure and threw it incomplete with pressure coming and good coverage by C.J. Henderson. On fourth down, though, Hubbard got free and scored a touchdown on a quick pass from Young. 7-0 Panthers. Olamide Zaccheaus took it back to about the 30. In play action, Rush was able to get the ball off with a man rushing free in his face and found Drake London, who got a first down with a nice move near the marker. Bijan Robinson then took it for three yards. Bijan on the right side stretch run got nowhere as any breathing room collapsed. Rush then hesitated in the pocket and threw an interception on third down on a tipped ball. Carolina had another false start. Young then threw it too high for McMillan. Young then missed a tightly covered McMillan again. On third down, pressure got to Young and had his arm hit and the ball fell to the turf. Fair catch on the punt. A yard or two on first down for Bijan. Robinson tried to make a cut and got three yards. On third down, Rush tried Kyle Pitts, but he couldn’t reel it in with a defender’s hand in there. The return from Jalen Coker got almost to the Atlanta 30, and a five yard penalty was added on for Atlanta. A quick hitter to Xavier Legette got nine yards. Young had to dirt the second down pass with Cameron Thomas nearly getting to him. A quick handoff to Hubbard went for a first down. On first down, Jonathon Brooks got two yards before the Falcons made the stop. CJ Henderson got to Coker immediately on a swing pass for a minimal gain. Young with pressure closing in launched it to the end zone but didn’t get it, with Henderson once again close by. They hit the field goal try to make it 10-0 Carolina. Zachariah Branch took it a short distance. A quick slant to London went for 13 yards and a first down. Brian Robinson Jr. then took it nine yards. Robinson followed that up with about seven yards and a first down. A quick screen to Zachariah Branch didn’t get great blocking and he got about three yards. Bijan then fought through contact and burst through the pile for four yards, but was stymied on the next carry for a one yard gain. They tried a reverse on fourth down to London and he was tackled well short of the marker. Carolina ball. Young hit McMillan for eight yards over the middle on first down. 2nd Quarter A penalty brought back the first down run, and then Bryce Young was brought down by Samson Ebukam and Gervon Dexter. They handed it off to Hubbard to set up a more manageable punt. Bijan took it a couple of yards, and then Rush hit Jahan Dotson for a slant and first down. Bijan then plunged ahead for three yards. A swing pass to Robinson went for another few yards. Rush then tried to scramble away from pressure and was taken down. Punt, and Coker took it back for a short return. A five yard plunge up the middle for Carolina to kick things off, and then Young missed his target downfield. On third down, Young had time and hit McMillan, with Mike Hughes tackling him after the first down grab. Then Young got McMillan again for about 20 yards. Then he aired it out to Coker for another 20 plus yards to put Carolina inside the 10. A quick pass went for a couple of yards before Xavier Watts got the stop. Hubbard then got a yard or so before Hughes got to him. Young then rolled way out and looked for McMillan, but couldn’t get him with Avieon Terrell in coverage. The field goal try made it 13-0 Carolina. Zaccheaus nearly had a very nice return but got tripped up by the last man who had a chance of getting him, and a holding call would’ve brought it back regardless (and backed them up anyways). Rush finally took a shot over the middle and got Drake London for a big gain, but a facemask on the offense brought it back. Bijan then took it about eight yards. On second down, Rush tried for Zaccheaus, but it was a little high and he couldn’t get it. Rush then rushed for 10 yards on a diving effort, getting Atlanta the first down, but then Kyle Pitts was hit with a false start. Rush then hit Pitts on the sideline for a first down. Bijan then got a seam and made it nearly nine yards. Rush then tried London but threw it too far inside. Rush found London on the next play, though, with a short slant turning into a major gain over the middle as London outran multiple defenders. Bijan then gained two yards on the ground, but followed that up with ten yards as he got quality blocking. Rush under pressure was able to hit Bijan but it wasn’t close, so Robinson was lucky to pick up two yards on the play. He went right back to Bijan for five yards. On third down, Rush missed badly over the middle and nearly had it picked off. Nick Folk hit the 41 yard attempt, though, to make it 13-3 Carolina. John Metchie made it to the 28 yard line with 1:02 on the clock. A quick pass over the middle to Darren Waller got a first down, and an illegal use of hands call on the Falcons was declined. On the next play, several Falcons converged on Young for a sack, but Xavier Legette got wide ass open downfield and Young aired it out for a huge gain. Young threw it away with pressure on the way on first down. A crosser to Coker went for five yards before he was tackled. Young then hit Waller for a touchdown to make it 20-3 Panthers. Zachariah Branch had a solid return, but the Falcons had no time on the…

title: Intriguing players to watch in Falcons vs. Panthers
summary: After a disappointing Week 1 loss, the Atlanta Falcons return home to clash against NFC South rival Carolina Panthers. The winner will get an early lead in the division, and it sets up perfectly for the Falcons to have a “get-right” game. Most of the intrigue in this matchup comes from getting back on track, […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - AUGUST 14: Atlanta wide receiver Drake London (5) warms up prior to the start of the NFL pre-season game between the Denver Broncos and the Atlanta Falcons on August 14th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After a disappointing Week 1 loss, the Atlanta Falcons return home to clash against NFC South rival Carolina Panthers . The winner will get an early lead in the division, and it sets up perfectly for the Falcons to have a “get-right” game. Most of the intrigue in this matchup comes from getting back on track, as several established Falcons stars look to rebound and several newcomers look to impress in front of the home crowd. We’re naming five Falcons to watch this Sunday. Drake London The Falcons need more from Drake London, who was targeted only four times in the team’s debut. His workload should be at least double that, given that he’s now among the NFL’s highest-paid wideouts . Fortunately, London historically shines against the Panthers. He has 38 catches, 435 yards, and 3 touchdowns in his last four outings against Carolina. If the Falcons can’t get him going against this Panthers secondary that he usually shines against, it may raise questions about whether this investment will pay off. Jake Matthews Another player who is due for a bounce-back game after a disappointing Week 1 performance is left tackle Jake Matthews, who earned the lowest PFF grade since his rookie season in 2014. Matthews gave up two sacks and drew a holding call, raising questions about whether the 34-year-old has lost a step. However, Matthews has usually played well against the Panthers lately, earning PFF grades of 69 or higher in his last five matchups. Za’Darius Smith Edge rusher Za’Darius Smith did not disappoint in his 2026 debut, tallying two sacks. Both takedowns came when Smith rushed from the left side of the defense against the opposing team’s right tackle. If he keeps getting similar opportunities this week against Carolina, he’ll be squaring off against rookie right tackle Monroe Freeling. This is a golden opportunity for Smith to baptize Freeling and give him a not-so-warm welcome to the NFL. Avieon Terrell No one benefits more from Smith’s steady pressure than rookie cornerback Avieion Terrell. He’ll be facing a tough test in Week 2, going up against Panthers wideouts Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan. Coker is Carolina’s primary slot option and is coming off an impressive two-touchdown performance in Week 1. However, McMillan has done plenty of damage specifically against the Falcons when operating from the slot. According to PFF , McMillan averaged 4.9 yards per route run from the slot against the Falcons, while averaging just 1.4 yards per route run against all other opportunities last season. Terrell has his work cut out for him against this double whammy. But if he can slow down both Coker and McMillan, it’ll do wonders for his confidence and the team’s hopes that he will grow into the transformative presence in the nickel they envisioned. Nick Folk Falcons kicker Nick Folk hasn’t missed a kick indoors since 2015, and that streak needs to continue as he makes his debut in Mercedes-Benz Stadium after a disappointing Week 1, when he missed two field goals. Folk has been the NFL’s most accurate kicker for the last few seasons and was signed to solidify a troublesome Falcons kicking spot. If he has more uncharacteristic misses this week, it’ll look like the Falcons’ kicking troubles are here to stay. If these five players’ performance matches the level of intrigue, the Falcons will be in prime position to claim an early lead in the NFC South. Can you name any more Falcons who intrigue you in this matchup?

title: Falcons vs. Panthers: What will Week 2’s win or loss mean for Atlanta?
summary: For the eighth time in the last nine seasons, the Falcons have stumbled out of the starting gate with a defeat in their opening game of the season. It was a rock fight between Atlanta and Pittsburgh, and one where an inept Cooper Rush-led offense was too much for the defense to overcome. Now, the […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - NOVEMBER 16: The Carolina Panthers snap the football during overtime in the Sunday afternoon NFL game between the Atlanta Falcons and the Carolina Panthers on November 16, 2025 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by David J. Griffin/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For the eighth time in the last nine seasons, the Falcons have stumbled out of the starting gate with a defeat in their opening game of the season. It was a rock fight between Atlanta and Pittsburgh, and one where an inept Cooper Rush-led offense was too much for the defense to overcome. Now, the Birds welcome the division rival Carolina Panthers to town for their home opener, in a midst of a tumultuous week at Flowery Branch where (as of this writing) we still have no idea who the starting quarterback will even be. It’s only September, but it feels like things could start heading south fast if the Falcons don’t take control of this ship’s steering wheel. Here is the scenario the Falcons face if they beat the Carolina Panthers in Week 2, as well as if they lose. If the Falcons win A lot of the noise around Flowery Branch will begin to calm for the time being, as the team has been routinely making national headlines due to the quarterback uncertainty. It’s feasible that the uncertainty remains even after this game, but winning games is the cure for many issues. They will also mark an end to a three game losing streak the Falcons currently have in games against the Panthers. They have also lost four of the last five matchups. Carolina has owned this game over the last couple of years and Kevin Stefanski’s first real impact would be stopping that bleeding. The difficult part of the schedule in October and onward still looms, and the Falcons will be doing themselves a great service with a victory, ahead of their Thursday Night Football game in Green Bay next week. They likely need to be able to scrounge two wins by the end of the first quarter of the season and this would get them halfway there, while also giving them a big division win early on. We’re still in the “way too early” part of the season when the division standings are in question, but Atlanta would come out of Sunday in first place in the NFC South due to their superior division record, even if Tampa and New Orleans both win to match their 1-1 overall record. If the Falcons lose Things could start going sideways really quickly. That difficult part of the schedule I referenced begins in Week 5, and the team really can’t afford to be sitting at anything worse than 2-2 going into that stretch. Starting in an 0-2 hole puts immense pressure on them to win primetime road games at Green Bay and New Orleans over the next two weeks, and I could argue that this game against Carolina will be their easiest until Week 14 in Cleveland. Stefanski will follow in the footsteps of Arthur Smith in 2021 as a new Falcons head coach to endure losses in his first two games. He’s on a five year contract and this is a very long term project with 2026 maybe not being a win now year, but that won’t relieve the angst from a fanbase which is creeping closer and closer to a full decade without seeing any success. For the first time in their respective histories in this matchup, the Panthers will have beaten the Falcons on four consecutive occasions. It will also be just the second time in which they won this specific game five times over the course of six tries. the first coming between 2012 and 2015, in the middle of Cam Newton’s prime.

title: Falcons’ Michael Penix could be starting QB vs. Packers on TNF Week 3
summary: When will Michael Penix be ready to start? That’s the question that’s been on everyone’s minds since at least Day 1 of this year’s training camp. According to reports from national insiders, that day may be coming up very soon. According to Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport, Penix is ‘nearing a return’ and could take […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Atlanta, Falcons, USA; Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. (9) talks to the media during the first day of training camp at IBM Performance Field. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect When will Michael Penix be ready to start? That’s the question that’s been on everyone’s minds since at least Day 1 of this year’s training camp. According to reports from national insiders, that day may be coming up very soon. According to Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport, Penix is ‘nearing a return’ and could take over as Atlanta’s starting quarterback as early as this Thursday night against the Packers in Lambeau. Michael Penix Jr., the Falcons' preferred starter, is nearing a return and could make his 2026 debut on Thursday night against the Green Bay Packers, per @RapSheet and me. https://t.co/n0COusIxf4 — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) September 20, 2026 What’s that mean for the future of Tua Tagovailoa? For now, he’ll stay on the roster, according to Rapoport. The #Falcons have no plans to release Tua Tagovailoa, sources say. From the story: https://t.co/VYkE0aZ89n pic.twitter.com/hRJEtvziP7 — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 20, 2026 I didn’t think Penix was genuinely an option for this week, regardless of what Stefanski said Wednesday about all quarterbacks being on the table to start this week. I don’t see a world where Penix starts on a Sunday and takes his first full-speed contact just four days before the next game. It’s just not smart. Starting in Week 3 and having a week and a half to rest up and prepare for the Saints in Week 4 on Monday Night Football is the smart play if Penix really is ready to go. People may be surprised by the reporting around Tua and the team’s plans to retain him for now, at least. The quarterback room has pretty good vibes with its current construction (even though it’s still wild to me that they’re carrying four quarterbacks on the active roster), and with both Penix and Tua’s injury histories, having enough backup is a must. I’ll feel sorry about it after he got trotted out there against the Steelers last week with a bad back, but if the Falcons get to a point where they feel comfortable with Penix’s health and availability I could see them moving on from Cooper Rush. The team seems high on Jack Strand’s potential, which … same. I don’t think they can stash him on the practice squad and realistically expect to keep him. This quarterback saga has been quite the ride, and I’m ready for this ride to be over. Here’s hoping Penix is able to take over as the starter for Week 3 and that he stays healthy through the season.

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 2: Low usage for rookie pass-catchers and Chidobe Awuzie
summary: The Baltimore Ravens dropped to 1-1 after losing at home to the New Orleans Saints in Week 2. Here is a breakdown of the team’s player snap counts on offense and defense from the 24-17 defeat. Offense Jackson was protected by his starting offensive line for the entire game with the exception of Ronnie Stanley, […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Juwan Johnson #83 of the New Orleans Saints runs after catch against Malaki Starks #24 of the Baltimore Ravens in the fourth quarter of a game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens dropped to 1-1 after losing at home to the New Orleans Saints in Week 2. Here is a breakdown of the team’s player snap counts on offense and defense from the 24-17 defeat. Offense QB: Lamar Jackson 58 RB: Derrick Henry 31, Justice Hill 27 WR: Rashod Bateman 54, Chris Moore 32, LaJohntay Wester 31, Devontez Walker 17 TE: Mark Andrews 41, Durham Smythe 32, Matthew Hibner 19, Josh Cuevas 5 OL: Ronnie Stanley 46, John Simpson 58, Jovaughn Gwyn 58, Vega Ioane 58, Roger Rosengarten 58, Carson Vinson 13 Jackson was protected by his starting offensive line for the entire game with the exception of Ronnie Stanley, who was replaced by Carson Vinson for the last 13 snaps. Stanley’s toe injury forced him to exit the game early and he was the only injury casualty for the offense. Derrick Henry was nearly matched in snaps by Justice Hill and played 53% of the share. Henry notably only received five carries in the second half with the Ravens trying to protect a lead. He had 87 scrimmage yards and a touchdown. Rasheen Ali has not been a factor in the running back rotation to begin the season. At wide receiver, Chris Moore (32 snaps) and LaJohntay Wester (31 snaps) saw elevated playing time with Zay Flowers absent. Devontez Walker returned from injury and only received 17 snaps despite making a long 47-yard reception in the first half. Rookie Elijah Sarratt was activated to play but did not receive any offensive snaps. Rashod Bateman played all but four snaps and had a team-high seven catches for 88 yards with a touchdown. Like Sarratt, fellow rookies Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas played limited roles on offense. Hibner’s 19 snaps were slightly down from last week and neither saw a target in the passing game. Mark Andrews dominated the snap share (71%) at the position and caught six passes for 49 yards. Durham Smythe played over 50% of snaps as a blocking piece. Defense DL: Calais Campbell 40, Travis Jones 38, Broderick Washington 27, John Jenkins 21, Aeneas Peebles 8 EDGE: Tavius Robinson 53, Trey Hendrickson 36, Mike Green 32, Zion Young 23 ILB: Roquan Smith 68, Trenton Simpson 42, CB: Nate Wiggins 67, Marlon Humphrey 67, Chandler Rivers 24, Keyon Martin 1, Chidobe Awuzie 1 S: Malaki Starks 68, Kyle Hamilton 67, Jaylinn Hawkins 64, Keondre Jackson 1 Veteran Calais Campbell led all defensive lineman in snaps with 40, closely followed by Travis Jones (38). The Ravens distributed defensive reps to all five players in the rotation again, with Aeneas Peebles bringing up the rear with eight snaps. Broderick Washington and John Jenkins ate up a combined 48 snaps. On the edge, Tavius Robinson’s 53 snaps were by far the highest of the group. Trey Hendrickson played 53% of defensive plays while nursing a broken finger injury, but still managed to record a sack — as did Robinson. Mike Green saw a huge jump in playing time from last week (32 snaps) and made an impact with a team-high two quarterback hits, two tackles for loss and a sack. Zion Young saw a slight uptick in playing time (23 snaps). Roquan Smith did not leave the field. Next to him, Trenton Simpson’s 62% snap share saw him make a couple notable plays including a big tackle for loss. It will be interesting to see how Simpson’s playing time changes when Teddye Buchanan makes his return from injury soon. Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey each played all but one play at cornerback. Rookie nickel Chandler Rivers jumped Keyon Martin in the pecking order in this game, playing 24 snaps with a tackle for loss. Surprisingly, veteran Chidobe Awuzie was once again iced out of the defensive game plan and saw just one snap. The Ravens seem to be opting for three-safety looks and giving their young slot corners reps over Awuzie. Malaki Starks played the entire game and Kyle Hamilton left the field for one play. Jaylinn Hawkins had another near every-down role with 64 snaps. The Ravens struggled with missed tackles on defense in this game, particularly over the middle of the field.
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens vs. Saints: 4 winners and plenty of losers
summary: The Baltimore Ravens fell back to earth this week with a humbling loss to the New Orleans Saints. There was plenty of blame to go around in this one, with a few bright spots mixed in. Winners Rashod Bateman: The Ravens needed their former first-rounder to step up in Zay Flowers’ absence this week, and […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Rashod Bateman #7 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the New Orleans Saints during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens fell back to earth this week with a humbling loss to the New Orleans Saints. There was plenty of blame to go around in this one, with a few bright spots mixed in. Winners Rashod Bateman: The Ravens needed their former first-rounder to step up in Zay Flowers’ absence this week, and Bateman answered the call with 88 receiving yards and a touchdown on seven catches. Bateman was the intended target on Lamar Jackson’s game-sealing interception, leading to questions about whether he ran the correct route, but both players were quick to shut such speculation down after the game. Trenton Simpson: Simpson’s contract season is off to a strong start through two games. The athletic linebacker was everywhere against the Saints, making six tackles and one tackle for loss. Simpson helped end several plays close to the line of scrimmage throughout the game. Mark Andrews: Andrews started the game on the wrong foot with a drop on third down, leading to a three-and-out on the offense’s first series. The veteran tight end rebounded afterwards, though, moving the chains on multiple plays and helping to spring several runs with key blocks. Andrews finished the day with 49 yards on six catches. While he may not be the explosive threat he once was, Jackson’s career go-to target can still be a reliable option through the air. Devontez Walker: Walker had just one catch on the day, but it was a big one. Backed up in their own end zone, Jackson connected with Walker on a 47-yard bomb. Walker has done nothing but make big plays when called upon so far in his career. Losers Secondary: Just about every member of the secondary shares some blame, from allowing Chris Olave to convert multiple key first downs to missing crucial tackles throughout the game. Safeties Malaki Starks and Jaylinn Hawkins seemed to be the worst offenders, with both missing tackles that led to extended drives for New Orleans. Starks appeared to be responsible for Olave’s touchdown catch as well. Special teams: The Ravens’ special teams had multiple gaffes on the day, the first being a blocked field goal that would have given Baltimore a 10-0 lead in the second quarter. Perhaps the bigger blunder, though, was allowing a 53-yard kick return before the end of the first half that allowed the Saints to cut the lead to eight with a field goal. Coaching staff: The honeymoon period for the Ravens’ new coaching staff is officially over. Sunday’s loss featured multiple questionable decisions on both sides of the ball. Possibly the biggest head-scratcher of the day was opting for a deep shot to wide receiver Chris Moore on third-and-one instead of handing the ball to Derrick Henry. The incomplete pass led to a three-and-out while the game was tied in the fourth quarter. Jesse Minter also had a questionable challenge on an Olave catch on the previous drive, which led to the Ravens only having two timeouts with just over a minute left on their final drive of the game. Chris Moore: Moore was the surprising hero of Week 1, but things did not go as well this week for the veteran receiver. Moore was the intended target on the aforementioned third-and-one deep ball, failing to haul the pass in. Moore was also flagged for holding earlier in the game, which negated a signature Jackson scramble for a first down. Moore nearly fumbled on a kickoff return as well, but he was ruled down on replay.
author: Dustin Cox

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 2: Coming up short across the board in upset loss
summary: The Baltimore Ravens suffered an upset defeat in Week 2, falling to the New Orleans Saints at home by a score of 24-17. The Ravens led for most of the game before being outscored 15-0 in the fourth quarter and squandering an eight-point lead. It was a disappointing follow up to a resounding victory in […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens scores a touchdown against the New Orleans Saints during the first quarter of the game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens suffered an upset defeat in Week 2, falling to the New Orleans Saints at home by a score of 24-17. The Ravens led for most of the game before being outscored 15-0 in the fourth quarter and squandering an eight-point lead. It was a disappointing follow up to a resounding victory in the regular season opener. Here are report card grades for each position group from the losing effort. Quarterback: C+ Lamar Jackson was mostly sharp throwing the ball in this game. He wound up connecting on 67% of his 31 pass attempts for 235 yards through the air with a touchdown, while adding 34 running yards on four rushes. The game-sealing interception to end the game leaves a sour taste, however. Whether it was simply a bad throw or a case of route miscommunication with Rashod Bateman is unclear — either way it erased the chance of a vintage game-winning drive or game-tying drive. Jackson played a fine game within structure, but the Ravens could have used more off-script magic from him without Zay Flowers on the field. Running Back: B Derrick Henry’s longest run of the game went for only eight yards. He averaged 4.3 yards per rush with a touchdown and 87 scrimmage yards. The Ravens puzzlingly only gave Henry five carries in the second half when they were leading by more than a touchdown. He likely would have been able to grind out some much-needed first downs to help sustain drives. Justice Hill turned four touches into 18 total yards behind him. Wide Receiver: B In the first game without Flowers or Ja’Kobi Lane, Bateman stepped up with a team-high seven catches on nine targets for 88 yards — the most of any player on both teams — and a touchdown catch. Bateman unfortunately was the target on Jackson’s intercepted pass to end the game. Devontez Walker had a highlight reel 47-yard catch early in the game in his season debut but was targeted only one either time. Walker’s involvement likely should have been greater. LaJohntay Wester and Chris Moore each had one catch. Rookie Elijah Sarratt was not involved in the game plan and was out-snapped by both Moore and Wester. Tight End: C+ Mark Andrews had an effective pass-catching game with six catches, second-most on the team. Andrews recorded 49 receiving yards for the second straight game and had multiple first down conversions over the middle. Rookies Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas were not targeted at all. Some anticipated more tight end usage given the wide receiver deficit from injuries, but that was not the case. Durham Smythe was targeted one time but did not have a catch. The tight ends collectively did not seem to make a huge impact in the run game, as Henry was not able to hit any significant running lanes on the outside. Offensive Line: D+ It was another uneven performance from the Ravens’ offensive line. Their pass protection was shaky for the second straight week, and this time the run blocking was not as dominant to compensate. Jackson was sacked three times and the Ravens surrendered six quarterback hits as well. The Saints were able to generate pressure to make key plays in the second half. Ronnie Stanley was replaced by Carson Vinson after he aggravated a toe injury and the interior of the offensive line was suspect. Jovaughn Gwyn and Vega Ioane each allowed multiple pressures and John Simpson had a notable missed block as well. Defensive Line: C The front seven did a good job against the run, limiting the Saints to only 65 rushing yards on 27 carries. Alvin Kamara and Travis Etienne Jr. were held in check. They were not able to create much interior pressure against Shough in the pocket. Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, Broderick Washington and company were quiet in the box score. Jones did have one pass breakup, but there were not any notable plays in terms of pass rush. Edge Rusher: B The Ravens were able to get pressure against Tyler Shough but allowed him to evade sacks a few times. Trey Hendrickson had his first sack as a Raven to accompany a tackle for loss. Mike Green had a big performance with a team-high two tackles for loss and two quarterback hits, along with a sack as well. Tavius Robinson had another sack for the second straight game. It wasn’t the best showing for rookie Zion Young, who missed a couple notable tackles. The Ravens’ edge rushers did a good job containing outside runs and limiting any explosive rushing plays. Linebacker: C + Roquan Smith had eight total tackles but the impact plays he made last week were not there to the same degree. Trenton Simpson had a tackle for loss and a huge stop on the Saints’ two-point conversion attempt, which would have been a game-altering moment if not for a holding penalty that negated the play. The Ravens’ linebackers similarly deserve credit for the defense’s effectiveness against the run, but also share blame for missed tackles over the middle of the field. Saints’ tight end Juwan Johnson had 66 receiving yards. Cornerback: C + The Ravens had some difficulties covering Chris Olave, who made big catches and conversions in one-on-one situations. Olave finished with eight receptions for 86 yards and a late fourth-quarter score. Marlon Humphrey was beaten a couple times in lone coverage. Devaughn Vele, the Saints’ No. 2 wideout, also had a couple notable catches and finished with 64 receiving yards and a long catch of 29 yards. Humphrey had one pass breakup and Nate Wiggins finished with six tackles and was solid in coverage again. Rookie Chandler Rivers had a huge tackle for loss attacking a screen pass from the nickel spot. Safety: D+ Kyle Hamilton easily led the defense in tackles with 13 (seven solo tackles), one of which was a tackle for loss. It was not the most memorable performance for Malaki Starks and Jaylinn Hawkins, who appeared to miss multiple timely tackles in open space. Hawkins was called for a holding penalty on the Saints’ unsuccessful two-point conversion attempt, which they then converted on the re-try to knot the game up at 17-17. The Ravens need Starks to make more impact plays on the ball consistently. Special Teams: D + This was a forgettable game for the Ravens’ special teams unit and a disappointing follow up to a great outing in Week 1. Tyler Loop’s first 49-yard field goal attempt was partially blocked, forcing a miss that would have given the Ravens a 10-point lead in the second quarter. Just before halftime, their kick return coverage unit gave up a huge return that put the Saints in position to add another field goal, which made it a one-possession game.
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens Roundtable: reacting to Baltimore’s Week 2 loss to the Saints
summary: The Baltimore Ravens dropped their home opener to the New Orleans Saints in dramatic fashion, giving up a late goal-line touchdown followed by a Lamar Jackson interception to seal the loss. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s reactions to the game: This felt like a trap game all week, and boy, did it deliver. Quarterback Tyler Shough […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough (6) attempts a quarterback sneak in the fourth quarter against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: James Lang-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens dropped their home opener to the New Orleans Saints in dramatic fashion, giving up a late goal-line touchdown followed by a Lamar Jackson interception to seal the loss. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s reactions to the game: This felt like a trap game all week, and boy, did it deliver. Quarterback Tyler Shough had a lights-out game under pressure, and a number of calls went against the Ravens throughout the game. Baltimore established a foothold early in the game, but sputtered into the half with the ground starting to give way beneath their feed. After halftime, the offense was held to just three points, and the defense could not get off the field on third down. New Orleans churned yards on the ground and in the underneath game, and Baltimore’s offense simply had no answer. This is a tough, tough loss for Jesse Minter’s squad in their home opener after emphasizing the need to re-establish dominance at M&T Bank Stadium. Unfortunately, it felt like a time-travel trip back to disappointing early-season losses of past Ravens teams. – Nikhil Mehta It’s an embarrassing loss. There’s simply no excuse. The referee show was awful but there are problems beyond that. The defense was far too soft for most of the day and let Tyler Shough and the receivers bully them. Lamar Jackson and the offense weren’t good enough, even if they were missing Zay Flowers. The run game wasn’t utilized nearly enough against a team that couldn’t stop the run at all last week. Falling short of 20 carries when you are missing your top wide receiver is criminal. Special teams is the real deciding factor here. The blocked field goal and the massive return that allowed the Saints to score three before halftime are the real difference in score. It’s a bad coaching loss in my opinion and you have to hope it’s only a speed bump for a new coaching staff that they take responsibility for. – Zach Canter Not much to say here but unfortunately, these first two weeks of the year have looked very similar to the old regime: dominant win followed up by home stinker vs an inferior opponent. The Ravens led the Saints 14-3 at one point, but let the Saints slowly climb back into it and took the Ravens down in their home opener. This felt a lot like their week two loss at home vs the Raiders in 2024 where the Ravens also led in that game but just couldn’t seal the deal against an inferior team. The Ravens defense looked good out of the gates but simply couldn’t get off the field on 3rd down. The pressure was good, but Tyler Shough was able to push all the right buttons down the stretch. As is usually the case, there are multiple things to point to – penalties, controversial calls, and a poor challenge. If there is a silver lining, the Ravens were missing Zay Flowers, Nmandi Madubuike, and others but this still feels like a game they should have won. – Stephen Bopst The euphoric high of the new coaching staff lasted just one game for the Ravens as the team squandered yet another fourth-quarter lead against a team they had no business losing to. Baltimore’s offense went stagnant in the second half while the defense failed to get to Tyler Shough and contain Chris Olave in the passing game. There is plenty of blame to go around in this loss, from poor special teams play, third-down defense, penalties, and a failure to get anything going offensively in the second half. The season is long and losses like these are bound to happen, even to the best teams, but this is still a disappointment for a team looking to exorcise demons from failing to close these types of games in years past. Getting Zay Flowers back will be a massive boost to the offense and Nnamdi Madubuike will hopefully do the same for the defense. – Dustin Cox The Ravens entered this game as 8.5 favorites, opening their home slate against an NFC opponent quarterbacked by a player that had never faced them. There were plenty of reasons that this game shouldn’t have been close, but here we are. It’s early in the year to be concerned, but depending on how the division shakes out, they’re going to really want this one back. The coaching staff veered away from Derrick Henry after a few non-starter plays, and in doing so, lost all control of a two-pronged offensive flow to the game. The defense, meanwhile, gave up several third and longs, giving the Saints life and keeping their tired defensive legs on the field to get worn down on long scoring drives. I think I’m most surprised by Declan Doyle seemingly playing things tentatively. That’s absolutely not what I expected from him in a tight game. I know one thing, I’d hate to be in that locker room right now or in the facility on Tuesday, because there are going to be a lot of uncomfortable conversations. – Kevin McNelis The Ravens allowed the Saints to hang around in this game and paid the price late. They sputtered offensively in the second half and strangely did not use Derrick Henry for more than five carries over the final two quarters. The defense could not get off the field on third down and allowed Tyler Shough to escape pressure and make too many throws under duress. In addition, the Ravens’ special teams was subpar. Their poor kick return coverage and missed field goal in the first half were notable swing moments in the game. This was a disappointing showing from Jesse Minter and the team’s coaching staff. One of the biggest hopes under this new regime was that the Ravens would no longer lose games in which they were leading by multiple scores, often at home to inferior opponents. Unfortunately, today felt like more of the same script we’ve seen in prior years. — Frank Platko

title: Buffalo Bills off to an elite pace disrupting quarterbacks
summary: Just to start off a candid note, nothing you’re about to read suggests that the Buffalo Bills’ defense doesn’t have room for improvement. It very obviously does, allowing 31 points in both of their first games. Now Week 1 is known for “lying” about a team’s identity, and Thursday Night Football is similarly wonky, but […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Greg Rousseau #15 and Bradley Chubb #9 of the Buffalo Bills sack Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions during the first quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just to start off a candid note, nothing you’re about to read suggests that the Buffalo Bills’ defense doesn’t have room for improvement. It very obviously does, allowing 31 points in both of their first games. Now Week 1 is known for “lying” about a team’s identity, and Thursday Night Football is similarly wonky, but neither is wonky enough to make me dismiss all that. They’ve also not recorded an interception yet, have the sixth worst points per drive in the league, and the ninth worst scoring rate; allowing their opponents to score 50% of the time. But the pass rush! That’s been a delight and something to build off of. Buffalo has seven sacks on the season so far and 19 QB hits. It’s early yet and forecasts should be considered as accurate as the weather ones in Western New York, but that would put Buffalo on pace for about 60 sacks and 160 quarterback hits. Those numbers aren’t unachievable, with the Broncos breaking the 60-sack mark the last two seasons (63 and 68) and 164 QB hits last year. Let’s take a look at some of their work so far this and see if it’s a lucky streak, or likely to be replicated.. The Film! pic.twitter.com/Bshv0SAIG0 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 20, 2026 Alright, so the question was if what was happening can be replicated and the answer so far seems to be “yes.” Breaking down the plays, here’s a quick rundown of what I see. Greg Rousseau is leading the way for the team. His success is largely dependent on his use of space and subsequent ability to disengage from the block to get after the quarterback. Rousseau’s long arm has been his bread and butter but as seen in the plays above, he’s been able to generate leverage and collapse the pocket. That’s benefitted himself directly and doesn’t exactly hurt the chances for the rest of the team either. Groot is currently on pace for 34 sacks this season which would shatter the current single-season mark of 23. I don’t expect that to continue, but would clearly be happy if it did. Deone Walker has been the talk of the town, and for good reason. For a big man, he’s been showing off good finesse techniques. The shimmy and swim move in the clips above are good examples of that with Walker starting to get a reputation as a menace up the middle. Bradley Chubb I described earlier this year as “capable” which was in no way intended as an insult. While I didn’t gush over anything I felt was “elite” I did indicate he could make a bigger impact than Von Miller or Joey Bosa if he remained healthy. Put differently, I felt he might be a tier below those players’ peak, but actually being present snap-to-snap would elevate him higher than those guys. So far I’m not backing off that analysis and his steady presence has been paying off for himself directly, but also the rest of the team. Chubb is currently trending toward double digit sacks himself. Michael Hoecht is a player I was excited to see suit up for Buffalo, feeling he could become the chaos piece like Lorenzo Alexander used to be. He had a great debut last year, and was sadly injured pretty much right away. So far this season, he’s been living up to what I hoped for and he’s another player that a full season of play from would likely pay off in a big way. The Final Straw Yeah, it’s way too early to make sweeping declarations, but as of right now the defensive front seems legit. The team may have an emerging star in Greg Rousseau, and a strong supporting cast around him. If they can keep it up, it’ll be the first time they broke the 50-sack mark since 2023 when Leonard Floyd and Ed Oliver led the team’s 53-sack campaign. That was the only time they hit the 50s in the McDermott era, despite several years with excellent pass rush rates.
