title: Buffalo Bills Week 2 game balls following 41-31 win over Detroit
summary: The Buffalo Bills are 2-0 after defeating the Detroit Lions 41-31 in the inaugural regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium. Buffalo’s offense delivered 41 points against Detroit, led by another nearly unstoppable performance from Josh Allen. James Cook controlled the game on the ground, while Greg Rousseau continued his dominant start to the season […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are 2-0 after defeating the Detroit Lions 41-31 in the inaugural regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium. Buffalo’s offense delivered 41 points against Detroit, led by another nearly unstoppable performance from Josh Allen. James Cook controlled the game on the ground, while Greg Rousseau continued his dominant start to the season on the other side of the ball. Following the win, head coach Joe Brady awarded game balls to all three players. Game ball: QB Josh Allen Allen completed 20 of 31 passes for 248 yards and three touchdowns. He added two more touchdowns on the ground, along with 69 yards rushing. Through two weeks, Allen has once again shown why there aren’t many (if any) quarterbacks you would take over him. Whether Buffalo needed him to deliver through the air or finish a drive with his legs, Allen found a way to keep the offense moving. Game ball: RB James Cook Cook carried the ball 21 times for 135 yards and a touchdown, averaging more than six yards per attempt. His performance gave Buffalo the offensive balance it needed against Detroit. Cook was patient when necessary, decisive when the running lanes opened, and consistently put the offense in manageable situations. Allen will understandably receive plenty of attention after accounting for five touchdowns, but Cook’s work on the ground helped make the entire offense more difficult to defend. Cook absolutely delivered. Game ball: DE Greg Rousseau As Brady prepared to present the final game ball, he explained just how rare Rousseau’s start to the season has been. “This has only happened once in history,” Brady said. “And the first one was Bruce Smith…” Rousseau recorded two sacks against the Houston Texans in Week 1 and added two more against the Lions. He became the first Bills player since Pro Football Hall of Famer Bruce Smith in 1996 to record at least two sacks in each of the season’s first two games. The four sacks are impressive enough, but they only tell part of the story. Rousseau has also forced three fumbles through two games, becoming a consistent source of disruption for Buffalo’s defense. Three game balls, one historic afternoon As Brady ended the locker room speech, Allen quickly handed his ball to Bills owner Terry Pegula in recognition of the franchise’s inaugural game in the new stadium. “I want to give my ball to Mr Pegula.” Celebrating the first win in the new stadium. It was a fitting gesture on a historic day for the organization. Allen may have led the Bills to the victory, but he understood that this game ball represented something much bigger than his performance. It was a historic evening in Buffalo, and there was no shortage of players worthy of taking home a game ball. My Honorable mentions: TE Dalton Kincaid Kincaid gave Allen a reliable target throughout the night, finishing with seven receptions for 95 yards and a touchdown. He consistently found openings in Detroit’s defense and came just five yards short of the second 100-yard receiving game of his career. Kincaid’s production was another encouraging sign of the role he can play in Buffalo’s passing attack this season. WR Keon Coleman Coleman may have been the unsung hero of the night, especially after DJ Moore left the game. He caught all six of his targets for 63 yards, with four of those receptions moving the chains. Coleman did not find the end zone, but he delivered every time Allen looked in his direction and helped keep multiple scoring drives alive. It was exactly the type of dependable performance Buffalo needed from the third year player. WR Joshua Palmer Palmer has only two receptions through the first two games of the season, but he has certainly made them count. Both catches have gone for more than 30 yards, and both have resulted in touchdowns. Palmer has not needed significant volume to make a difference. Through two weeks, every reception has produced an explosive scoring play. Bills Mafia, who earned your game ball following Buffalo’s 41-31 victory over the Lions?
author: Sara Larson

title: Buffalo Bills can’t forget about this common tendency in NFL before Chargers game
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers will enter this Week 3 contested headed in diametrically opposed directions, which can often spawn a rather silly assumption. That we are sure of something in the NFL, especially in September. Now, should the Bills have confidence going into this game? Yes. Plenty of it. And, I’ll never […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 13: Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel of the Los Angeles Chargers takes the field during a preseason game against the Houston Texans at Reliant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers will enter this Week 3 contested headed in diametrically opposed directions, which can often spawn a rather silly assumption. That we are sure of something in the NFL, especially in September. Now, should the Bills have confidence going into this game? Yes. Plenty of it. And, I’ll never blame for a team for, internally, feeling good about their chances against a team spiraling as opposed to an opponent firing on all cylinders. But we can’t simply assume this game is over before it begins. There’s too much parity in today’s NFL. And many times, right when we collectively feel like we have a team or teams figured out, the unexpected strikes. Justin Herbert defenders are going through it to begin the 2026 season. He’s completed 59.3% of his throws, with two touchdowns and three interceptions and has been sacked six times in this 0-2 start. That comes after another dud of a playoff game last January. Mike McDaniels’ widely regarded reputation as an offensive genius is continuing to lose luster, fast, and it’s fair to start to wonder if Jim Harbaugh, at this age, can be a Super Bowl-caliber coach. But Herbert has insane big-time throw ability in him. McDaniels did coach a Dolphins team that, with plenty of talent, saw Tua Tagovailoa lead the NFL in passer rating. Derwin James has been a first or second team All-Pro six times. And Harbaugh has won everywhere he’s coached, from FCS football to Stanford to Michigan to the 49ers. Heck, McDaniels’ rather hapless Dolphins trounced the Bills 30-13 in November last season. And, for the Bills, the Patriots are coming to town in Week 4. This Sunday could be referred to as a “trap game.” Buffalo can’t get caught looking ahead. Because for as much as the Chargers may very well be already into a season-long implosion with some polarizing yet previously successful characters at the top of their organization, the bounce-back tendency of the NFL cannot be forgotten before this Week 3 game. It’s very real. Sure, favorites can cruise. But more often than we initially believe, two teams playing each other one week do not resemble what we’ve previously seen from them. However, I’ll end with this — if Buffalo can get out to a sizable lead in the first half, this does feel like a Chargers team that won’t have nearly as much fight in it as the Lions showed in Week 2.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills pass rush has improved in one overlooked but key area
summary: Despite clearly not playing particularly well through two weeks, there is one vital area in which the Buffalo Bills defense has improved from years past. Converting pressures to sacks. Through the vast majority of the Sean McDermott era, the Bills pass-rush unit was rarely one of the league’s better units actually sacking the quarterback. We […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Bradley Chubb #9 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates with Greg Rousseau #15 after sacking Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions during the second quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Despite clearly not playing particularly well through two weeks, there is one vital area in which the Buffalo Bills defense has improved from years past. Converting pressures to sacks. Through the vast majority of the Sean McDermott era, the Bills pass-rush unit was rarely one of the league’s better units actually sacking the quarterback. We never really hear or read about this metric for a defense — it’s strictly reserved for quarterbacks — and I’m not sure why. Don’t get me wrong. Disruption is production for a pass rush. But, of course, sacks are most valuable. Let’s check the Bills’ pressure-to-sack rate through two games in 2026 and compare to the last few seasons. Last season, the pressure-to-sack rate of Buffalo’s defense was 19.0% via Next Gen Stats. The season before it was only 12.8%. The best figure Buffalo’s defense managed since 2020 in this metric was 23.2% in 2023, when as a team, the Bills had 54 sacks during the regular season. It was the only time they reached or eclipsed the 20% mark in McDermott’s tenure. Two weeks into the 2026 campaign, the Bills defense has managed a pressure-to-sack rate of 29.1%. Yes, I know. Sample size. But it ranks third in the NFL behind the Texans (30.4%) and Steelers (36.8%). The Bills are currently one of five teams with a pressure-to-sack rate as a defense over 25%. In short, they’re not just pressuring quarterbacks, they’re getting quarterbacks on the ground. Leonhard’s defense has been far from stellar, allowing 31 points in each contest. And the unit’s pressure rate is only 27.1% per NGS, which is distinctly in the bottom fourth of the NFL. But if it’s felt like the Bills pass rush has been better than previous seasons through these first two weeks, it’s because they’re converting those pressures to sacks at a noticeably higher rate than the past two seasons. This is a not often used metric I’ll be tracking with the Bills throughout this season, particularly after the pass rush’s torrid start.

title: Buffalo Bills at forefront of efficiency-boosting personnel grouping movement through two games
summary: We already suspected the Buffalo Bills loved their tight end group, but when they kept four tight ends and five receivers on their initial 53-man roster after the preseason, we should have realized they planned on frequently using those bigger bodies this season. And it hasn’t just been the most common double tight-end look — […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills runs with the football during the first half of the NFL game against the Detroit Lions at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images We already suspected the Buffalo Bills loved their tight end group, but when they kept four tight ends and five receivers on their initial 53-man roster after the preseason, we should have realized they planned on frequently using those bigger bodies this season. And it hasn’t just been the most common double tight-end look — 12 personnel — from Buffalo. No. It’s been the significantly more rare three-tight end grouping — 13 personnel — the Bills have featured offensively. Through two weeks, the Rams (36.4%) and Bills at 33.8% are lapping the field in 13 personnel. The Ravens are third in 13 personnel usage at 18.3%. Dalton Kincaid’s bulked up physique has a two-fold benefit to his game and this Bills team. There’s the idea that added strength, particularly around his knee, will help his durability. Also, with more power, Kincaid can become a more stable, people-moving blocker. He’d demonstrated clear improvement in that aspect in these opening two weeks. And check this takeaway from Max Toscano on Twitter/X: Have charted both Dalton Kincaid games. One big, interesting takeaway He's an obvious run/pass tell in everything except for 13 personnel. 11: 76.7% pass 12: 70% Pass 13: 50% pass He's being used in both neutral and obvious pass situations unlike last year, BUT personnel… — Max Toscano (@maxtoscano1) September 19, 2026 Remember, in the first three seasons of his NFL career, Kincaid was one of the league’s most glaring tells that it was going to be a pass . Through two games, while 13 personnel — with Kincaid on the field of course — the Bills have an exactly even 50-50 run-pass split. In my five takeaways article after Bills-Lions , I wrote about the showcasing of Buffalo’s real-time adaptability in the second half of Week 2’s win after DJ Moore’s injury. And they were able to roll out plenty of 13 personnel looks to keep the defense honest when they really wanted to lean on the ground game without their No. 1 wideout on the field and holding a sizable lead. Over the past few years, as analytics has taken the NFL by storm, teams have discovered they can generate tremendous efficiency throwing the football from heavy personnel in large part due to the personnel groupings defenses feel obligated to counter with. One example — the Rams’ 331 plays in 13 personnel netted a considerably higher Expected Points Added per drop back than the No. 1 EPA per drop back offense (Packers) in 2025 on all plays. Of course, sample-size difference matters here. But that fact alone is very noteworthy. Los Angeles’ used 13 personnel on 30.4% of their snaps last season, the first time in at least four years in the NFL any team deployed the three tight-end look on more than 17% of the time. I ran my own study, using the nflverse play-by-play database and FTN’s participation data from 2018 – 2025, and this is what note how much more EPA per drop back teams have generated throwing out of 13 personnel than the other most commonly used groupings with tight ends on the field: Use Rate Pass Rate Overall EPA / play EPA / dropback EPA / run 11 personnel 60.2% 70.3% +0.002 +0.020 -0.041 12 personnel 19.7% 51.1% +0.005 +0.093 -0.086 13 personnel 3.6% 39.7% -0.005 +0.122 -0.088 *other groupings accounted for 16.7% of offensive snaps in this large sample The other noteworthy observation from that chart is this — offenses are less efficient running the ball from 13 personnel. BUT, the simple presence of those three tight ends on the field brings larger, less-coverage capable defenders onto the field, thereby inviting the offense to actually pass the football. For clubs like the Bills with at least one tight end who’s a dangerous receiving threat, not a blocking liability, and their presence on the field doesn’t telegraph run or pass, 13 personnel has become the ultimate efficiency creator for an offense. And Joe Brady’s team has joined the Rams at the forefront of this movement.

title: DJ Moore, Ed Oliver avoided serious injuries on Thursday night in Week 2
summary: The Buffalo Bills got a huge scare in the first half of their 41-31 Thursday Night Football victory over the Lions in Week 2, when DJ Moore stayed down after diving for a throw from Josh Allen in the end zone. A few hours before that, Ed Oliver was shockingly on the inactive list after […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - DECEMBER 23: Ed Oliver #91 of the Buffalo Bills looks on from the sideline before an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on December 23, 2023 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Ryan Kang/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills got a huge scare in the first half of their 41-31 Thursday Night Football victory over the Lions in Week 2, when DJ Moore stayed down after diving for a throw from Josh Allen in the end zone. A few hours before that, Ed Oliver was shockingly on the inactive list after tweaking his hip in warmups. Now we have more clarity on the severity of their injuries. Appearing on NFL Gameday before Sunday’s action in Week 1, Ian Rapoport gave the following updates on Moore and Oliver. First on Moore: “Not considered to be a serious injury. It is an AC joint sprain for DJ Moore. It’s considered day-to-day. I expect him to practice next week. That is a good sign. We’ll see if he plays. But I expect him to practice.” On Oliver: “Is considered day-to-day, and has a chance, though, for next week.” Oliver not being on the field was hugely impactful against Detroit, as Buffalo’s defense is clearly getting its legs early in the season. The Bills did deviate to a more run-heavy approach once Moore was sidelined on Thursday, but it’s not as if the aerial was completely stagnant for the rest of the contest. However, we all understand how vital Moore is to the Bills pass-game plans this season. The news that these veterans are day-to-day instead of week-to-week or month-to-month is majorly positive from the Bills as they begin preparing for the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3. While I won’t be shocked if either don’t play in week — and wouldn’t necessarily be against the precautionary route this early in the season — we will get a good sense of how the Bills are approaching their respective injuries during practice this week.

title: The Optimist: Do it again, Bryce
summary: They were the best of teams. They were the worst of teams. Then we reflected on the fact that the Carolina Panthers 34-3 win over the Atlanta Falcons was, pending the results of Monday Night Football, the largest margin of victory in the NFL in Week 2 by a mile and a half and we […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers passes the ball against the Atlanta Falcons during the second quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images They were the best of teams. They were the worst of teams. Then we reflected on the fact that the Carolina Panthers 34-3 win over the Atlanta Falcons was, pending the results of Monday Night Football, the largest margin of victory in the NFL in Week 2 by a mile and a half and we determined that the Panthers are, at the very least, not the worst of teams. In fact, the 1-1 Panthers have a positive score differential through two weeks in spite of giving up a franchise record number of points in Week 1. That is true because they played an incredibly inept Falcons offense without a quarterback to speak of and because the offense has largely started out strong in the 2026 season. That strong start has been keyed by none other than the very much maligned Bryce Young. We’ll detail his rise more later on, but suffice it to say that he is passing the eye test at a level many of us had long since given up on. We’re not ready to crown him as a franchise quarterback, but we will be if he keeps up this pace through the season. Kudos are also due to the management of the team and the defense as a whole. Let’s get into it. What I liked The linebackers Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke have transformed this defense from last season. The unit as a whole has a lot of the same problems that it did last season, largely thanks to injuries undoing some of the gains they made through free agency, but one weakness is well on its way out the door. These guys are heads up players who are only going to get more comfortable playing in this scheme and with their new teammates as the season goes on. Both of them had incredible interceptions that were largely due to their ability to pay attention to the football and make the play in front of them. Lloyd and Okereke shared the team lead with nine tackles on the day. For Lloyd that included one sack, two additional tackles for loss, one additional quarterback hit, three passes deflected, and two interceptions. He returned the second pick 16 yards for a touchdown. Yes, they did this against Cooper Rush so well that they also got the opportunity to do it against Jack Strand in the same game. Yes, they were picked apart by the same Caleb Williams last week who only managed three points against the Minnesota Vikings in most of four quarters before suffering a severe looking hamstring injury. Like I said, they are only going to get better the more time they have to gel with their new team. This week isn’t their floor so much as a glimpse of a possible ceiling. It’s a ceiling worthy of the history of Carolina Panthers linebackers. All they have to do is reach it. The receivers This is what we wanted to see this year. Tetairoa McMillan had a 100-yard day, Jalen Coker was a reliable, productive target, and Xavier Legette made a positive impact. Sprinkle in a couple targets to running backs and tight ends in appropriate situations, add some broth and a potato and the Panthers look like they got a stew going. Unlike their offense, the Falcons defense is a real unit made up of professional football players. This was what they did against real competition and it was great. Neither the Falcons nor the Bears are likely to be near the top ten of defenses by the end of the season, but neither unit is laughably bad, either. These were great games to ramp up into the rest of the season. Question marks abound around Young, Legette, Jonathon Brooks, and the meaning of life, but right now the Panthers have an honest to goodness strength in their wide receiver room and that’s fantastic to see. Do it again, Bryce. No player is going to be beloved by their team’s fans when they are acquired via a trade that involves sending away a first overall pick, other high future picks, and a fan favorite wide receiver. Young’s path was further inhibited by awful coaching as a rookie, comparisons to Williams, and his own awful, awful play in the first three years of his career. The bright side for him has been the coaching and encouragement he has received from head coach Dave Canales and offensive coordinator Brad Idzik. Both of those mentors are young in their own rights and are growing into their current roles at about the same rate that Young is. That is to say that it is equally unsurprising that it took a minute to for them to find success together as it was frustrating to watch them struggle along the way. These past two weeks to open the season have qualified as success for Young and Idzik. Over two games, Young has averaged 324 passing yards, three touchdowns, 0.5 interceptions, a 63% completion rating, and 8.86 yards per attempt. In his career prior to this season, he average 180 passing yards, one touchdown, 0.65 interceptions, and 6 Y/A per game. This season has provided a small sample size so far, but we can only judge off of what he has shown. He is throwing the ball further down field, keeping drives alive for longer, getting in scoring position more, and turning the ball over less. Outside of the box score, his pocket presence, movement, vision, general demeanor, and touch have all dramatically improved. Bear with me for one of the biggest “ifs” in the history of the Carolina Panthers. IF Young can keep this up, IF Young can keep playing at this level then he will be who the Panthers drafted him to be. He will have absolutely spoiled his rookie contract window. From a team building perspective, that’s like shooting yourself in the foot to make sure you can walk in a few years. But compared to where the Panthers were for the six years prior to drafting Young, that seems like fine logic to me. What’s next? That all depends on Young. Two games are hardly a trend. Thus we cannot say definitively that Young, Canales, and Idzik have “Arrived”. We can say, however, that so far they are passing the eye test. The little things are adding up in their favor. Play calls are in and Bryce Young is at the line of scrimmage with time to spare. Penalties, like the many we saw in the first quarter of yesterday’s game, aren’t complete drive killers. These are great things that we have now witnessed twice against pretty poor defenses. If we see them again against better defenses, like the Browns and the Lions before the bye-week, then we’ll probably be in for a fun season. The Panthers offense that showed up the last two weeks at least makes a game out of their next two contests. The Panthers defense that we saw yesterday won’t show up again, but it may look closer to that than who they were against the Bears. Time will tell. For now, I’m focusing on Young’s statistical improvements to buoy my optimism through the week. Forgive me if this is a little pie in the sky. It’s been a minutes since we got to start the season talking about nice things. so I’m just going to do that until the nice things go away and we have to spend weeks on end cursing the Kellen Moore/Tyler Shough Saints. Let’s go back to what we were talking about after the preseason. The Carolina Panthers were traditionally a team to start the season slowly under Bryce Young and Dave Canales. By all accounts, that’s not what we’ve seen so far. Let’s look at Young’s average first two games of the season: Young first two games average Yards Comp% Attempts Y/A TDs INT 2023 149.5 0.60 35.5 4.24 1 1 2024 122.5 0.56 28 4.30 0 1.5 2025 241 0.58 45 5.36 2 1.5 Average ‘23 – ‘25 171 0.58 36.17 4.63 1 1.33 2026 324 0.63 36.5 8.86 3 0.5 Difference ‘26 – (’23-‘25) 153 0.05 0.33 4.23 2 -0.83 153 more yards per game. Two more touchdowns per game. A 5% improvement in completions isn’t exactly world changing, but the nature of his passes have changed. 4.23 more yards gained per pass attempt show a more aggressive passer. Combine that with a higher completion…

title: Panthers 34 Falcons 3: The Panthers returned to normalcy
summary: After a 59 point blowout to open the season, the Panthers found themselves in the familiar Misery and Sadness Bowl with the Falcons. They proved they might be a team team to watch out for once again. First Quarter The Panthers started off the game with a nice turnover, as regular season starting knight Nick […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Chuba Hubbard #30 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates with Bryce Young #9 after scoring a touchdown against the Atlanta Falcons during the first quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a 59 point blowout to open the season, the Panthers found themselves in the familiar Misery and Sadness Bowl with the Falcons. They proved they might be a team team to watch out for once again. First Quarter The Panthers started off the game with a nice turnover, as regular season starting knight Nick Scott recovered a Cooper Rush fumble. Carolina responded with Bryce Young hitting Chuba Hubbard on a short pass for a score. The next drive for the Falcons ended with another turnover, as Bobby Okereke snagged a tipped ball for an interception. Carolina could not capitalize which forced a punt. Another Falcons punt later and a nice Jalen Coker return had the Panthers in scoring distance again, but they fell short. 10-0 Panthers. The Falcons engaged on a somewhat productive drive that got them into the RedZone, but a nice tackle by Devin Lloyd on 4th down ended those hopes. Second Quarter The second quarter didn’t start well, as a holding penalty and then a sack basically shut down the Panthers drive. Sam Martin punted a nice ball to trap the Falcons inside their 20 despite the offensive struggles. A Devin Lloyd sack ended the Falcons ensuing drive. A couple Tetairoa McMillan catches and a really special Jalen Coker reception put the Panthers back in scoring distance. They failed to score a TD so the game got to 13-0 following another field goal. The Falcons tried to push into scoring distance on their next drive, and managed a field goal, 13-3 Panthers. Bryce Young hit Xavier Legette on a HUGE pass to get the Panthers right back to scoring range in the waning moments of the half. The Panthers capitalize with a Bryce Young strike to Darren Waller, 20-3 Panthers! Third Quarter The Panthers opened the second half with the ball, and they ate with a nice 73 yard drive capped off with another Darren Waller TD pass. 27-3 Panthers. Devin Lloyd made an instance interception on the following drive that once again put the Panthers in scoring distance. The Panthers could not put any points on the board and lost possession on an incomplete pass by Bryce. The Falcons took over and brought in Jack Strand at QB, who subsequently threw a ball that Jaycee Horn got a hand on and Devin Lloyd picked off and took to the house for a TD. 34-3 Panthers. Strand took over but it didn’t go well, as the Falcons went into 4th down to end the quarter. Fourth Quarter The Panthers continued to have issues with holding penalties, but things were academic at this point. The Panthers punted with about 10 minutes left in the final quarter. They trotted out the second string defense at that point. The Falcons also got Bijan Robinson out of the game and also seemed to settle in to the end of the game. Nick Folk missed on a sad field goal attempt that perfectly encapsulated the Falcons efforts on the day. Kenny Pickett took over on offense for the Panthers. They still managed to turn the ball over, so the Panthers won on a victory formation as they kneeled the clock out. Overall, solid win by this Panthers unit. They certainly have things to clean up (those penalties, man) but a blowout win over a division rival puts them in great position to take the NFC South once again. I think we;lol have a better idea of who this team is in the next two weeks, but we can at least celebrate now. A win is a win! KEEP POUNDING!

(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images That massive *sigh* you just heard is from the entire Chicago Bears fanbase welcoming the good news just published about their young franchise quarterback. Bears QB Caleb Williams avoided any major injury to his hamstring Sunday, tests confirmed today — and the team isn’t even ruling him out for next Monday’s game against the Eagles, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . A massive sigh of relief in Chicago. pic.twitter.com/mfCT5x0JWR — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) September 21, 2026 Ultimately, there still should be precaution exercised here, as hamstring injuries can be tricky to both diagnose and treat without risking setbacks. That being said, there is a chance Caleb Williams does not miss any time due to what is being considered as a mild hamstring pull. It’s certainly better than what Dak Prescott of the Dallas Cowboys recently underwent, as he missed an entire season due to the required surgery. It’s also not the first time in Caleb Williams’ football career that he’s pulled a hamstring. In December of 2022, he suffered a similar injury in his left leg and would not be back to full speed for a month. As teammates have described, Caleb is a very resilient baller who will push to return as soon as possible. Ben Johnson will be speaking to the media in the near future. And, chances are, we should expect Tyson Bagent at quarterback against the Philadelphia Eagles on Monday Night Football unless the Bears are 100% convinced Caleb Williams is good to go in one calendar week. Still… I can speak for many of us when I say, “Thank God.” UPDATE: Ben Johnson did a morning spot with Jeff Joniak on ESPN1000 and said , “It sounds like it’s going to be a week-to-week deal for him. … But he will likely miss some time.”

title: Bears vs. Vikings: Inside the Snap Counts, Stats, and so many mistakes
summary: Luckily, the Chicago Bears have a 24-hour rule that gives them a day to either celebrate a win or get over a loss, because this is a game the Bears would like to forget. But before they move on to the Philadelphia Eagles, they’ll need to dissect some of the worst tape this regime has […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 2026: Minnesota Vikings safety Joshua Metellus (44) and safety Theo Jackson (26) jared the ball from Chicago Bears tight end Sam Roush (87) in the fourth quarter at Solider Field in Chicago, Illinois, on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) Luckily, the Chicago Bears have a 24-hour rule that gives them a day to either celebrate a win or get over a loss, because this is a game the Bears would like to forget. But before they move on to the Philadelphia Eagles, they’ll need to dissect some of the worst tape this regime has ever had with their 9- 3 loss to the Minnesota Vikings. Chicago’s 3 points were their lowest output since December 26, 2024, and if you were wondering when a Ben Johnson-led offense had this few points, you’d need to go back to October 9, 2022, his first year as the full-time play caller in Detroit, when the Patriots shut out the Lions. The Bears gained more yards (297 to 246) and had more first downs (17 to 11), but they deserved to lose this game. They were penalized 8 times for 58 yards, while the Vikings were penalized just 3 times for 25 yards. The Bears got into the red zone three times and got to a goal-to-go situation twice, but a fumble on the one-yard line and a blocked field goal doomed their chances of winning. The defense, which looked bad a week ago, bounced back against a lesser opposition in the rain, but everything else that could have gone wrong did. Minnesota defensive coordinator Brian Flores threw a lot of looks and pressure at the Bears, and he dictated the game to Ben Johnson, who didn’t have an answer. Let’s look at the Bears’ playing time breakdowns and a few individual stats from the game. OFFENSE Caleb Williams had a game he’d like to forget, with his lowest passer rating since the aforementioned 12/26/24 game against the Seattle Seahawks. Kalif Raymond was the Bears’ most productive wide receiver for the second consecutive week. Which, you know, is good for Raymond, but with Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III on this team, it’s not a good look for them. Tight end Colston Loveland has 1 catch and 3 yards in two weeks and was pass blocking on the final play of the game instead of running to the end zone with his 6’6″, 241-pound frame. Chicago’s offensive line, which was so good a week ago, wasn’t moving people yesterday, and center Garrett Bradbury was called for 4 penalties (3 accepted, 1 offsetting). Bears TE Colston Loveland said postgame that Caleb Williams broke down the team and didn't mention his injury. Per Loveland, Williams told them: "Let it hurt, let it sting, watch the tape, clean it up, get back and be 1-0 next week." — Kalyn Kahler (@kalynkahler) September 21, 2026 DEFENSE Chicago held the Vikings to just 3 for 13 (23.1%) on third downs. Rookie safety Dillon Thieneman toed for the team lead with 7 tackles. He also had a pass defended. Defensive lineman James Lynch, who got the start, also had 7 tackles Tyrique Stevenson had 5 tackles, a tackle for loss, and a PD. Cam Lewis had 5 tackles. Rookie Malik Muhammad II recorded the first sack of his career to go along with 3 tackles and a TFL. Dayo Odeyingbo had a TFL, a sack, and 2 QB hits. Austin Booker had a TFL and a sack. SPECIAL TEAMS* *The above image has players who only played in the third phase. Cairo Santos made a 50-yard field goal but had a 23-yarder blocked. Rookie tight end Sam Roush missed his block on the play. Tory Taylor had 4 punts for a 48.8 average (46.0 net), with 3 punts inside the 20. Jack Sanborn had 2 tackles. Raymond had 30 punt return yards on 3 returns. Zavion Thomas had 3 kickoff returns for 68 yards. To check out the complete Bears vs. Vikings box score, I find ESPN’s site is easy to navigate. All statistics and snap counts, as well as the accompanying pictures, are taken directly from the NFL’s Game Statistic and Information System.

title: 5 Bears Takes: Waiting on a Williams update, red zone failures, and good defense?
summary: Week 2 of the NFL delivered another outstanding weekend of football, but the offense was much harder to find for most teams. Unfortunately, the Chicago Bears were one of those teams, putting up just three points over 60 minutes of football. Despite a final score of 9-3 not going their way, all eyes are on […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 2026: Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) was hurt and was replaced by Chicago Bears quarterback Tyson Bagent (17) in the fourth quarter of an NFL game against the Minnesota Vikings at Solider Field in Chicago, Illinois, on Sunday Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) Week 2 of the NFL delivered another outstanding weekend of football, but the offense was much harder to find for most teams. Unfortunately, the Chicago Bears were one of those teams, putting up just three points over 60 minutes of football. Despite a final score of 9-3 not going their way, all eyes are on the health of quarterback Caleb Williams, who left in the fourth quarter what appeared to be a serious hamstring injury. At (1-1) and (0-1) within the division, how they fare over the next few weeks (or maybe more) will determine how competitive they can be in November and December. For more on a disastrous Sunday and how to move forward, let’s dive into our weekly postgame Bears Takes. 1. Although head coach Ben Johnson was noncommittal during his postgame presser, Monday’s MRI results for Caleb Williams might dictate how serious of a contender the Bears can be moving forward this season. The early reports are promising, though. Even with a strong performance from the defense on Sunday, it was fair to say that the Bears’ ceiling was going to be dictated by how well they were able to settle in after a rough Week 1 against the Carolina Panthers. With Williams out for the foreseeable future, the road back to the playoffs became that much harder. According to NBC Sports’ Mike Florio, there’s optimism that Williams suffered a Grade 1 sprain, which would keep him out only a few weeks. Outside of Florio, both Johnson and the top insiders have echoed the same information: Williams will have an MRI on Monday to determine the severity of his hamstring injury. Given how bad it looked in real time, anything short of season-ending would feel like a big “win” for the long term. That said, anything that avoids injured reserve should keep the Bears in the playoff race. For what it’s worth, the Seahawks are in a very similar position with Sam Darnold leaving Week 1 with a glute injury. They are also trying to keep their heads above water, but the initial thought is that Darnold will return before Williams. Sunday’s loss (which we’ll touch on more later) was tough enough, but it’s worth keeping in mind that navigating this at 2-0 with a divisional win is a lot easier than what they are currently facing. To muddy the waters even more, this will be the first time that Johnson will be calling plays relying on a backup quarterback. The offense will need to change moving forward, but relying on their run game will be key to finding offensive success. For now, we’ll wait for a more concrete timeline and hope it’s on the shorter end of everyone’s feared timeline. 2. Even before Williams’ injury, the offense was getting their brains beat out by Vikings’ defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Like we pounded home last week, overreacting to Week 1 rarely works out well. Plenty of other teams struggled around the league to follow up their season-opening performances. All week, we heard about the battle between Johnson and Flores. For outside observers, I’m sure it’s a great chess match to watch twice a year, but for Bears fans, it hasn’t been overly fun since Johnson came over from Detroit. Despite their 59-point performance last week, the offense struggled all day to move the ball. Even when they were in position to score, it backfired every time except for their first-quarter field goal. Williams had one of his worst games in quite some time, but he was far from the only disappointment on Sunday. The run game struggled to get going consistently. For all the explosive plays they had last week, many more runs went for less than two yards in their home opener. More concerning, their receivers weren’t getting open, and the offensive line wasn’t holding up in pass protection against the blitz. To be fair, Flores blitzed over 70% of the time, but even so, this offense has proven it can succeed against that approach in the past. The offensive line is down two starters from last season, but even so, they looked disjointed for most of the game. Despite all their issues, they still had multiple chances to put points on the board and simply couldn’t. The goal-line fumble from D’Andre Swift felt like a back-breaker in the moment, but the blocked field goal felt like a week-long issue in the making. Rookie long snapper Beau Gardner has shown a tendency to snap the ball high, but the blocking off the edges was shaky last weekend against the Panthers, too. While these are the types of games that feel like they are simply impossible, Johnson and this offense will now be tasked with getting back on track against another tough defense on a national stage next Monday night. Figuring out the penalties will be key, but their execution in “scoring position” must also vastly improve. Now they’ll be doing that with a backup quarterback under center. 3. The defense was far from perfect, but if you had told anyone earlier in the week that they gave up just nine points and no touchdowns, everyone would have assumed the Bears won in a blowout. There aren’t going to be many “pretty” performances from this defensive group, but this was about as good a day as anyone should realistically ask for in 2026. Allowing an aging Aaron Jones to go for 105 yards on 23 carries isn’t ideal, but allowing just 127 total passing yards, three sacks, and no touchdowns should be enough for almost any team to win a game. That said, maybe we shouldn’t be as surprised. After all, Carson Wentz has been responsible for handing some ugly losses to the Bears. Before Sunday, the last time he started a game and beat the Bears was when the Bears couldn’t overcome a 12-point defensive effort, in which they had multiple cracks inside the five on Thursday night football. Regardless of the Brock Osweiler-type black magic, the defense played more than well enough to come out with a victory on Sunday. Still, it didn’t happen thanks to some very uncharacteristic struggles from the offense. On the plus side, their performance should give fans hope that they won’t set bad records and that being closer to league-average isn’t out of the question. If we are being honest, their best shot at staying afloat might be playing as close to league-average as possible, with Williams expected to be on the shelf for a while. 4. For years, we’ve heard how good of a backup Tyson Bagent is. With Williams out for the foreseeable future, we’ll see if he can keep the Bears in the mix. It’s also worth noting that this will be Johnson’s first time navigating these waters, too. Simply put, the Bears’ immediate playoff hopes (even heading into Week 3) will ride on how much Johnson can get out of his backup quarterback. The team has loved him since he came in as an undrafted free agent from Shepherd. He’s survived through two head coaches and is just a little over a year removed from signing a two-year extension. Regardless of what anyone wants to believe, the difference between Williams and Bagent is very different. While Bagent has some mobility in his game, the stark difference in arm strength will be extremely noticeable. That doesn’t mean Bagent can’t succeed. In fact, Johnson’s vote of confidence in him should give Bears fans plenty of hope that with some modifications to the offense, they can still do more than enough to win games. I expect the offense will become more of a “quick strike” unit that relies on quick, decisive reads and, of course, a strong run game. That might help the offensive line get into a better rhythm, but the big-play aspects of this unit might be less consistent. Think more of what Johnson did in Detroit with Goff as a better example. How long Williams is out will also matter. Initial…

title: Bears lose Caleb Williams, and the season is now in question
summary: Sunday was about as bad as it could’ve gotten for the Chicago Bears. They fell to the Minnesota Vikings 9-3, putting together a lackluster outing on offense after a stellar Week 1 performance. But most importantly, quarterback Caleb Williams suffered a non-contact injury to his right hamstring, taking him out for the rest of the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears is carted off the field after an injury against the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday was about as bad as it could’ve gotten for the Chicago Bears. They fell to the Minnesota Vikings 9-3, putting together a lackluster outing on offense after a stellar Week 1 performance. But most importantly, quarterback Caleb Williams suffered a non-contact injury to his right hamstring, taking him out for the rest of the game. As of this writing, it’s still unclear how long Williams will be out. That said, his scream in pain, the fact that he needed help to get off the field, and the Bears’ carting him off, doesn’t bode well for his outlook, both in the short term and in the long run. EDITOR: We’ll know more about the injury later today, but for what it’s worth, last night’s report was good news. It’s tough to find optimism in how this game played out. That said, here are some of my notes from the Bears’ loss to Minnesota, breaking down both the good and the bad. Brian Flores: mastermind Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores utterly outcoached Ben Johnson on Sunday. Flores predictably dialed up the blitz heavily, and the rain made it significantly easier for Minnesota to dial up the pressure and disrupt Chicago’s passing attack. The offensive line struggled in pass protection, and there were clearly major issues with penalties up front. Garrett Bradbury and Braxton Jones seemed to struggle in particular. The Vikings ranked No. 11 in the NFL in PFN Defense Impact Scoring in Week 1, and they’ll surely rank higher in Week 2. It was uncharacteristic of Johnson’s offense to see such a straightforward defensive philosophy and not adjust accordingly to find a way to exploit it. That says a lot about how well the Bears’ offense has fared with Johnson as their head coach that it’s taken this long for that to happen, but that doesn’t mean he can’t be held accountable for a poor performance. Reassuring play from rookie DBs On the bright side, the Bears got encouraging play out of rookie defensive backs Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad. Thieneman was everywhere in run support and was flying all over the field, and Muhammad tallied the first sack of his NFL career on a nickel blitz. The All-22 will tell all, but upon first watch, both looked good in coverage. If Williams is out for a significant amount of time, you’re not expecting the Bears to make a playoff run like they did last year. Now, the focus is on the future. Any encouraging play you can get from young players will be beneficial as Chicago aims to come back into the Super Bowl hunt in 2027. Thieneman and Muhammad were two bright spots in an otherwise disappointing season. 2026 might be a dud year As deflating as it is to admit, if Williams is seriously hurt and will miss a significant part of the 2026 regular season, the Bears will not make the playoffs. They have a questionable defense to begin with, and their entire hopes relied upon having one of the best offenses in the NFL to remain at the top of the NFC North. With Williams injured, that very likely will not be the case. It’s so frustrating to see the Bears’ season go up like this. I’m trying to stay optimistic and talk myself into thinking Tyson Bagent will keep this team competitive, but Williams’ physical attributes have gotten him out of so many sticky situations and allowed him to make plays most other NFL quarterbacks cannot. Bagent, respectfully, does not have those same attributes. It’s possible Chicago’s offense will still be serviceable with him at the helm, but Sunday feels like it marked the beginning of the end for this season. Again, Williams’ severity of injury hasn’t been revealed, as of this writing. If it turns out he’ll only be out for a few weeks, it’s entirely possible they stay afloat in the meantime and could still make the playoffs. I hope I’m wrong, but it looked serious. Today’s MRIs will tell a lot about not only Williams’ outlook on the season, but the Bears’ season as a whole.

Making the task even more daunting for the Bears is the likely absence of starting quarterback Caleb Williams, who left today’s game with a hamstring injury. One week after dropping a record-setting 59 points in the season opener, the Bears could muster only 3 lousy points today at sloppy Soldier Field in a 9-3 loss to the Minnesota Vikings. title: Chicago Bears Drop Home Opener to Vikings in Downpour and Lose Caleb Williams to Injury
summary: Hello…Chicago Bears Fans. This is my first post-game writeup, as the Dean of WCG had to step in for me last week as I was stuck abroad in tournament baseball hell. Speaking of hell, let’s get to our postgame, shall we? FIRST QUARTER Vikings take the ball to start the game. They drive down as […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Head coach Kevin O'Connell of the Minnesota Vikings and Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears shake hands after the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello…Chicago Bears Fans. This is my first post-game writeup, as the Dean of WCG had to step in for me last week as I was stuck abroad in tournament baseball hell. Speaking of hell, let’s get to our postgame, shall we? FIRST QUARTER Vikings take the ball to start the game. They drive down as the Bears seem unable to put pressure on Carson Wentz. Tyrique Stephenson had good coverage on the big pass play to JJ down the sideline but didn’t get his head turned around, and JJ makes the catch. The Vikings drive into the red zone, and we get the first “downpour” effect on the game – and it goes against the Bears (it’s going to be a theme), as Devin Bush has an easy interception that he drops – three times – due to the rain. On the Bears’ first drive of the first half, we see what will remain a theme – operational errors that put the Bears behind down and distance. That said, Caleb does one of his Houdini impressions as he somehow escapes a massive yardage sack and turns it into a four-yard gain. Santos for the field goal – which is almost blocked from the edge (we will come back to that) – and it is a 3-3 tie. On the Vikings’ ensuing possession, we get the one and only rain event that will go for the Bears in this game, as the Viking center snaps the ball well over Wentz’s head – Wentz goes back and covers within the 10-yard line, and the Vikings will punt from the shadow of their own end zone. The Bears get the ball, and nothing goes well – we have a terrible sequence of plays. We are gifted an offside that moves the ball to 3rd and 7 (manageable), and instead of calling a timeout, we take a delay of game – back to 3rd and 12. Calebel then scrambles to his right and just chucks the ball up – nowhere close to Rome, the intended receiver – and Byron Murphy intercepts it. The interception does work a bit like a punt, as the Vikings have it on their own 35-yard line. Bears manage to hold – while the Vikings pick up the Bears’ blitz, Wentz misses Jordan Addison on a fade route badly. Muhammad was in coverage. SECOND QUARTER So far this game, the defense has been particularly unimpressive. For a defense predicated on penetration, they mostly do not get penetration – not on run fits – and not on passing downs. Vikings get a first down on 4th and short with a Wentz sneak. But the very next play Tyrique Stephenson and Dillon Thineman combine to stuff a stretch play for a loss. Bears force a Vikings punt. On the Bears possession, Caleb hits Kalif Raymond for a big hit on the checkdown over the middle. The Bears are in business. Caleb again dumps off to Raymond and the Bears get a “Roughing the Passer” call on the forcible contact to Caleb’s head. The Bears are forced into a 4th and 3, but Caleb floats a beauty of a swing pass out to what should be an easy first down for Swift – but he slips. Luckily, he gets back up and earns the first down. Vikings challenge and the play stands. But penalties are still absolutely killing the Bears. An illegal shift kills a big gain to Colston Loveland, then a holding call puts them further back. The Bears Tax is showing up again in 2026. It was an utterly terrible sequence for the Bears with four straight penalties. We are forced to punt. Flores is winning the battle by quite a bit so far. On the ensuing Vikings drive, we get a coverage sack for Austin Booker, who thankfully finishes the job, and the Bears are able to get off the field. With 40 seconds left the Bears get the ball back and do nothing with it. The half ends with several unblocked defenders sacking Caleb Williams. HALF TIME – THIRD QUARTER The Bears seem to have learned a few things at half as their run game comes uncorked. We get big-time runs by Swift to move the Bears into Vikings territory. Sam Roush, who had previously been penalized and easily had one of the worst rookie games in Bears history today, drops an easy pass from Caleb. But Caleb picks him up with a scramble for first down. And then the Bears remember they have Kyle Monangai. Several big chunk runs from KM put the Bears in the Red Zone. Once there we again see some bad operation plays, which bring up 3rd down and long. But then an amazing play to get the ball to Raymond – who on a dry day would have easily turned that pass into the end zone- gives the Bears a first down and first-and-goal within the one-yard line. But then disaster strikes, perhaps due to the wet conditions, as Swift has the ball punched out and its Vikings ball on the one and the Bears are again denied points. I have to question the personnel decision there – KM hasn’t fumbled since high school, and he is the obvious short-yardage back. Seems like BJ overthought that choice. On the Vikings possession, they manage to get out of the shadow of their own end zone with a few first downs, but ultimately they must punt the ball. On the ensuing Bears possession, we again suffer from operational mistakes (TE off the line uncovering Braxton Jones), and we are forced to punt the ball back to the Vikings. The Vikings get the ball back and rip off their biggest pass of the day for a 22-yard gain to their third tight end. But then on 2nd down Stephenson has blanket coverage, forcing Wentz to dirt the ball. And then on 3rd down, Muhammad blitzes and gets a sack. 4TH QUARTER Bears get the ball back, and it’s another bad penalty by Garret Bradbury. Bradbury wasn’t great in the Panthers game, and he has been downright awful in this game. Five penalties in two games and multiple missed blocks in the run and pass game. Hard to see why Logan Jones remains on the sidelines. Luther Burden makes a big catch that somehow wasn’t pass interference despite the defender being draped over him (it’s going to be a busy “Upon Further Review” this week, Bears fans). Bears end up punting, and Vikes also end up punting – it is a punt fest. On the punt, Raymond clearly has both feet out of bounds and takes a massively late hit that the refs do not call. Mike Periera, the rules analyst, for once calls out the refs and states that it was an obvious penalty that should have been called. The Bears get the ball back, and Caleb hits Swift on a perfectly timed screen, and it goes for a big game. Caleb then completes a big pass to Rome and the Bears are in business. Caleb hits Roush on what should have either been a touchdown or the ball down at the one-yard line, but Roush drops it as he is pancaked. Terrible day for Roush. On the next play we have a great roll-out- might have been a designed run or at least a run-pass- and Caleb is going to easily scamper for the go-ahead touchdown and…wait…oh. Oh no. Caleb is down. Non-contact. He grabs his leg and is screaming. (My note in my journal is just massive capital letters: “OH SH*T!!!”) This…does not look good. Not merely for the game – but for the season. Bagent comes in, and he is unable to get the Bears in the end zone. The Bears set up for a chip shot field goal, and, well, remember how I noted that the Vikings nearly blocked the first field goal from the edge? Well, they get there this time. Blocked field goal. Game is still 6-3 Vikings. Caleb is on the cart with the towel over his head – he is carted off the field. Before he leaves, the towel comes off, and he tries to rally the crowd. I am in shock. Vikings take the ball down the field and kick a field goal. I think. I don’t know. I can barely pay attention to the screen (and I have a big one). The field goal doinks off the upright and in (because of course it does), and it is 9-3 Vikings. Bears take over – good kick return by Raymond sets the Bears up. Bagent leads us down the field – we get into the Red Zone. He makes a pass to the pylon that is nearly intercepted – replay shows the defender was…

title: Bengals News: 2-0 and it feels so good
summary: Wow what a difference a year makes. The Cincinnati Bengals are once again 2-0, and this time there is actual optimism to go along with that. It also hasn’t been Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins carrying the team on their back to the wins. In fact, quite the contrary. The defense has been […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; Cincinnati Bengals defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II (97) celebrates after defeating the Houston Texans at Reliant Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Wow what a difference a year makes. The Cincinnati Bengals are once again 2-0, and this time there is actual optimism to go along with that. It also hasn’t been Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins carrying the team on their back to the wins. In fact, quite the contrary. The defense has been holding up the offense, and that has not gone without notice from the quarterback. “It feels like early on in 2021,” Burrow told Geoff Hobson from Bengals.com . “We’ve got a really good defense, and try to stay in front of the sticks, not turn the ball over, kick field goals, put points on the board, we’re going to win with our defense.” Back in 2021 you had players like linebackers Germaine Pratt and Logan Wilson as well as several secondary guys like Jessie Bates, Chidobe Awuzie and Mike Hilton who could make the defensive plays at the end of the games to seal things out. That is something this team hasn’t really had these past few seasons. It takes so much pressure off an offense when you don’t have to assume the other team is going to score nearly every time. Bengals News Postgame Quick Hits | Bengals Deliver Statement In Bruising Complete Game Win Over Texans It certainly shows how far this defense has come the this team can win only scoring 20 points. It used to be iffy if they scored 30. It shows this team doesn’t have to treat every offensive possession as a do-or-die situation needing to score points. Especially when they are playing such a great defense like that of the Houston Texans. Dexter Lawrence is changing the game plan for the Bengals and their opponents Box score watchers will always be disappointed in Lawrence. But you simply have to understand that this guy absolutely is having a massive impact when he is out there. The Texans had to abandon the run because they simply couldn’t get away from Lawrence or anyone freed up by trying to block him. Not to mention the amount of pressure the defensive line is getting with just four rushers is no mistake. Joe Burrow played ‘incredibly average.’ That could be scary for AFC Some fans may get riled up by this, but truly this offense has not bloomed yet. It mostly looked to not make the big mistake against Houston. That means there should be another level to this team where Burrow and this offense is able to get going and score those big points while also having this defense behind them. NFL News Todd Monken fires back after win over Buccaneers: ‘Browns are the Browns, (expletive) that’ The Cleveland Browns certainly got their first win pretty early this season. They also looked generally good on the day, but we will have to see how long that continues. To have this kind of rant after their recent history with Deshaun Watson at quarterback is kind of comical. Jim Harbaugh ‘not deterred’ by Chargers’ 0-2 start following double-digit loss to Raiders Things are not great for the Los Angeles Chargers. A vast majority of people would have expected them to start 2-0, but instead they sit at 0-2 with a huge hole to dig out of. So much for that Justin Herbert finally having that year their fans have dreamed about. 2026 NFL season, Week 2: What We Learned from Sunday’s games The Bengals did not allow a single touchdown in Week 2 at the Texans, their first game allowing no touchdowns since Week 3, 2022, at the Jets. Cincinnati broke a franchise-long and NFL-long streak of 65 consecutive games allowing at least one touchdown. The Bills now own the longest active streak in the NFL, having allowed at least one touchdown in 47 consecutive games. Just a crazy, crazy stat. It isn’t exactly surprising given the fall off this team had defensively over that time. However, it feels good to have that monkey off their back I’m sure.

title: Zac Taylor applauds the Bengals in “hostile territory”
summary: There were a lot of eyes on the Cincinnati Bengals heading into this week’s matchup with the Houston Texans. With Houston at 0-1, nearly nobody in the national media saw the Bengals leaving Houston with a win, but they got to board the plane as 20-6 winners to take a 2-0 record back home to […]
full_text: Bengals Head Coach Zac Taylor speaks at a press conference at Paycor Stadium on Wednesday September 16, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co There were a lot of eyes on the Cincinnati Bengals heading into this week’s matchup with the Houston Texans. With Houston at 0-1, nearly nobody in the national media saw the Bengals leaving Houston with a win, but they got to board the plane as 20-6 winners to take a 2-0 record back home to Cincinnati. Texans fans certainly showed up, making it a true road environment, and after an uneventful start, the Bengals’ big-play ability finally showed up. After the game, Bengals head coach Zac Taylor praised his team’s performance in “hostile territory.” “We talked last night about what type of team we’re gonna be,” said Taylor. “We’re gonna pack up, take on the road, get off the bus, send a message in hostile territory. Our defense set the tone for that, doing a great job early in the first half, getting them off the field, helping the offense with the field position. The Bengals are now 2-0 for the second-straight season and sitting atop the AFC North ahead of next week’s matchup with the Pittsburgh Steelers. “We couldn’t capitalize on it early,” Taylor said. “Then they had the field goal that we may have influenced the snap. Who knows? And then Dexter (Lawrence) getting that fourth-and-1stop. So he may have impacted two plays right there just from where he’s at. So, really proud of the way that our defense played, all the sack production, all the plays on the ball. Really proud of our team overall.” The offense hasn’t found its rhythm yet, which is something we have seen early in the season many times, but until they do, they finally have a defense that can have their backs.

QB-WR duos in NFL history to reach 50 touchdown connections while both players were under 30: 🏈 Dan Marino — Mark Clayton 🏈 John Hadl — Lance Alworth 🏈 Daunte Culpepper — Randy Moss 🏈 Joe Burrow — Ja’Marr Chase That’s the entire list. — Arye Pulli (@AryePulliNFL) September 21, 2026 Again, Burrow hasn’t been prolific yet. Not ideal going up against the Texans’ defense. But Burrow wasn’t mincing words or backing down earlier this week when he said he was good to go. On Sunday in Houston, Burrow went out and withstood five sacks, delivering a performance that helped the Bengals to a massive road win. We’ve seen Burrow deliver performances like this while banged up and taking several hits in a game. Houston’s defense is ferocious, and they sacked Burrow five times on Sunday. Yet Burrow extended plays, including the second touchdown to Chase and a 16-yard third-down pass to Samaje Perine. Despite back tightness and Houston’s defense, Burrow overcame it all, and the Bengals are now 2-0. title: Bengals take AFC North lead after Ravens’ Week 2 blunder vs. Saints
summary: There’s no denying the AFC North is one of the toughest divisions in football. Three of its four teams entered the 2026 season with legitimate playoff aspirations, and two weeks into the season, there’s already a little separation at the top. For now, at least, the Cincinnati Bengals stand alone. The Bengals moved to 2-0 […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson (8) throws while pressured by New Orleans Saints linebacker Kaden Elliss (55) in the second quarter at M&T Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: James Lang-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect There’s no denying the AFC North is one of the toughest divisions in football. Three of its four teams entered the 2026 season with legitimate playoff aspirations, and two weeks into the season, there’s already a little separation at the top. For now, at least, the Cincinnati Bengals stand alone. The Bengals moved to 2-0 with their Week 2 road win over the Houston Texans, and they got a little help from around the division. Both the Pittsburgh Steelers and Baltimore Ravens lost on Sunday, leaving Cincinnati as the AFC North’s only undefeated team. Pittsburgh wasn’t favored against New England, but the Steelers didn’t put up much of a fight, falling to the Patriots 20-3 in Foxborough. The loss dropped them to 1-1. Things were a little more painful for Baltimore, who entered Week 2 as one of the biggest favorites in the entire NFL. Almost no one saw the Saints coming into Baltimore and beating the Ravens, but that’s why the games aren’t played on paper. The Ravens took a 17-9 lead into the fourth quarter against the Saints before watching it disappear. New Orleans scored two touchdowns in the final quarter, including a successful two-point conversion, to hand Baltimore a 24-17 loss and drop the Ravens to 1-1 as well. That leaves the Bengals sitting at 2-0 with sole possession of first place in the AFC North. The Browns join Pittsburgh and Baltimore at 1-1 after beating the Buccaneers 23-19 in Tampa Bay, where the game was interrupted by a weather delay. Obviously, there’s an absurd amount of football left to play. Nobody wins a division in September, and the Bengals know better than most how quickly things can change over the course of an NFL season. But after two weeks, they’ve done exactly what contenders are supposed to do: win their games and take advantage when the teams around them stumble. For the first time this season, the rest of the AFC North is chasing Cincinnati.

title: Browns Week 2 win: Building blocks moving forward
summary: The Cleveland Browns Week 1 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars was extremely disappointing for the players and fans alike. There weren’t many positive moments to build on, making it difficult to find much hope for the season. After the Browns’ Week 2 win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, some of that hope and optimism have […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Tampa, Florida, USA; Cleveland Browns wide receiver Denzel Boston (12) celebrates scoring a touchdown with quarterback Deshaun Watson (4) and head coach Todd Monken during the second half against the Cleveland Browns at Raymond James Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kim Klement Neitzel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Cleveland Browns Week 1 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars was extremely disappointing for the players and fans alike. There weren’t many positive moments to build on, making it difficult to find much hope for the season. After the Browns’ Week 2 win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers , some of that hope and optimism have been restored. In this 23-19 win, what are the most important things the team should try to build on to keep the momentum going into Week 3? Denzel Boston got heavily involved in the offense against the Buccaneers, finishing with five receptions for 95 yards and one touchdown. There was a lot of excitement about the rookie receiver going into this season. His Week 1 performance, two receptions for 59 yards and a touchdown, flew somewhat under the radar following the tough loss to the Jaguars. With the win over Tampa Bay, there is a lot more to get excited about with Boston. Deshaun Watson was efficient, with only 6 incompletions, and rushing for 22 yards. On the other side of the ball, the defense appeared to find its footing in Week 2 after a frustrating performance the previous week. They made life difficult for Baker Mayfield , recording three sacks, an interception, and three passes defended. While it wasn’t perfect, the unit looked far more cohesive and played with greater purpose compared to the Week 1 performance. They will have an opportunity to build on this performance in Week 3 against the Carolina Panthers, who are coming off of a dominant 34-3 win against the Atlanta Falcons. Let me know what you think in the comments – What are the most important moments for the Browns to build on from this Week 3 win?

full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Mike Tomlin, NBC Sunday Night Football analyst, looks on prior to the game between the Indianapolis Colts and the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Mike Tomlin left the Pittsburgh Steelers after 19 seasons as their head coach, and joined the Football Night in America crew on NBC as analyst. Cleveland Browns fans are used to a boatload of battles against him, but how did he play a factor in the Cleveland Browns’ 23-19 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers? Have a listen to this from Todd Monken’s postgame press conference: Todd Monken: Browns are gonna Browns. F— that! pic.twitter.com/loDcRzzF9T — Daniel Oyefusi (@DanielOyefusi) September 20, 2026 Was was Monken referring to? At first, it made me think of when former Steelers WR JuJu Smith-Schuster said ‘The Browns is the Browns’ back in 2021, prior to a playoff match. What I didn’t realize is that last week, after the Browns’ loss to the Jaguars, Tomlin made a reference to it on national television. As a highlight of QB Deshaun Watson being picked off by the Jaguars played, Tomlin quoted his ‘friend’ Smith-Schuster and repeated his infamous quote. Apparently, Monken must have used that quote as bulletin board material in the Browns locker room this week, and they responded. On Sunday evening, Tomlin and the NBC crew played a recap of both quotes, with Tomlin being happy that he could provide bulletin board material in his new role without consequence: Mike Tomlin last week: "The Browns is the Browns" Browns HC Todd Monken: "Browns are gonna Browns. F— that!" Tomlin today: "I love my new role. That's what I have to say for myself. You know why? Because I can provide bulletin board material with no personal consequence"… — Oh No He Didn't (@ohnohedidnt24) September 21, 2026 Can someone say that quote every week? For some reason, it’s the one thing that seems to actually motivate this club toward a win.

full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Devin Lloyd #55 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates with teammates after an interception against the Atlanta Falcons during the fourth quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns opened as 2.5-point underdogs for their home opener against the Carolina Panthers ahead of their Week 3 match-up, according to FanDuel Sportsbook . The over/under on the game is 40.5. The Browns (1-1) are coming off of a 23-19 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers . It was obviously a way better performance than their first game. The defense came to play, and seemed to show more man defense — although it was a zone drop by CB Myles Harden that led to an interception. And then, QB Deshaun Watson played perhaps his best game as a member of the Browns, including a very solid second half with two touchdown drives. Before the game, it seemed like a foregone conclusion that QB Shedeur Sanders was about to start the opener against the Panthers. But now, Watson remains the guy and gets credit for a solid effort. The Panthers (1-1) blew out the Atlanta Falcons 34-3, a week after they lost a shootout to the Bears 59-37. It’s an unusual team to have a pulse on right now, because statistically, they’re essentially the hottest offense in football. But they also had a horrible defensive effort against the Bears, but a great one against one of the worst offensive teams in the NFL. For both teams having .500 records, and Cleveland being at home, it’s a marginal surprise that the Browns aren’t the slight favorites. Maybe Vegas doesn’t know what to think of Watson and the Browns looking good after that abomination in Week 1. The over/under for the game is 40.5. What odds would you take if you were placing a bet?
