title: Packers Week 2: Stats from Green Bay’s victory over the Jets
summary: Every week, we’re digging into some stats from the Green Bay Packers game by using SumerLive, a new product from SumerSports that tracks a bunch of stats in real time. Last week we got a loss. This week we got an overtime win. So that’s fun. Offense This week saw an uptick in usage of […]
full_text: (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) Every week, we’re digging into some stats from the Green Bay Packers game by using SumerLive , a new product from SumerSports that tracks a bunch of stats in real time. Last week we got a loss. This week we got an overtime win. So that’s fun. Offense This week saw an uptick in usage of 11 personnel. This week, the Packers were in 11 personnel on 55.1% of their snaps, up from 47.8% last week. They were in 12 personnel 30.6% of the time, 13 personnel 14.3% of the time and “Other” 2% of the time (I’d say that’s likely their package with an extra o-lineman, but I’ll know a little better when I finish my charting). Just as a refresher, personnel tells you who is on the field. The first number is the number of running backs, the second number is the number of tight ends, and the number of wide receivers is assumed based on there being 5 available skill players. So 11 personnel would be 1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR. In the run game, the Packers leaned heavy in gap scheme runs this week. A third of their runs were in the Zone family (11.1% inside zone, 22.2% wide zone), while the rest was a mix of gap/power scheme. Nothing they ran was particularly effective. On the day, they had 18 attempts for 63 yards (55 of those yards coming after contact) for -0.48 EPA per Play. Their best performance of the day was on Inside Zone runs, in which they had a -0.06 EPA per Play. Their power run game was bad from an efficiency standpoint (-0.76 EPA per Play), but it worked really well from a Success Rate perspective (60% Success Rate). Not particularly efficient, but it kept them ahead of the chains. Just like last week, we got a pretty nice run/pass ratio from the Packers. They passed on 64% of their offensive snaps this week, after passing on 68.7% last week. After an offseason of begging for LaFleur to let Love loose a bit more, it looks like they’re starting this season by leaning into the passing game more than we had previously seen. I’m taking that as a positive sign. The pass game wasn’t particularly good (-0.17 EPA per Play, 34.4% Success Rate), but I like that they’re looking to push it. Between the rain and Love’s numb fingers, it wasn’t quite as smooth in the passing game as I would have liked, but I’ve seen enough from Love to believe he’ll have a bounce-back. The more encouraging thing from the passing game is that protection held up better this week than it did against the Vikings in Week 1. This week, the Jets blitzed on 28.13% of snaps (0.3% above the NFL average), but had a pressure rate of 31.25% (7.86% below NFL average). From his pass performance by zone chart, Love kept more to the short-to-intermediate portion of the field this week. We just talked about the offense being more pass-heavy this week, but one area they were not was on 1st and 10. On that down, they had a run rate of 64%. Were they good at it? Dear Reader, they were not! They had an EPA per Play of -0.60 and Success Rate of 29%. They weren’t exactly burning down the house when passing on 1st & 10 (-0.07 EPA per Play, 33% Success Rate), but it was an improvement over the run game. Their 1st & 10 run rate in Week 1 was 48%, so I’m curious to see if this run-heavy approach on 1st & 10 is a product of a very rainy afternoon or whether that’s going to be their approach going forward. Please let this run-heavy approach on 1st & 10 just be a blip. Matthew Golden had himself a nice day. He had 4 catches (on 6 targets) for 58 yards, good for +1.27 EPA per Reception. He had an ADOT (Average Depth of Target) of 13.33 yards, and averaged 8 yards after the catch. His YAC ability keeps showing up, and I’ve really been enjoying watching him with the ball in his hands. Four of his targets came when he was aligned wide (+1.2 EPA per Reception) and two of his targets came from the slot (+1.48 EPA per Reception). The play that got the Packers into chip-shot field goal range saw Golden aligned outside. this is really good stuff. https://t.co/pMiTBnCpke pic.twitter.com/v3CmG7xxYR — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) September 20, 2026 Defense Last week, the Packers were pretty balanced in terms of defensive personnel used (49.2% Base, 49.2% Nickel, 1.6% Dime). This week they leaned much heavier into Nickel. They used Nickel personnel on 72.2% of their defensive snaps, 11.02% above the NFL average. That likely is a response to the Jets personnel (69.4% 11 personnel), but it’s something to monitor going forward. In terms of their coverage menu, the Packers were predominantly in Zone coverage (87%) zone. Here is their breakdown of zone coverages: Cover 3: 32.6% Cover 4: 32.6% Cover 2: 13% Cover 6: 8.7% The rest was either Cover 1 (10.9%) or Cover 0 (2.2%). As expected, a lot of stuff based in the Quarters family. The Packers had a blitz rate of 34.69% this week, 6.87% above the NFL average. There was a lot of talk about Gannon’s lack of blitzing during his time as a defensive coordinator, but we’ve seen him more willing to blitz for his first two weeks in Green Bay. He has been actively looking for ways to use his best players to impact the game, and that’s been extremely encouraging so far. Lukas Van Ness had himself a day , man. On the day, he had 5 solo tackles, 5 assisted tackles and 3 tackles for loss (including 1.5 sacks). As a pass rusher, he had a 23.3% pressure rate, with an average time to pressure of 2.6 seconds. His 3 tackles for loss has him tied for the Week 2 lead in that category with Will Anderson, Elijah Ponder and Nick Herbig. His 7 pressures has him tied for 4th this week and his 3 stuffed runs has him tied with Will Anderson for the lead in week 2. Lukas Van Ness MAKING PLAYS in OT 💪 GBvsNYJ on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Z3hFEusKVF — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 Dani Dennis-Sutton also had a pretty nice day. He played 40% of the Packers defensive snaps and, while the box score numbers aren’t eye-popping (2 solo tackles, 4 assisted tackles) some of the underlying numbers are very good. He had a 29.4% pressure rate and an average time to pressure of 2.4 seconds. That pressure rate was good for 4th overall in week 2 among players who played at least 25 snaps. He has looked really impressive so far this season. Albums listened to: beabadoobee – Pylon ; Orville Peck – Mule

title: Skyy Moore had more yards than all other Packers combined vs. the Jets
summary: You’re going to see some insane stats from the Green Bay Packers win over the New York Jets, because they managed to win the game while having a shaky offense, getting no turnovers and also being penalized heavily. On paper, they never should have won that game. One of the major factors in why they […]
full_text: (Photo by Tyler Schank/Clarkson Creative/Getty Images) | Getty Images You’re going to see some insane stats from the Green Bay Packers win over the New York Jets , because they managed to win the game while having a shaky offense, getting no turnovers and also being penalized heavily. On paper, they never should have won that game. One of the major factors in why they were able to survive that overtime game with a win was receiver Skyy Moore. Moore had four kick returns for 116 yards (29.0 average, long of 43), four punt returns for 92 yards (23.0 average, long of 63) and also added two receptions for six yards on offense. Perspective: the Packers’ longest kick return last year was 36 yards, while their longest punt return was 20 yards. For what it’s worth, Moore was also the offensive substitute for Jayden Reed, who left on a backboard , as the team’s slot receiver on Sunday. In total, Moore had 214 total yards (even with just six yards of total offense), while the rest of the Packers combined had 193 yards on the day. You can’t understate how much Green Bay needed Moore to move the football into scoring range in Week 2. There’s no chance they would have won against the Jets if they hadn’t gotten an all-time returner performance from Moore. Previously, I was a little skeptical that Moore would hold down the kick returner job (I thought he was for sure going to be the punt returner, though) once second-year third-rounder Savion Williams returned from the injured reserve, potentially as early as Week 5, but it’s going to be impossible to take him off the field now. For what it’s worth, Moore didn’t return kicks last week (Bo Melton and Kaleb Johnson got kicked to), and he had two punts for 17 yards against the Minnesota Vikings. It will be interesting to see if the Packers lean out of three-receiver sets in favor of two-receiver sets, though, as Green Bay’s receiver rotation has been very rigid this season. The X position has only been played by Matthew Golden and Melton, the Z position has only been played by Christian Watson, Williams (IR) and J. Michael Sturdivant and the slot position has only been played by Reed and Moore, dating back to the preseason. Maybe the team will adjust some of that, allowing a player like Melton or Sturdivant to play some slot reps moving forward, which would allow Moore’s legs to be fresh for returns. At the moment, there is no timetable for when Reed will be back on the grass after his injury on Sunday.

title: Packers vs. Falcons odds: Opening lines for Week 3 matchup
summary: Two games into the 2026 season, the Green Bay Packers find themselves with a 1-1 record, having just mounted a come-from-behind overtime victory over the New York Jets in week two. That game saw the Packers fail to cover the 3.5-point spread, however, as they elected to kick a field goal after holding the Jets […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Cooper Rush #13 of the Atlanta Falcons throws a pass against the Pittsburgh Steelers during the first quarter of the game at Acrisure Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Two games into the 2026 season, the Green Bay Packers find themselves with a 1-1 record, having just mounted a come-from-behind overtime victory over the New York Jets in week two. That game saw the Packers fail to cover the 3.5-point spread, however, as they elected to kick a field goal after holding the Jets scoreless in New York’s overtime possession rather than trying to punch the football into the end zone. That sends the Packers into Week 3 0-2 against the spread, though they started the season with back-to-back road games. The Packers’ home opener finally arrives in Week 3, and it will take place on Thursday Night Football as they host the 0-2 Atlanta Falcons. The Falcons have started Cooper Rush at quarterback in each of their first two games, thanks to injuries to Michael Penix, Jr. and Tua Tagavailoa, and they have scored just 16 total points over their first eight quarters of football this season. Atlanta lost their opener 20-13 to the Pittsburgh Steelers, then got absolutely trounced by the Carolina Panthers on Sunday in Week 2, losing 34-3. With all of those factors combined — along with injuries to Jayden Reed and Zach Bako-Bewele for Green Bay — the Packers open up this week being favored by nearly a touchdown. According to FanDuel Sportsbook , Green Bay is favored by 6.5 points after the conclusion of most of Week 2’s games. Although the first Thursday Night Football game of the year, Week 2’s matchup between the Bills and Lions, was a shootout, these games are often low-scoring affairs. The books are expecting a fairly low point total in this one as well, with 44.5 set as the line for total points. The Packers were last favored by a number that high back in Week 13 of last year, which was also the last game they had won prior to their win over the Jets on Sunday. That game saw the Packers as 6.5-point favorites over the Chicago Bears at home, and they held on to win that game 28-21, just barely covering the spread. Atlanta and Green Bay last faced off in Week 2 of the 2023 season at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. That game, which was Jordan Love’s second start as the Packers’ full-time starting quarterback, feels all too familiar — the Packers blew a 24-12 lead that they held early in the fourth quarter, eventually falling 25-24. Atlanta was favored by three points heading into that game, giving the Packers the cover, but Green Bay was held to just 224 yards of total offense and went three-and-out four times in the game. title: Packers Winners and Losers: Week 2 vs. the Jets
summary: Folks, the Green Bay Packers have finally won a game in the year 2026. After six straight losses dating back to December of last year, the Packers traveled to New Jersey to face off against the New York Jets, and gave us the ugliest win I’ve ever seen. The game started off on an extremely […]
full_text: (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) | Getty Images Folks, the Green Bay Packers have finally won a game in the year 2026. After six straight losses dating back to December of last year, the Packers traveled to New Jersey to face off against the New York Jets, and gave us the ugliest win I’ve ever seen. The game started off on an extremely rough note, with a scary neck injury suffered by WR Jayden Reed which saw him transported to a local hospital. Not long after, the team’s best offensive lineman, RT Zach Bako-Bewele, went down with a potentially long-term leg injury. The offense looked dejected on every drive, but the defense kept them in it until the very end. The Packers clearly aren’t trying to break the scoring record (even though I think they scored more than 3 against the Vikings? Someone confirm?), but they got the job done with 20 points this week. Let’s explore the good and bad from the team’s 20-17 win in OT. Winner: Trey Smack With the other kicker who will not be named, I’m not sure the Packers win this game. The Packers rookie was perfect today, nailing both of his XP attempts, as well as a 34 yard FG, and the game-winning 26-yarder. He had one job. He did it. FOR THE WIN! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/6SaV3LwqmI — Green Bay Packers (@packers) September 20, 2026 Winner: Javon Bullard The Packers safety turned in one of the better games of his career on Sunday. He was there at the point of catch to prevent some big plays, and broke up a couple of passes as well. He nearly had a pick, a play I’m sure he’d love to get back, but overall, he helped limit any major damage from the Jets’ passing game. Bullard finished the game with 7 tackles (2 TFL), and 2 PDs. Others probably won’t agree, but I’m very unmoved by the taunting penalty he was given in the first quarter—I think most taunting penalties are very silly, and that Jets drive ended with a punt anyways. No harm, one (1) foul. Packers get a flag for taunting. pic.twitter.com/i1s2UPN3BH — Rate the Refs (@Rate_the_Refs) September 20, 2026 Winner: Lukas Van Ness The former first round pick had the game of his LIFE on Sunday, and it was a huge reason for the team’s win. With Micah Parsons set to miss at least a few more weeks, fans have been hoping and praying someone will step in so his loss isn’t so deeply felt. Van Ness has been doing a stellar job so far. Lukas Van Ness generated a career-high nine pressures against the Jets in Week 2, recording five in under 2.5 seconds, tied for the third-most by a Packers defender since 2020. #GBvsNYJ | #GoPackGo pic.twitter.com/A3avmr0stl — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) September 20, 2026 The edge rusher had stop after stop today, and when he wasn’t making tackles, he was making Jets QB Geno Smith run for his life. One of his biggest plays of the day came in OT, as the Jets were dealing with 2nd and 16, when Van Ness led a host of defenders into a game-changing sack. Lukas Van Ness MAKING PLAYS in OT 💪 GBvsNYJ on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Z3hFEusKVF — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 He put it all out there today, the Packers are reaping the benefits. Van Ness tied with Evan Williams for a team-high 10 tackles (3 TFL), 1.5 sacks, and 4 QB hits. He also generated a career-high 9 pressures. Baby’s First Touchdown: MarShawn Lloyd Welcome to the club, MarShawn. FIRST CAREER TOUCHDOWN FOR MarSHAWN LLOYD! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/ucVN1sqt2Y — Green Bay Packers (@packers) September 20, 2026 Loser: *gestures wildly* I don’t think the Green Bay Packers are a good football team. The offensive line puts QB Jordan Love at risk of injury each time the ball is snapped. Losing Zach Bako-Bewele long-term makes an already-bad line even worse. There’s no feasible way to play a winning season like this—the offense is not a threat to anyone they play, until the line improves. The line will not magically improve. With a line as detrimental as Green Bay’s, Matt LaFleur’s abilities as a play caller are extremely limited, and I’m left wondering what the Packers offense can even do at this point to continue to win games. The organization has put together an extremely talented young roster, except perhaps where it matters most. Because of the lack of reliable bodies on the line, Jordan Love and Co. are suddenly unable to make any mistakes without the team suffering some disastrous consequences. I’m not done with Matt LaFleur! The play calling! I understand things are a mess up front, but it seems like every play is still the wrong one. When games are close or tied, and the Packers have the opportunity to score a dagger of a touchdown, LaFleur always seems to play for the tie, or for the FG. There’s no punch. Case in point: one of the Packers’ final drives of the game, when the team was down by 3. With under 5 minutes to play, WR Skyy Moore returned a punt 63 yards, an unheard of feat in Green Bay. The Packers offense was already on the Jets 19-yard line—a gift to an offense who struggled all game to move the ball past their first set of downs. The call on 1st and 10? A Chris Brooks run, good for 4 yards. The call on 2nd and 6? A Chris Brooks run, for a loss of a yard. The drive would end in a FG, and overtime began shortly thereafter. Will Matt LaFleur punch someone in the mouth already? Good news everyone: we get to do this all over again in just four short days, as the Packers finally play their home opener against the 0-2 Atlanta Falcons on Thursday Night Football at 7:15 PM local time. Can the team claw their way to a 2-1 record during a short week? *fart noise*
author: Sam Kallien

title: How the Packers can move forward on the offensive line
summary: You’re going to hear a lot about injuries and numbers on the offensive line for the Green Bay Packers this week. Not only did all eight of the Packers’ game-day active players at the position get in against the New York Jets in Green Bay’s unlikely (considering the context) win on Sunday, but three of […]
full_text: (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images You’re going to hear a lot about injuries and numbers on the offensive line for the Green Bay Packers this week. Not only did all eight of the Packers’ game-day active players at the position get in against the New York Jets in Green Bay’s unlikely ( considering the context ) win on Sunday, but three of those players, Zach Bako-Bewele, Aaron Banks and Donovan Jennings, all left with injuries. We don’t know the extent of the Banks (toe, was previously dealing with knee tendinitis) or Jennings (hand) injuries, but head coach Matt LaFleur did say that Bako-Bewele, who was limited in practice coming into this game because of his recovery from a patellar tendon surgery, was going to miss some games in his post-game presser . For what it’s worth, Bako-Bewele left the game in an air cast, which usually means that a player has either a bone injury, a break and/or a dislocation. Who starts for Green Bay? Post-Bako-Bewele, the Packers’ preferred offensive line is : Jordan Morgan (left tackle), Banks (left guard), Sean Rhyan (center), Jacob Monk (right guard) and Anthony Belton (right tackle). Obviously, though, Banks (and his replacement, Jennings) and his status are up in the air. If both Banks and Jennings are out, rookie fifth-round pick Jager Burton, who got his first snaps in the regular season in Week 2, would be the next man up at left guard. How do they account for injuries? Shoutout to Cheesehead_In_Paradise, who brought up the Packers’ options at the position in The Feed . I was actually going to reply to his post, but my answer was going to be long, so I figured I should just make it into a full post. Alright, so what happens if Green Bay is incredibly injured up front? First of all, I want to state that we don’t know the situation there, besides ZBB. We’ll learn more on Monday, when the Packers have to release their first injury report of the week (Green Bay plays on Thursday Night Football in Week 3). With that being said, if only one of Banks/Jennings is out (along with ZBB), the Packers can sort of handle these injuries with their 53-man roster. People don’t want to hear about internal options, but that’s what’s most likely to happen. Even though the line was so banged up that tight end Tucker Kraft almost had to move to offensive tackle in-game, it needs to be said that the only two healthy scratches (NFL teams can only carry 48 players into game action) from Week 2 for Green Bay were both offensive linemen: tackle/guard/center John Williams and tackle/guard Travis Glover . The Packers like these players enough that they didn’t get rid of them at the cutdown deadline to add other players from around the league (or keep other internal talent). Essentially, the team has “extras” on the offensive line, and really only the offensive line right now. The Packers have numbers – if one of Banks/Jennings can go So if the injury situation means that ZBB and one of Banks/Jennings are out, the Packers should be fine (from a numbers perspective) to have a line of: Morgan (LT), Banks/Jennings (LG, as long as one is healthy), Rhyan (C), Monk (RG), Belton (RT), Burton (backup), Williams (backup) and Glover (backup). Eight healthy offensive linemen are basically par for the course in the NFL. If you want to get really specific about the league’s rules about the 48-man roster, it’s really a 47-man game-day roster (this includes practice squad additions; practice squad additions just mean you have to scratch another 53-man roster member for a game) with an exemption for the 48th roster spot. The way it’s worded in the NFL’s rules, you only get that 48th player if that player is an offensive lineman. Because of that rule, it’s logical to go into games with either six offensive linemen (on a 47-man gameday roster) or eight offensive linemen (on a 48-man gameday roster). There’s no reason to just keep seven players at the position, since it would mean that a team would be passing up a free exemption for a 48th man/8th offensive lineman. As long as one of Bank or Jennings can go, the Packers’ 53-man roster holds up, because they were sort of “oversigned” at the position already. If Bako-Bewele, Banks and Jennings can’t go, they need to make a move Where the situation gets tricky is if all three of Bako-Bewele, Banks and Jennings aren’t able to play on the quick turnaround on Thursday. If that’s the case, the roster is at just seven healthy offensive linemen, including the two players who were scratched today. That’s firmly in the no-no zone, because of the NFL’s eighth offensive lineman exemption on game days (to bring a 47-man roster to 48). Personally, I think the Packers like a couple of their internal options on the practice squad, and it would take five total injuries for that new “eighth” lineman to get on the grass (including ZBB, Banks and Jennings). It’s unlikely that we’ll ever see that player on anything other than special teams on field goal protection. With that being said, here are the internal options for Green Bay: Dalton Cooper Josh Gesky Dillon Wade Cordell Volson Cooper is a second-year player who the Packers have had their eyes on for a while, as they brought him on a pre-draft visit but were unable to sign him in 2025 as a post-draft free agent (likely because the Kansas City Chiefs were willing to give him $259,000 in guarantees on his UDFA deal). When Cooper was cut from the Chiefs last August at the cutdown deadline, Green Bay quickly signed Cooper to the practice squad, where he remained for the entire 2025 season. Both Gesky and Wade were big free agent signings for the Packers this draft class. Both went undrafted, despite getting some draft buzz, and received $215,000 in guarantees to sign as UDFAs. For perspective, that was only bested by edge defender Nyjalik Kelly’s $262,500 in guarantees (a franchise record for a UDFA). $215,000 in guarantees is also how much Green Bay paid receiver J. Michael Sturdivant, who made the Packers’ 53-man roster. For perspective, defensive tackle Nazir Stackhouse got $165,000 in guarantees last year, the most of any Green Bay UDFA in 2025, and only two other Packers got more than $45,000 in guarantees (linebacker Jamon Johnson and Johnathan Baldwin — who got $115,000 guaranteed). Usually, the guarantees tell us how interested the Packers are in on UDFAs. Stackhouse made the team in 2025, but was waived this year and claimed by the Tennessee Titans at the cutdown deadline. He probably would have been on Green Bay’s practice squad, had he passed through waivers. Johnson and Baldwin both were called up for games in 2025, but Johnson was waived with an injury designation this offseason and Baldwin, who at the time was working in as the team’s number two option in the slot in camp, suffered a season-ending knee injury this summer. For added perspective, Kelly, Sturdivant, Gesky and Wade are the only UDFAs from Green Bay’s initial 2026 class who remain on the roster right now. They were paid an average of $226,875 in guaranteed money when they signed. The other six UDFAs who were initially signed by the Packers are not even on the practice squad anymore, and they averaged guarantees of $37,500. In short, the Packers have three young UDFAs who got paid a lot of guaranteed money (for UDFAs), and they are probably the best bets to be called up in case of three linemen being out against the Falcons, especially since it’s a short week. The other internal option is Volson, who was signed to the practice squad last week after failing to make the Tennessee Titans’ roster after signing a one-year, $3.2 million contract this offseason that included $2 million in guarantees. He obviously has some pedigree, as he was drafted in the fourth round in 2022 and has started 48 games, but he earned a 29.1 grade from Pro Football Focus in true pass-protection snaps in 2024 with the Cincinnati Bengals (Volson missed the entire 2025 regular season with a shoulder injury that…

title: Jordan Love says his throwing hand went numb vs. the New York Jets
summary: During the broadcast, CBS’ team highlighted that Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love was favoring his throwing hand, shaking it out and had it worked on while he was on the sideline. In his post-game press conference, Love stated that the issue actually started with a hit to his elbow. On one of the Packers’ […]
full_text: (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images During the broadcast, CBS’ team highlighted that Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love was favoring his throwing hand, shaking it out and had it worked on while he was on the sideline. In his post-game press conference, Love stated that the issue actually started with a hit to his elbow. On one of the Packers’ five (that’s right, five) fumbles of the day, Love took a shot to the elbow, which apparently caused his hand to go numb. After the hit, he got it checked out on the sideline. Love was able to push through the injury and had a 16-of-29 for 145 yards and two touchdowns performance on the game, good for a passer rating of 91.9. It wasn’t his best game that he’s ever played, but it wasn’t a disaster-class effort, either. Those incompletions also came with several dropped balls, as each side of the game struggled with the wet conditions in MetLife Stadium. The fact that Love was able to push through the final whistle in overtime probably means that Love will be able to suit up against the Atlanta Falcons, but keep an eye on his progression on the injury report next week. Green Bay will begin releasing injury reports on Monday, as their matchup against Atlanta will be a Thursday Night Football contest. Love’s backup is Tyrod Taylor, who was signed by the Packers to a one-year deal this offseason. Taylor has a 29-31-1 record as a starter over his career and has played in 100 total games. The third quarterback in Green Bay, who would be the second-string option if Love isn’t ready to go, is Kedon Slovis, a practice squad player who was signed by the team from the Arizona Cardinals after the cutdown deadline.

title: Texans vs. Colts odds: Opening lines for Week 3 matchup
summary: The Houston Texans’ 20-6 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals stung in a way that is a bit rattling to those that were hoping for a breakthrough season. It’s still a bit early, but maybe the Texans’ 0-2 start has shaken your faith in this team and their championship ambitions. They’ve played poorly enough to warrant […]
full_text: The Houston Texans’ 20-6 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals stung in a way that is a bit rattling to those that were hoping for a breakthrough season. It’s still a bit early, but maybe the Texans’ 0-2 start has shaken your faith in this team and their championship ambitions. They’ve played poorly enough to warrant this doubt, but one of the great things about the NFL is that they’re one good game away from turning the page on this rough start. Next week, the Texans will play their first road game when they travel up north to play the 0-2 Indianapolis Colts in an early divisional bout to determine who’s racing to the bottom of the AFC faster. It’s an early-season battle between the AFC South’s disturbing cousins, and FanDuel has got their opening odds for the game: What may have been seen as an easier game for Houston before the season started has now become far more intimidating, especially after Indy’s overtime loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. FanDuel is narrowly favoring the Texans to win over the Colts in this game, meaning the Texans haven’t quite returned to the underdog status that they occupied for the majority of last season. They certainly aren’t the world-beaters many expected of them coming into 2026, and FanDuel has taken note of the disappointing results, but despite it all, they are still favored in this game. THE SPREAD: TEXANS -2.5 Since the Texans are -2.5, FanDuel is expecting the Texans to win, but still expects the game to be close. That’s encouraging for Houston, and historically, this era of the Texans have been dominant against the Colts. They swept the Colts last year, and in his career, Texans QB CJ Stroud is 5-1 against Indianapolis, his only loss coming in 2023. This season, Stroud has been one of the few bright spots on the team thus far, and I expect him to continue his dominance over the Colts and their suspect pass-defense. Jonathan Taylor will likely feast on the Texans, but Houston’s offense should be able to maintain a lead on Indianapolis. Colts WR Pierce’s status for Week 3 following the team’s loss to the Chiefs Sunday night is in serious doubt, so I think the Texans will rebound and get this season back on track. I’m taking the spread here! Watch out! C.J. Stroud vs. the Bengals today via @NextGenStats & @SumerSports : 30/55 353 Passing Yards 29 Rushing Yards -0.08 EPA/Play 42.6% Success Rate Stroud threw the ball very well in a game where Houston did not have a successful run from an RB and had multiple opportunities from… pic.twitter.com/6hLXfJvASI — Jacob Barzilla (@JacobBarzilla) September 21, 2026 THE MONEY LINE: Texans -146 Between these two admittedly sloppy and injured squads, the Texans are narrowly favored. If you were to bet $14.60 on the Texans winning, you’d net $10.00 in return. After that Bengals game, I don’t blame you if you’re against betting on the Texans to win any game, but last time the Texans played the Colts, they won in a shootout in the 2025 season finale 38-30 on just 339 total yards – 35 less than they gained against the Bengals yesterday. That Texans win came from the efforts of a lot of backup players that Houston plugged into the game following the first half – which may bode well considering the amount of backups that will be playing next week’s game due to Houston’s alarming number of injuries. KPRC2’s Aaron Wilson reported that it’s possible both WR Nico Collins and RG Ed Ingram miss two games following their respective hamstring and groin injuries, so Houston’s depth at those positions will be tested yet again. #Texans Nico Collins has a Grade 1 hamstring injury, per league sources. Status for next week vs. #Colts still being determined. Replacing Collins is a committee approach. Ed Ingram, out vs. #Bengals and expected to miss at least two games, per sources. Next man up for Ingram:… https://t.co/hYebjZHCKx — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) September 18, 2026 Still, Houston’s recent history of success against Indianapolis gives me optimism despite the critical injuries. Their history against the Colts must be influencing FanDuel since Houston is still favored despite all of their warts. They should have at least a moderately improved rushing attack against the Colts, and that should grant the Texans a far more complimentary offense – so give me the Texans to win it! OVER/UNDER: 44.5 Honestly, as much as I wish for the over to occur, I expect this game to actually stay below 44.5 total points. Both the Texans and Colts have had a lot of drives end in field goals in the first two games, and, following Colts WR Alec Pierce’s injury during Sunday Night Football, both teams will now be missing their #1 receiver in this Week 3 matchup. That means a lot more handoffs and loaded boxes. Both teams will get production from their quarterbacks, but I expect a lot of drives to stall in the red zone. Give me the Texans to win 23-20. omg this is a brutal stat is this necessary 💀💀 pic.twitter.com/hHtjbd16PW — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) September 21, 2026 Of course, this is all just my opinion, and you should take the gambling advice from me or any other sports blog seriously. Remember to gamble responsibly and, of course, go Texans! They’ll travel to play the Indianapolis Colts in Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday, September 27th at 12:00 PM CST. title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: Two weeks of football and two losses for your Texans. Every victory and every loss comes with its own set of circumstances. The key is to take down the data and figure out the patterns in what you see. If you see the same things in defeat then you can avoid defeat by avoiding those […]
full_text: Two weeks of football and two losses for your Texans. Every victory and every loss comes with its own set of circumstances. The key is to take down the data and figure out the patterns in what you see. If you see the same things in defeat then you can avoid defeat by avoiding those things. There are other things that are more or less random, For instance, week one was largely on the defense where week two was more on the offense and special teams. However, we can begin to see some similarities when we look at the numbers. Of course, we will also do our customary good, bad, and ugly along with our special look at C.J. Stroud. The scoreboard says it was a 20-6 game, but watching it live and the numbers in the aftermath says it was a lot closer than what the final score would indicate. These games are usually decided by a play here and a key decision there. We will get to those as well. The Numbers Total Yards: Texans 78/374, Bengals 59/267 Rushing Yards: Texans 18/60, Bengals 23/85 Passing Yards: Texans 60/314, Bengals 36/182 Third Down Conversion: Texans 5/17, Bengals 5/15 Fourth Down Conversion: Texans 0/4, Bengals 0/0 Sacks: Texans 5, Bengals 4 Penalties: Texans 9/83, Bengals 12/78 Turnovers : Texans 0, Bengals 0 Time of Possession: Texans 29:11, Bengals 30:49 So, let’s get this straight. The Texans had more yards than the Bengals. They possessed the ball for more plays than the Bengals. They had more first downs than the Bengals. They got into the red zone more often than the Bengals (called penestrations back in the good ole days). They didn’t turn the ball over. Yet, somehow did they not only lose, but they got blown out on the scoreboard. The Texans have gained 755 yards of total offense and have produced 37 points. That is over 20 yards per point scored. We are going to keep a look at that number throughout the season as it the highest sum in the league and a good predictor of team success. The Good Will Anderson got paid a lot of money to play football this offseason and he showed up to play football on Sunday. He was second on the team with eight tackles including multiple tackles for loss in the running game. He also added his first sack of the season. Anderson and Danielle Hunter both got to Joe Burrow and Burrow was harassed all game including on his two touchdown passes. Those were plays that superior players make. The second touchdown had some shaky defense from Reed Blankenship, but it was still a good play where Burrow was chased and narrowly avoided the rush. Great players make great plays. Great offenses will put some points on the board. When you hold a team like the Bengals to 20 points then you usually feel good about your chances. We can’t say great because this is still a defense that has generated zero turnovers. Sometimes a quarterback is just better and that might have been the case during these first two weeks, but the defense showed up on Sunday. The Bad It is hard to decide on what to peg here, so I will peg what is not a normal occurence for this team. Frank Bush might kill someone in practice this week if they look at him sideways. You had a muffed field goal and Fairbairn missed a 58 yarder. I’m not holding that one against him, but it is what it is. There was also a bad punt followed up by a targeting penalty that gave the Bengals the ball in Texans territory. This is a day they will want to have back, but in the grand scheme of things it wasn’t the reason why the Texans lost the football game. The Ugly I can see the wheels spinning in DeMeco Ryans head and that is the problem. On a key fourth and one play he decided to attempt a low percentage 58 yard field goal rather than go for it. The math geeks would all tell you to go for it. The math geeks haven’t tried to watch a Nick Caley offense try to gain a yard. This team was a combined five for 21 on third and fourth down. Sure, the Bengals defense is much improved, but this wasn’t the 2000 Ravens or the 1985 Bears out there. In the grand scheme of things this is probably a mediocre defense which is evidenced by the fact that the Texans gained nearly 400 yards in total offense without Nico Collins. This qualifies under the ugly column because we’ve seen it all before. We get new linemen. We get a new featured back. After year two of the Ryans era we even got a new offensive coordinator. This team is still soft in short yardage situations. I honestly don’t know how it can be fixed and whether it could during the year. I’m not happy that Ryans decided to kick in that scenario, but I can’t be mad at him either. He’s watched this team fail repeatedly in short yardage and had just seen them fail on third and one the previous play. Who wouldn’t be gun shy after watching that yet again? Focus on Stroud There are a couple of things I need to say first. First, this is one data point out of 17. No one should make any declarative statements based on one or two data points. Secondly, we live in a hot take world where people want to go with superlative statements one way or another. That is radically inappropriate in this case. Based on the two data points, Stroud has shown himself to be a good NFL quarterback. He definitely should be on the the 32 starters and would start for probably half of the teams in the league. All that being said, these first two weeks showed us something up close and personal. Two of the QBs that are considered among the elite made plays that Stroud simply did not make. We can blame the offensive line, receivers, offensive coordinator and the alignment of the planets if we wish. Some of that is valid and that is why these discussions are a lot more nuanced than we let on. Elite quarterbacks make plays to win games. Good quarterbacks don’t. It really is that simple. What makes life hard is that we have seen Stroud make plays before. We have seen those elite guys fail to make plays. Nothing is ever black and white. We are looking at rates of success and those guys just make those plays more often than Stroud. Again, we can argue the whys and what fors if we like. There are always reasons, but if you are going to pay a guy 60 million then he needs to be one of those guys that makes plays to get his team over the hump. When he is playing good football, Stroud manages a game well, but he hasn’t been that guy since his rookie season. Sometimes it really is that simple.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Texans lose a let down game to the Bengals
summary: Since 1990, 12 percent of teams have gone 0-2 and made the playoffs. The Texans have done that on a few occasions and they will have to do it again after the Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Houston Texans 20-6. It was a game that felt a lot like last season. The Texans defense harassed Joe […]
full_text: Since 1990, 12 percent of teams have gone 0-2 and made the playoffs. The Texans have done that on a few occasions and they will have to do it again after the Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Houston Texans 20-6. It was a game that felt a lot like last season. The Texans defense harassed Joe Burrow all afternoon and got to him a few times, but ultimately fhe former Heisman Trophy winner was too much for the Texans on this day. He and his former teammate JeMar Chase made one too many big plays on this one. However, the bigger story was the Texans offense. They seemed to live in Bengals territory, but they managed only six points on the afternoon. That included a missed field goal, a muffed snap on a field goal attempt, and a failed fourth and one run from inside the Bengals 20. Those results were eerily similar to a season ago when the offense seened to move freely inside the 20s, but bogged down in the red zone. It was not a bad game for C.J. Stroud. He threw for over 300 yards again despite the absence of Nico Collins. Unfortunately, the run game was non-existant, so the Texans offense became one-dimensional fairly early on. That also felt eerily familiar. The Texans are now in familiar position as they start the season 0-2 yet again. I suppose if there is any consolation, the score was not indicative of how close the game really was. The key was a few key plays the Bengals made and the Texans did not make. If there are any stars from this game for the Texans it could very well be Dalton Schultz. He had twelve catchers for 140 yards which qualifies as a star performance in a game where you score six points. The tight ends in general were very productive as Foster Moreau added two catches for 34 yards. That hopefully is a bright spot to focus on in the future as we look for signs of life in the Nick Caley offense. We have not reached the pitchforks stage in the season quite yet. This is particularly true for a franchise that has come back from these deficits before. We are probably at the side eye stage of the proceedings. Stroud and Caley came into the season on the hot seat and the seat might be getting a little warm for Caley. Stroud has done enough to question some of the critics, but quarterbacks are paid to win football games and he hasn’t done that this season. Look here for more coverage on this game and the Indianapolis Colts this week at Battle Red Blog.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Colts receive initial encouraging injury update on Alec Pierce, but further evaluation coming on Monday
summary: According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler (which was later confirmed by head coach Shane Steichen post-game), the x-rays on Indianapolis Colts wideout Alec Pierce’s reinjured ankle/heel were negative last night: However, further medical evaluation will be undergone on Monday, and given that Pierce was seen leaving Arrowhead Stadium in a boot and using crutches, I’m no […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Alec Pierce #14 of the Indianapolis Colts is tackled by Marlon Humphrey #44 of the Baltimore Ravens during the fourth quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler ( which was later confirmed by head coach Shane Steichen post-game ), the x-rays on Indianapolis Colts wideout Alec Pierce’s reinjured ankle/heel were negative last night: X-rays on Colts WR Alec Pierce's heel injury were negative, per source. Further evaluation coming Monday. — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) September 21, 2026 However, further medical evaluation will be undergone on Monday, and given that Pierce was seen leaving Arrowhead Stadium in a boot and using crutches, I’m no doctor, but him missing time here again seems like a realistic possibility. It’s the same injured ankle/heel that kept him out of all of training camp and preseason. Pierce left late in the first quarter on a non-contact play and was unable to put weight on his aggravated left ankle/heel, as he limped off to the sideline. He was eventually helped to the medical tent with the help of Colts team trainers before exiting the field entirely along the sidelines on a medical cart. While he was initially designated as “questionable,” which seemed overly optimistic for any sort of return, he was quickly downgraded to “out” by the Colts medical staff—and obviously, was not available again last night. Of course, it’s a big blow to the Colts offensively, as Pierce is one of their unit’s most explosive playmakers, and their best downfield threat—especially with their AFC South rival Houston Texans coming to town in Week 3. The Colts absolutely want to avoid an 0-3 start and make an already increasingly large loss deficit, grow even bigger. Even though the Texans defense has struggled a bit out of the gates, allowing the 24th most points (28.0 avg. ppg.) through two games in the 2026 campaign, reputationally, they’re still regarded as one of the league’s best. With Pierce potentially absent, it could mean more looks for rookie Deion Burks downfield situationally, as well as Ashton Dulin (ankle), who’s also mending from an injury which kept him out of action last night. Without Pierce’s deep speed and vertical separation, the Colts become a lot easier to cover, as none of the group of Keenan Allen, Josh Downs, or Tyler Warren are burners, which also means heavier boxes for Jonathan Taylor.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts-Texans opening odds: Colts seeking lone victory against the Lone Star State
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are set to return home and begin divisional play against the Houston Texans. After these starts, this one will be huge. 0-2 starts to the year have created a sense of desperation for both teams. FanDuel Sportsbook sees the Colts as underdogs in this one at +2.5. The money line is +124 […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - AUGUST 28: A Texans helmet during a preseason NFL football game between the Houston Texans and the Carolina Panthers on August 28, 2026, at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C.(Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are set to return home and begin divisional play against the Houston Texans. After these starts, this one will be huge. 0-2 starts to the year have created a sense of desperation for both teams. FanDuel Sportsbook sees the Colts as underdogs in this one at +2.5. The money line is +124 with the over/under at 45.5. Oof. That one hurt. After a rough opener, the Colts responded in Kansas City. Another beautiful drive to start the game was followed by a blow by blow affair. Each team traded punches, but the defense once again struggled immensely. It took overtime to decide this one, and after a fortuitous reversal of a fumble call, the Colts had hope. Patrick Mahomes had other ideas, however, as he swiftly worked down the field for the game-winning field goal. The Texans welcomed the Bengals into town for their second home game to start the year. So far, the season hasn’t gone as planned, but after a slow start in 2025, you can’t count them out. C.J. Stroud threw 55 times with no touchdowns as the Texans fell behind early and could never catch up. After putting up 31 on the Bills, they could only muster 6 points against Cincinnati. This is the battle for relevancy, a chance to save a season. 0-2 is a bad start. 0-3 might be a death sentence. The season and jobs could be on the line if the Colts don’t turn this one around. It’s time to get in the winning column.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Should the Colts have kicked the Field Goal or gone for it?
summary: I have been hard on Shane Steichen plenty of times over the last few years, so I have no problem saying when he gets something right. Sunday night against Kansas City was the best coaching performance of his Colts career. Indianapolis still lost 33-30 in overtime and fell to 0-2, so there are no moral […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Head coach Shane Steichen of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates a touchdown with Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images I have been hard on Shane Steichen plenty of times over the last few years, so I have no problem saying when he gets something right. Sunday night against Kansas City was the best coaching performance of his Colts career. Indianapolis still lost 33-30 in overtime and fell to 0-2, so there are no moral victories to celebrate. Still, this was about as close as one gets. The Colts went into Arrowhead, played one of the best teams in football into the final seconds of overtime and did it while Kansas City’s best players were playing extremely well. Patrick Mahomes finished with 382 passing yards and three touchdowns, Kenneth Walker III ran for 117 yards and Travis Kelce looked like the Kelce of a few years ago with nine catches for 101 yards and a touchdown. Kansas City did not give Indianapolis an opening by playing poorly. The Colts also lost Alec Pierce early in the second quarter after already entering the game without Ashton Dulin, yet Steichen continued to find ways to move the offense. Jonathan Taylor scored twice, Josh Downs consistently came through on third down and Laquon Treadwell, of all people, ended up making the biggest offensive play of overtime. The Colts scored 27 points in regulation and had a chance to win a game in Arrowhead that very few people expected them to be in late. That is why I have a hard time with the criticism Steichen is getting for the decision that followed Treadwell’s 48-yard catch in overtime. There is absolutely an argument for going for it on fourth-and-8. I understand it. I just do not agree with it. The case for going for it The easiest argument is also the most convincing one: keep the ball in your own hands. Kansas City had already taken a 30-27 lead on Harrison Butker’s 31-yard field goal. The Colts answered immediately when Daniel Jones found Treadwell for 48 yards, moving the ball from their own 35 to the Kansas City 17. Three plays later, Indianapolis was facing fourth-and-8. Go for it, pick up the first down and the Colts are suddenly in position to win the game themselves. Convert and they can continue draining the clock before either scoring a touchdown. It’s also worth noting that getting the 1st down does not ensure that they will win the game. However and more importantly, Patrick Mahomes never gets the ball back unless the Colts decide to give it to him. That last part is going to drive most of the criticism. Who wants to voluntarily give Mahomes another possession in overtime? He had already thrown for nearly 400 yards. Walker was running extremely well. Kelce was finding openings throughout the game. Kansas City had just driven 55 yards on its first overtime possession before Indianapolis finally forced a field goal. Mahomes getting the ball back is obviously not the preferred scenario. There is also something to be said for deciding the game yourself rather than asking the defense to save it. If Jones converts fourth-and-8, nobody is talking about whether the Colts should have kicked. Steichen probably gets praised for being aggressive on the road against Kansas City. The historical numbers do not make going for it ridiculous either. NFL teams converted fourth-and-8 at a 39.4 percent rate in play-by-play data from 2013 through 2022. In a vacuum, that is close enough to four out of every 10 attempts that an aggressive coach can justify keeping the offense on the field. The problem is that this was not a fourth-and-8 in a vacuum. This was a very difficult fourth-and-8 Field position changes everything. The Colts were already deep in Kansas City territory, which meant the Chiefs did not have much field left to defend. The closer an offense gets to the goal line, the less vertical space there is for receivers to threaten. Safeties do not have to respect a route going 40 yards over their heads because there are not 40 yards available. Kansas City also showed no obvious intention of bringing heavy pressure. If the Chiefs rush four and drop seven, Jones is looking at seven defenders covering five eligible receivers in a condensed part of the field. The Colts needed eight yards for the first down, and there were only about 20 yards of field behind the line of scrimmage. Spread seven defenders across a space roughly 20 yards deep and 53⅓ yards wide, and that works out to about 152 square yards of field per defender. Each player could realistically only be 6 yards away from everything… that is nothing! Obviously, football coverage is not divided into equal boxes, but it gives you an idea of how crowded that part of the field becomes. The Chiefs could sit around the sticks, keep everything in front of them and not worry nearly as much about being beaten deep. The third-down play right before it showed exactly how difficult that area of the field was to throw into. On third-and-13, Jones dropped back and never even had a clean window to get the ball out. Kansas City flooded the short field, took away the routes and forced him to hold the ball. If the Colts could not find anything on third-and-13, there was little reason to think fourth-and-8 was suddenly going to offer an easy answer. That is why I do not think the normal fourth-and-8 conversion rate tells the whole story here. Around midfield, the offense has much more space to stretch the defense vertically. Near the red zone, that space disappears. This was a much tougher fourth-and-8 than the average one. That is a completely different fourth-and-8 from one around midfield, where the defense has to respect the entire field. Could Steichen have drawn up something that worked? Of course. Downs is excellent underneath, Taylor can create after the catch and Tyler Warren is a difficult matchup. Jones had also made several good throws on third and fourth downs during the game. It still would have been a very low-percentage play against a Chiefs defense that knew exactly where the Colts needed to get. It would have been much much less than 39%. If the Colts fail, the game ends immediately. There is no second chance and no opportunity for the defense to make one play. Kansas City wins 30-27 and everyone spends Monday asking why Steichen passed up a 38-yard field goal. That risk is being glossed over too easily. Kicking gave the Colts another path to win The field goal was almost automatic. Shrader had already made kicks from 42 and 49 yards earlier in the game, and his 38-yarder in overtime tied it at 30. The decision essentially became this: attempt a difficult fourth-and-8 in a condensed field or make the short kick and ask the defense to keep Kansas City from gaining roughly 30 to 40 yards. I will take the second option. The Colts did not need the defense to shut Mahomes down for an entire quarter. They did not need a turnover. They did not even necessarily need to force an immediate three-and-out, although that would have been ideal. They needed to keep Kansas City outside comfortable field-goal range long enough to get the football back. If the Colts force a punt, Jones gets another possession with enough time to move into Shrader’s range. Indianapolis had already watched Shrader make a 49-yarder with plenty of room to spare that night. Asking the offense to move 25 or 30 yards on multiple plays for a potential winning kick is a much more comfortable proposition than asking it to convert fourth-and-8 against eight defenders sitting in a short field. Kansas City eventually moved 46 yards after the kickoff and Butker won it from 40 yards as time expired. Walker did most of the early work on the drive before Mahomes found him for 22 yards on third-and-1, which was the play that effectively put Kansas City into winning…
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Colts drop heartbreaker to Chiefs as overtime expires behind Butker’s game-winner
summary: The Indianapolis Colts walked into Arrowhead facing all the doubters and were almost too much to handle in an attempt to steal a road win. The Sunday Night Football primetime clash against the Kansas City Chiefs turned into a classic shootout that refused to end in regulation. The Colts leveled the score at 30-30 after […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts runs for a touchdown during the fourth quarter against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts walked into Arrowhead facing all the doubters and were almost too much to handle in an attempt to steal a road win. The Sunday Night Football primetime clash against the Kansas City Chiefs turned into a classic shootout that refused to end in regulation. The Colts leveled the score at 30-30 after quarterback Daniel Jones connected a deep shot to Laquon Treadwell on their first offensive play of overtime. The referees initially ruled the play a fumble, because Treadwell rose up from the turf and tried to gain more yards before getting the football punched out Nohl Williams. It would have won the game for Kansas City, but replay review changed the call to Treadwell being down by contact and allowed for the Colts to settle for a chip shot with just three minutes left to play. Both teams had 10 true drives until the Colts kicked it off for the final time and had to try and stop Mahomes from leading a game-winning drive in the waning minutes of overtime. Chiefs’ Harrison Butker ultimately kicked a 40-yard field goal as extra time expired, which sent Indianapolis home with a 33-30 OT loss Sunday night. Indianapolis walked into the noise of Arrowhead and instantly silenced the crowd with another brilliant opening drive that ended in the end zone. The Colts were able to move the chains on four consecutive plays to march into Chiefs territory. On third-and-4 from inside the red zone, Jones found receiver Josh Downs on a slant for 11 yards before a roughing-the-passer penalty allowed the Colts to set up shop at the goal line. Taylor was stuffed on the next play, so Steichen went away from the obvious run. Jones faked the pitch and waited just long enough to throw a dart to tight end Tyler Warren, who ran a slick slant to get behind L’Jarius Sneed and found open space to catch a 1-yard touchdown. Tyler Warren under the lights! #INDvsKC on NBC pic.twitter.com/rLiPmsdUPy — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 21, 2026 It took just one play for the Chiefs to breach Colts territory as Kenneth Walker ran into a scrum, but was able to spin outside of the reach of defensive end Arden Key and burst down the left side for an explosive 19-yard run. Not only was the opening play the longest run of the game for the Chiefs, but it put the brutal missed tackles on full display. Kansas City answered with a field goal on its opening possession, then took advantage of a major mistake from the visiting stampede. For the second straight game, the Colts second possession lasted just two plays. Jones tried to squeeze a slant to receiver Keenan Allen, but Chiefs cornerback Kris Fulton intercepted the forced pass to seize possession inside the red zone. Two plays later, Mahomes found tight end Travis Kelce on an out route for a 13-yard touchdown, which was the 81st TD connection in the careers of the golden jacket duo, the most in league history. Indy opened the game with possession of the football for 15 of the first 20 minutes, controlling the pace of play. The Colts were able to rely on kicker Spencer Shrader, who delivered a pair of field goals from 42 and 49-yards out to momentarily take a 13-10 advantage. Each time the Colts landed a significant strike, the Chiefs were able to respond with some shots of their own. Mahomes showcased his ability to step up inside the pocket and flawlessly spread the football to his trio of receivers including Rashee Rice, Tyquan Thorton and Travis Kelce to march downfield. The Chiefs punctuated the scoring drive with consecutive quick hits to speedster Xavier Worthy for a 1-yard touchdown to retake a 17-13 lead late in the first half. The Colts could have bled the clock out, but instead, took advantage of a blatant pass interference by Fulton to instantly get back inside Chiefs territory. It took the Colts just 86 seconds to run a 10-play scoring drive, capped by a 24-yard touchdown run from Jonathan Taylor as Indianapolis used some true grit to go into the locker room with a halftime lead. Taylor finished with 24 carries for 92 rushing yards and two touchdowns. ‼️ Prime time JT ‼️ #INDvsKC on NBC pic.twitter.com/n61zcxR5Wd — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 21, 2026 Kansas City opened the second half with a 16-play, 80-yard touchdown drive to regain control, ignited by a 45-yard deep shot to Thorton that allowed the Chiefs to set up at the goal line. Faced with fourth down, Mahomes rolled right and found receiver Jaylen Royals wide open in the back of the end zone for the go-ahead score. Trailing by a touchdown, the Colts continued leaning heavily on the play fakes as Jones hit Downs on a creative out route to instantly march back inside Chiefs territory. On third-and-6 from the Kansas City 30-yard-line, Jones recognized the all-out blitz and got the pass out quickly to Downs on a slant to convert the first down. Six plays later, Taylor burst left and crossed the goal line from 5-yards out to tie the game at 27 apiece with just 5:37 remaining in regulation. From there, the intensity rose each time Kansas City had the ball in its possession. When Indianapolis forced a punt with 3:15 remaining, the first chance to win the game laid in the hands of the offense, starting from their own 18. Jones first used the play action to dump it off to Taylor for 14 yards. The Colts were truly threatening to escape with a win after Jones hit Downs on a hitch to convert a first down following the two minute warning. But the drive stalled out near midfield after consecutive incomplete passes fell to the turf and Indy was forced to punt in the final minute of regulation. The Colts won the overtime toss, but team captain Cam Bynum tried to defer the choice, then ultimately chose to play defense first. A decision that certainly gave the Chiefs the 11th final drive necessary to bleed the clock for the game-winning kick. Indianapolis allowed 523 total yards in the Week 2 defeat as Mahomes finished 32 of 47 for 382 passing yards. Kenneth Walker rushed for 117 yards on 24 carries, while Kelce torched the secondary for nine catches, 101 receiving yards and a touchdown. For a night in Kansas City, the Colts stood toe-to-toe with the NFL’s perennial contender in perhaps the most difficult environment in football. The Colts had the Chiefs on the ropes twice, but just couldn’t land the final punch before time expired. The Colts host the Houston Texans next Sunday, with both AFC South rivals aiming to secure their first win of the 2026 season.
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: Colts finally get TKO’d in OT during heavyweight SNF fight against Chiefs
summary: For the second season in a row, the Indianapolis Colts fell in overtime to the Kansas City Chiefs, only this time around, the final score was 33-30—as Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker landed the 40-yard game-winning field goal blow in the closing seconds of overtime to crush Colts fans hearts again at the end of extra […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts runs the ball against Nick Bolton #32 of the Kansas City Chiefs during the first quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the second season in a row, the Indianapolis Colts fell in overtime to the Kansas City Chiefs, only this time around, the final score was 33-30—as Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker landed the 40-yard game-winning field goal blow in the closing seconds of overtime to crush Colts fans hearts again at the end of extra regulation in Arrowhead. There’s no moral victories in this, as the Colts will fall to 0-2, with pretty close to a must-win game against their AFC South rival Houston Texans coming to town—to avoid going 0-3 to start the 2026 campaign. That being said, the Colts did look night-and-day different compared to last weekend’s ‘egg laying’ against the Baltimore Ravens at home, and to be fair, in the NFL, you’re never as bad as your last loss, or as good as your most recent victory. It was truly a spirited road effort by Indianapolis, even if they came up just short. For whatever reason, the Colts seem to play the Chiefs very well historically no matter the odds. The Colts got off to a hot start with an opening drive offensive touchdown, which Tyler Warren capped off with a 1-yard touchdown reception. However, it was followed up by a Colts quarterback Daniel Jones interception, which was the exact same script as last weekend. The Colts would recover this go around though, as Indianapolis and Kansas City traded punches throughout this one, as neither team ever led by more than a single score throughout the Sunday night primetime matchup. Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor led the way for the Colts with 92 total rushing yards and 2 rushing touchdowns on 24 carries (3.8 ypc. avg.), as Indianapolis rightfully rode their workhorse in a tough road game. On the other side, Kenneth Walker III was arguably just as good with 117 total rushing yards on 24 carries, and it’s scary to see Mahomes paired with such a pure rusher in his backfield. Still working his way back from a torn Achilles, Daniel Jones was fairly good in this one on the road, completing 22 of 31 pass attempts for 210 passing yards, a passing touchdown and an interception, but he wasn’t Patrick Mahomes either, who completed 32 of a whopping 47 pass attempts for 382 total passing yards, 3 passing touchdowns, and 0 interceptions. The Colts secondary, who admittedly were banged up in this one, will have to do some further soul searching, as expected to be a strength of their defense, they were not good in this one against Mahomes (although it was a bit of a coming out party for undrafted rookie defensive back Kapena Gushiken, who made two big plays in relief). Injuries to veteran starting cornerback Charvarius Ward and Sauce Gardner (the latter who did later return) certainly did not help matters though, but they have to put up more resistance going forward as a unit. The Colts defense collectively surrendered a whopping 523 total yards defensively, which is 500+ offensive yards allowed for the second week in a row—both of which were losses. There’s a lot of work to be done defensively in all facets and all three levels of defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo’s unit. The status quo won’t cut it. Colts kicker Spencer Shrader went a perfect 3 for 3 from field goal range, including a long of 49 yards, as well as a pristine 3 for 3 from extra point range. Colts fans’ hearts had to have sunk, when wideout Laquon Treadwell had the football inexplicably punched out after getting up after connecting on a 48-yards pass from Jones to begin the Colts first offensive drive in overtime near the Kansas City 17-yard line. Fortunately, he was ruled down by contact, which looked like the right call after a number of slow motion replay angles, but it was close to being disaster and ‘night night’ for the Colts. For the Colts, the continued status of lead wideout Alec Pierce, who reinjured his surgically repaired left ankle/heel late in the first quarter on a non-contact play (and couldn’t put any body weight on it), will be of critical concern. Pierce went to the medical tent with the help of trainers before being carted off the field. He was eventually downgraded from questionable to out, and obviously, did not return to the football field. One final thought: The big national talking point from this game will be whether the Colts should’ve gone for it on 4th and 8 on the Kansas City 15-yard line with a chance to win, having 3:15 left in OT, and trailing the Chiefs 27-30. In my opinion, those same people should’ve been making the same argument then that the Colts should’ve gone for it on 4th and 4 on the IND 49-yard line with 34 seconds left in regulation, and tied 27-27, because if you’re “playing to win the game,” that’s actually the stronger play, because it’s not only a shorter distance to move the sticks, but a longer field for the Chiefs to cover as opposed to where things get tighter closer to the red zone. Personally, I liked the latter more than the former because the Chiefs defense was simply teeing off on Jonathan Taylor on the Colts final offensive drive in overtime, and I didn’t like how Indianapolis looked offensively to successfully convert a 4th and 8th with a shorter field. They looked shaky at that point in time. We ended up losing anyways by trusting a tired and clearly underperforming defense against the always dangerous “Mahomes and Company,” so maybe by kicking the field goal in overtime, we just prolonged our eventual agony however.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts WR Alec Pierce leaves game with heel injury and has been ruled out for return
summary: Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce was forced to leave Sunday Night Football’s game against the Kansas City Chiefs, as he reinjured his surgically repaired left ankle on a non-contact play. Pierce gingerly limped to the sideline, without being able to put his body weight on his reinjured heel/ankle, and headed directly to the medical […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 23: Alec Pierce #14 of the Indianapolis Colts makes a catch in the third quarter of the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce was forced to leave Sunday Night Football’s game against the Kansas City Chiefs, as he reinjured his surgically repaired left ankle on a non-contact play. Pierce gingerly limped to the sideline, without being able to put his body weight on his reinjured heel/ankle, and headed directly to the medical tent with the help of trainers before being eventually carted off the field. He was initially listed as “questionable” to return (which a return to this game never seemed realistic), but that designation was recently downgraded to “out.” Obviously, Pierce’s injury is concerning for the Colts, as it’s the same ankle that caused him to miss all of the team’s offseason training activities, veteran minicamp, training camp, and preseason. After inking a once historic 4-year, $114 million contract (with $84 million guaranteed) right before free agency, the thought was that Piece, after a breakout 2025 campaign, would take another step forward into becoming an even more complete, bona fide #1 wideout for Indianapolis going forward. Instead, the Colts could be without one of their most explosive big play threats offensively for quite a while again.

title: Week 2 Colts vs. Chiefs Game Thread

The offense started most of the day with terrible field position due to poor special teams play. They didn’t […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts reacts against the Baltimore Ravens during the fourth quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are on the road to take on the Kansas City Cheifs in week 2 of the 2026 season, kickoff is at 8:20 p.m. EST. Week one didn’t go how any Colts fan would have liked. The offense started most of the day with terrible field position due to poor special teams play. They didn’t have many answers for the Ravens blitz and couldn’t consistently sustain drives. Defensively it was a complete and total excrement show. The number of words I could use to describe and further explain the happenings of last weeks defensive performance is in the tens of thousands, so instead I’ll just say it was terrible. But wait! There is reason for hope! Jonathan Taylor was as good as ever and Daniel Jones played as well as an quarterback in his first game back from a torn Achilles. There is plenty of reason to believe the offense will improve as the season goes along. The same can be said for the defense. There are only two ways you haven’t heard or read some variation of “the green dot” five thousand times over the past week, but I’m going to use it one last time. Lou Anarumo’s plan to give play calling duties to Cam Bynum was amongst the worst he has had in Indianapolis but to the teams credit, they have identified the issue and given the green dot to Akeem Davis-Gaither. There’s a reason linebackers are almost always the guy given that responsibility and the Colts have made the change. Given how disorganized the defense was in week one it’s difficult to even begin to determine where the holes are. There are almost certainly holes but until all 11 guys know what they’re supposed to be doing on every play, it’s impossible to know where those holes are. The hope (if you can call it that) is that the defense will be organized enough today that we will be able to tell exactly what part of this defense needs work. Because right now if someone asked me “What are the holes in the Indy defense?” I would just say “yes”. Join Stampede Blue on game day! Stay on top of every Colts update and debate every snap with other diehard fans. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . The Cheifs are coming off of a nice week one win over a Denver Broncos team that expects to contend in a good AFC. Patrick Mahomes is coming off of his own late, season ending injury from a season ago (torn ACL), and week one was good for ole Pat but he wasn’t quite the Mahomes of old. Though I’m sure he’ll be there soon. Kenneth Walker III had a career day with something like 172 yards rushing, after contact. Defensively the Chiefs made Bo Nix and the rest of the Broncos offense look pretty rough. Their entire offense only mustered 176 total yards and 10 points on Monday Night Football. If Indy wants to keep this one competitive offensively they’ll need to find quick win answers for beating the blitz. Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo sent pressure on just over 30% of their week one snaps which is right around league average. But Spags’ blitz packages are famous for their ability to confuse offenses and get home, taking a quality over quantity approach. They’ll need to feed Jonathan Taylor the ball to control the pace of the game and they’ll need to try to generate touches for Tyler Warren. If they can get Warren matched up against Chiefs linebacker Nik Bonitto and exploit it, the Indy offense will have a chance to look much better in week two. Defensively, I’ll just focus on these Chiefs as there’s too much to say otherwise, Indy needs to wrap up and make their tackles. Kenneth Walker III will make teams pay if they don’t rally to the ball and make sure tackles. Travis Kelce remains the Chiefs most concerning pass catching threat, so making sure the defensive backs are on top of their game so they don’t let someone who is a league average receiver 16 games out of the season, have a career day, needs to be a priority. This game probably isn’t going to go great for our Colts. It may, but I wouldn’t bet on it. Ultimately the defense moved on from multiple long term leaders, replacing them with younger options. No matter how you felt about those old team leaders and their leaving, ultimately it will take time, actually on the field, to fill those roles and work out the kinks those moves created. We may not see this defense peak until the midway point, if it even does. This is the toughest stretch of the Colts season, expect turbulence. Prediction: Chiefs: 24 Colts: 20 As always, go Colts. Go wild (within reason)! Go Colts!
