title: Where to Watch: Colts at Chiefs on SNF for Week 2
summary: The Indianapolis Colts (0-1) travel to the Kansas City Chiefs (1-0)(-6.5) for Sunday Night Football (8:20 PM EDT) to try to avoid a difficult 0-2 start, after an embarrassment of a Week 1 showing last weekend. The primetime matchup can be viewed on NBC, where Mike Tirico (play-by-play), Cris Collinsworth (analyst), and Melissa Stark (sideline) […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 23: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs meets with Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts following the game, at Arrowhead Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (0-1) travel to the Kansas City Chiefs (1-0)(-6.5) for Sunday Night Football (8:20 PM EDT) to try to avoid a difficult 0-2 start, after an embarrassment of a Week 1 showing last weekend. The primetime matchup can be viewed on NBC, where Mike Tirico (play-by-play), Cris Collinsworth (analyst), and Melissa Stark (sideline) will be handling the national television duties. Meanwhile, Colts fans can tune in locally on 93.5 and 107.5 The Fan / 97.1 Hank FM or nationally on Sirius XM Channel 193. For those listening in, Matt Taylor (play-by-play), Charles Arbuckle (analyst), and Larra Overton (sideline) will be on the call as usual for the Colts. At Arrowhead, it’s expected to be partly to mostly cloud with temperatures in the high sixties/low seventies at kickoff, and a chance of later game rain or isolated storms. Anytime Indianapolis heads into a tough road environment like Arrowhead, especially against the future Hall of Fame duo of quarterback and head coach Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid, they’re going to be in a for a tough challenge. After Week 1, the Chiefs currently rank 8th in points scored (31.0 ppg) and 2nd in points against (10.0 ppg), which means the Colts will need a lot stronger and spirited of a showing than they demonstrated last week. In particular, the Colts will need to shore up their run defense, which another future Hall of Famer, Derrick Henry, carved up last weekend. Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker carries a lot of momentum into this one, having rushed for 173 total rushing yards and a rushing touchdown last weekend in a Chiefs win vs. Denver. Communication will also be key. The Colts suffered a number of miscommunication issues last weekend defensively, which resulted in a number of blown coverage assignments. The hope is that by transitioning the green dot and thus, the helmet transmitter duties, from safety Cam Bynum to veteran linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither that it’ll be cleaned up logistically. The officiating unit for this one will be Craig Wrolstad and his crew for tonight. Indianapolis leads the all-time series against Kansas City, 18-11-0, with the Colts narrowly losing to the Chiefs in Week 12 of last year, 23-20, on the road in overtime. To-date, superstar Chiefs quarterback Mahomes is 1-2 against the Colts in his Canton-bound career. The Colts enter this one pretty healthy after the regular season opener, with just wideout Ashton Dulin (ankle) declared out. With Dulin absent, on Saturday, the Colts elevated fellow wideout Anthony Gould from their practice squad to presumably help handle special teams return duties. Backup running back DJ Giddens is questionable, but was a full participant during team practice on Friday. title: Jaguars Winners & Losers From Week 2: Jags Fall Flat In Mile High
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars came out flat in a winnable game Sunday, surrendering 17 second half points to the Denver Broncos, falling 20-13 on the road for the team’s first loss. It doesn’t take this column to tell you this game was a dud. That was a winnable game in all versions of the phrase, but […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 20: Parker Washington #11 of the Jacksonville Jaguars is tackled by Brandon Jones #22 of the Denver Broncos during the second quarter of the game at Empower Field At Mile High on September 20, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars came out flat in a winnable game Sunday, surrendering 17 second half points to the Denver Broncos, falling 20-13 on the road for the team’s first loss. It doesn’t take this column to tell you this game was a dud. That was a winnable game in all versions of the phrase, but the Jags collapsed in the second half, specifically in the fourth quarter. Jacksonville wasn’t playing the Browns again and it showed. And that’s frustrating. Liam Coen’s team left much to be desired on the field in Denver, which will cause quite the week of discourse on what this team truly is. It’s only Week 2, so there’s plenty of football ahead for Jacksonville but that game leaves a bitter taste in the mouth for anyone who watched or played in it. No one particularly shined which might be the most damning aspect of that debacle. The season is far from over, but nonetheless that was a brutal watch for a team that had the game in control until it just flat out fell apart at the seams. WINNERS Perspective Let’s take a broader look at the loss because it was far and away the most respectable loss of the Sunday slate. We didn’t lose to the Cleveland Browns like Tampa Bay did. We didn’t lose our starting quarterback like Washington did. We didn’t bench our starter like Pittsburgh did. We lost to a good team by a touchdown on the road. It happens. By no means should the Jags hang a banner for “Hey, we didn’t lose that badly!” but it at least wasn’t like the team got killed. They just came out flat on the road. It actually might be a good thing that there’s a collective frustration with that game because for the first time in a while there’s real expectation with the Jaguars. Many people were talking about how this team could be a playoff favorite after last week. It isn’t like that’s gone away after one game. It can always be a lot worse. One game doesn’t automatically disqualify us from ever winning again. There’s concern, certainly. But the sky isn’t falling. Parker Washington Quietly, Parker Washington was probably the best offensive – or maybe best overall – player on Sunday. Washington hauled in seven catches for 98 yards on 12 targets which is respectable enough. His yardage was over half of the team’s total through the air. Dating back to last year, Washington has excelled against a typically solid Broncos secondary for almost 250 yards and 13 catches plus one score combined. He can’t help Trevor Lawrence’s hapless ball thrown his way for that one interception, too. If you have to find some sort of solace, you can find it in the trust Lawrence and the offense have in Washington. The Jags might want to pay this man before it becomes far too late. He has 181 yards, 12 catches and one score through two games this year. Parker Washington down to the 1! JAXvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/0oEhufCdDV — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 LOSERS Buster Brown This Losers section isn’t so much an indictment on Buster Brown as it is on the discourse surrounding Jaylen Waddle after last week. Because of one game, did everyone forget Waddle is a top flight receiver? He reminded the world of that, largely picking on Brown for his 138-yard afternoon. Brown, like most of the secondary, got cooked for large swaths of the game. Bo Nix and the Denver offense were able to get the medium-to-long passing game going in ways against the Jags that they were unable to against the Chiefs. Travis Hunter, Brown and even Jarrian Jones despite his pick all got bullied at points on Sunday. It was an ugly day on defense and the secondary was far from the only reason for it. But Brown specifically was the guy getting picked on by Nix and Waddle. To Brown’s credit, he has stepped in big ways in big moments. He didn’t in his most recent game. What a ridiculously accurate throw by Bo Nix to Waddle pic.twitter.com/YbJbAkvVXg — Fitz (@LaurieFitzptrck) September 20, 2026 Brian Thomas Jr. Ok, what the hell is wrong with this guy? Brian Thomas Jr. was back at it again dropping passes and it’s truly inexplicable why. He hauled in just three of his eight targets, dropping some balls that hit him square in the palms. An incompletion to Thomas Jr. led to Cam Little’s missed field goal and that was just about the end of the game for Jacksonville. This is a well documented problem dating back to last year that might just end the former rookie phenom’s time in Duval County before it ever really gets off the ground. It’s baffling. There could be an argument that the lack of catching ability from Thomas Jr. led directly to the Jags losing. That’s not going to fly for much longer. Perfect ball by Trevor Lawrence. BTJ has to make this catch. #Jaguars #Jags pic.twitter.com/IXs9X3LCQ7 — Clay Harbor (@clayharbs82) September 20, 2026 Emmanuel Pregnon Welcome to the NFL rook. Last week, it was all rosy for the third-round rookie. This week not so much, as Denver’s defensive line and specifically Zach Allen took Pregnon to church for 60 minutes. No one on the offensive line played well, but much like Brown’s performance in the secondary or Thomas as a receiver, the glaring issue all game was with the left guard. This is an understandable issue as this was only Pregnon’s second game. It’s going to happen to a rookie. Again, it’s not like the Broncos are akin to the Browns. However, it wasn’t a Baldy Breakdown level showing from Pregnon who is going to face an equally tough defense in New England’s next week. Emmanuel Pregnon gives up quick pressure to Zach Allen. Tough matchup for the rookie. Broncos front showed up today. #Jaguars #Jags pic.twitter.com/320uNEkne0 — Clay Harbor (@clayharbs82) September 20, 2026 The Defensive Line Two games in the past two years against Denver have resulted in one sack. As I said in our staff roundtable this week, it was going to be on the defensive line to cause havoc on the Broncos or Nix would be able to pick the team apart. With zero sacks Sunday, we saw what happened. As a result of those zero sacks, it was safety Antonio Johnson who led Jacksonville in pressures Sunday with two (!!!). This joins the laundry list of things that are downright unacceptable from this defense. When Nix is pressured, like he was against the Chiefs, he’s as volatile as the Chernobyl reactor when left unattended. When you don’t pressure him, he goes for almost 300 yards. It’s basically that simple. Dennis Gardeck played fine enough, but if that’s the guy you are highlighting on a defensive line that has the former number one overall pick and your franchise sack leader, it probably wasn’t a good day. Lo and behold, this was not a good day for the pass rush. The run defense was pretty good all around, but the pass rush game suffered greatly. To add insult to injury, defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton left the game with a weird back injury and we all know how touch and go that is with him. Defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile took an L this weekend plain and simple. Yet through it all, we lost by just one score. Well that sucked. Let us know your thoughts on the game down below and we will see you back here when the Jags face the former Super Bowl runner-ups next Sunday. Maybe by then someone will have tackled Waddle in the open field.

title: Jaguars Collapse in Second Half, Fall to Broncos
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars suffered their first defeat of the 2026 season, a tough 20-13 defeat at Mile High Stadium to the Denver Broncos. Following a two-possession third-quarter lead, a frustrating second half in all three phases contributed to the loss. Here’s everything you need to know from Jacksonville’s Week 2 defeat. In Case You Missed […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Denver, Colorado, USA; Jacksonville Jaguars head coach Liam Coen on the sidelines against the Denver Broncos during the first half at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Jacksonville Jaguars suffered their first defeat of the 2026 season, a tough 20-13 defeat at Mile High Stadium to the Denver Broncos. Following a two-possession third-quarter lead, a frustrating second half in all three phases contributed to the loss. Here’s everything you need to know from Jacksonville’s Week 2 defeat. In Case You Missed It In a game that began as a defensive slugfest, Jacksonville struck first to kick off the scoring. Following five straight punts by both offenses, the Jaguars offense put together a balanced 8-play, 72-yard touchdown drive featuring a 22-yard catch by Brian Thomas Jr. However, the highlight of the drive was a 32-yard deep ball to Parker Washington to move into the redzone. One play later, Bhayshul Tuten scored on a one-yard Wildcat carry to open the scoring. Parker Washington down to the 1! JAXvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/0oEhufCdDV — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 The Denver offense added a quick field goal and seemed ready to take a halftime lead after a 76-yard Broncos drive. However, Broncos quarterback Bo Nix attempted a contested, high-point pass to Cortland Sutton on third down, resulting in a hard-fought Jourdan Lewis interception to end the drive. Nix saw cover 0 and threw it up, but the Jags corners were playing with eyes on the QB so Lewis saw it all the way — Steven Ruiz (@theStevenRuiz) September 20, 2026 A Cam Little field goal ended the half to extend the Jacksonville lead to 7. Halftime Stats: Score: 10-3 Jaguars First downs: 12-7 Jaguars Time of possession: 15:25 to 14:35 Broncos Third & Fourth Down Offense: 3/6 Jacksonville (50%), 1/6 Denver (16.7%) Defensive Sacks: 0 for Jacksonville, 2 for Denver Turnovers forced: 1 for Jacksonville, 0 for Denver Rushing yards: 31 to 32 Broncos Yards per rush: 3.1 YPC Jaguars vs 2.9 Broncos Passing yards: 122 to 156 Broncos Redzone: 1/1 Jacksonville (100%), 0/2 Denver (0%) Penalties: 2 for 15-yards Jaguars, 6 for 35-yards Denver Points off turnovers: 3 points Jacksonville, 0 points Denver QB Trevor Lawrence ended the half 12/17 for 138 yards (8.1 avg), and a 94.7 passer rating, while RB Bhayshul Tuten led Jacksonville with five carries for 16 yards (3.2 YPC), and a touchdown. Following the half, both teams traded opening drive field goals, and the Jacksonville offense suffered its first turnover of the day – a seemingly predetermined throw from Trevor Lawrence to Parker Washington, resulting in a Riley Moss interception. Riley Moss picks it off! JAXvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/tefsQpqaZO — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 The Denver offense immediately made Jacksonville pay for the turnover, putting together a 10-play, 64-yard touchdown drive that took 4:46 off the clock. The Jaguars struggled to defend Denver’s multiple-tight-end formations, allowing the Broncos to consistently move the ball. After Denver’s touchdown, Jacksonville’s offense began to unravel. Brian Thomas Jr. dropped a pass, Trevor Lawrence narrowly avoided an interception on third down, and Cam Little missed a field goal. The struggles continued on the other side of the ball, as the Jaguars once again failed to force a third down while Denver marched 56 yards on just five plays to take its first lead with 7:21 remaining. From there, Jacksonville’s offense could barely sustain a drive, while the Broncos continued to roll. Denver scored 17 unanswered points following the Jaguars’ third-quarter interception, completely flipping the game as Jacksonville struggled to find an answer on either side of the ball. Live blog: Recap each of the big plays and real-time reactions from tonight’s game in our live blog ! Favorite Highlight: Jourdan Lewis climbing the latter to end the scoring drive was dominant. Jourdan Lewis jump ball INT in the end zone ‼️ JAXvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/4Ot8gMmBp2 — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 Biggest play(s) of the game: According to rbsdm.com, the biggest play of the game by Expected Points Added (-4.3 EPA) and Win Probability (-15%) was the Jourdan Lewis interception. Key stats (traditional): QB Trevor Lawrence: 17/29 for 189 yards (6.5 avg), 1 int, 63.7 passer rating WR Parker Washington: 7 catches for 98-yards (14.0 avg), on 12 targets RB Bhayshul Tuten: 13 carries for 65 yards (5 YPC), 1 TD LB Foye Oluokun: 7 tackles, 5 solo CB Jourdan Lewis: 4 tackles (all solo), 1 interception Notable statistical gaps: Time of possession: 31:17 to 28:43 Denver Defensive Sacks: 2 to 0 Denver Rushing yards: 104 to 95 Denver Passing yards: 392 to 268 Denver Redzone: Denver 2/5 to Jacksonville 1/2 Penalties: 4 penalties for 40-yards for Jacksonville vs 10 for 53-yards for Denver Turnovers forced: Tied 1-1 Points off turnovers: 3 points Jacksonville, 7 points Denver View the full box score here Game balls: Special Teams: Logan Cooke – 4 punts, 46.3 avg, a long of 55-yards Defense: LB Foye Oluokun – 7 tackles, 5 solo Offense: WR Parker Washington – 7 catches for 98-yards (14.0 avg) on 12 targets Post-game notables: 1. OL Struggles Rampant While the Broncos’ defensive line ended Sunday with just two sacks, it felt like much more as Lawrence struggled to get comfortable in the pocket for much of the game. Both tackles struggled, along with the interior offensive line. 2. A True Team Loss Brian Thomas Jr. suffered two clear drops while struggling to get free from Riley Moss for much of the game. On a third-down deep ball, while down by seven, Thomas failed to make a play on the ball or jump into the contact to force a penalty. LeQuint Allen also had a drop that could have cost the team 4 points. Cam Little missed a second-half field goal, and the defense struggled to get off the field just once in the second half. 3. Davon Hamilton’s Back Injury With his serious 2023 history of a back abscess and the lack of stout depth at nose tackle, the Davon Hamilton injury has the potential to be huge. That will be one to watch moving forward. 4. Dennis Gardeck’s Solid Day Despite the loss, I thought it notable that Gardeck had a quality performance in this one. In the first half he had a third-down quarterback pressure to force the first Denver punt and he also had a shoestring tackle of JK Dobbins on what looked like a huge run, otherwise. In the second he flashed again on Denver’s opening drive, with his second third-down quarterback hit (and pressure) to force a Broncos field goal. 5. Tough Day on O On a day where the team couldn’t score 21 points, it’s difficult to pin the majority of Sunday’s blame elsewhere. The run game didn’t seem prevalent enough after halftime, Jakobi Meyers and Brenton Strange, both who caught 100% of their targets, received just three combined attempts, and Lawrence threw for less than 200 yards with no touchdowns. In very many ways, this felt like one of Coen’s toughest performances to date. The red-flag connection between the four games of the Coen era where they did not score 20 points: all came against top defensive fronts Denver Houston Seattle 2025 Los Angeles — John Shipley (@_John_Shipley) September 21, 2026 Injuries As a note, the following Jacksonville players left Sunday’s game due to injury: DT Davon Hamilton left the game late (back) and did not return Pregame Notes: Inactives For the Jaguars: QB Quinn Ewers WR CJ Williams S Jalen Huskey LB Jack Kiser OL Daniel Faalele TE Tanner Koziol DE Wesley Williams The active/inactive list was somewhat interesting, as it featured four 2026 draft picks (3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th round picks), plus a 2025 4th round pick, all made inactive Sunday. title: 3 Reasons Why the Jaguars Lost to the Broncos in Week 2
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars will leave Denver wondering how they managed to let this one slip. For three quarters, Liam Coen’s team had done plenty right. The Jaguars led 10-3 at halftime, extended that advantage to 13-6 in the third quarter and had Denver’s offense struggling to find any sort of rhythm. Then everything changed. The […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 20: Malcolm Roach #97 of the Denver Broncos sacks Trevor Lawrence #16 of the Jacksonville Jaguars during the second quarter of a game at Empower Field At Mile High on September 20, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars will leave Denver wondering how they managed to let this one slip. For three quarters, Liam Coen’s team had done plenty right. The Jaguars led 10-3 at halftime, extended that advantage to 13-6 in the third quarter and had Denver’s offense struggling to find any sort of rhythm. Then everything changed. The Broncos scored twice in the fourth quarter, turning a seven-point deficit into a 20-13 victory and leaving Jacksonville with a second-half collapse that will sting considerably more than the final score suggests. Here are three reasons why the Jaguars came away from Mile High empty-handed. Second-half capitulation All tied up. 🙌 📺: @NFLonCBS / @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/fJ13wxU8WZ — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) September 20, 2026 This one is impossible to avoid. The Jaguars were 13-6 up with 15 minutes remaining. They had controlled the scoreboard, forced Bo Nix into an interception in the second quarter and, despite some struggles of their own, looked to be in command of the contest. Then they simply couldn’t finish it. Denver put together a 64-yard touchdown drive to tie the game at 13-13, with Nix finding Nate Adkins for a seven-yard score with 11:47 remaining. Just over four minutes later, the Broncos struck again, driving 56 yards in five plays before Jonah Coleman powered into the end zone from three yards. Suddenly, it was 20-13. And the Jaguars never found an answer. That is the brutal reality of this defeat. Jacksonville didn’t lose a game in which it was comprehensively outplayed from the opening snap. It lost one in which it held a seven-point lead entering the fourth quarter and was outscored 14-0 in the final 15 minutes. For a team with ambitions of competing deep into the season, that inability to close out a game it had largely controlled will be the biggest frustration of all. Mile High eventually became a factor First TD for the rook! 📺: @NFLonCBS / @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/lwtGesjhr4 — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) September 20, 2026 There is a reason playing in Denver is different. The altitude is one thing, the atmosphere is another. The Jaguars spent much of the afternoon doing a good job of silencing the crowd, but as the Broncos started to build momentum in the fourth quarter, Empower Field at Mile High became exactly the sort of environment Jacksonville knew it would be facing. Communication becomes more difficult when the crowd is at full volume, and that matters when an offense is trying to make adjustments at the line of scrimmage. Denver’s home environment has long been one of the more challenging in the NFL, and there was a noticeable shift once the Broncos got themselves back into the game. The Jaguars had already done the hard part by building a 13-6 advantage. But once Denver tied the game, the pressure changed. Every Broncos defensive stop became louder. Every Jacksonville mistake was amplified. And with Denver suddenly believing it could win, the home crowd became another problem for a Jaguars team trying to regain control. The noise didn’t lose this game by itself. But when the momentum swung, it certainly didn’t help Jacksonville stop it. The Jaguars didn’t put the game away Broncos defense forces a crucial incompletion 👀 JAXvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/X4nDb7wwx8 — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 This is perhaps the most frustrating part. Jacksonville had enough opportunities to make Denver’s comeback considerably more difficult. The Jaguars moved the ball well enough at times, but they couldn’t turn their control of the game into the kind of scoreboard advantage that would have forced Denver into desperation mode. Instead, the Broncos remained within one possession. That meant one good drive could completely change the complexion of the game; and that’s exactly what happened. Jacksonville’s offense also became increasingly difficult to sustain once Denver’s defense found its footing. The Broncos eventually generated the pressure and disruption needed to stop the Jaguars from putting together the sort of response required after Denver tied the game. Trevor Lawrence, so assured in the first half, started misfiring, throwing a regrettable interception and was lucky not to be picked off twice more. The Jaguars controlled this game for a large chunk of the sixty minutes. But they didn’t put it away. And when Denver finally found a way to seize the momentum, Jacksonville had no answer. The verdict There will be plenty for Liam Coen and his staff to digest from this one. The Jaguars showed enough during the opening three quarters to suggest they were capable of leaving Denver with a victory. They defended well, controlled the scoreboard and spent long stretches making life difficult for the Broncos. But NFL games aren’t won over three quarters. Being outscored, outschemed and outplayed for the final fifteen minutes essentially turned a win into a loss. The Jaguars competed, and when all is said and done this may not be a bad defeat within the context of a 17 game schedule. Jacksonville are a team that can now be considered amongst the best in the AFC, but Liam Coen will know this is one they should have had. We’re on to New England.

title: Chiefs’ Kahlil Benson is ‘winning over a lot of people,’ says Andy Reid
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs are 2-0 through two weeks of the NFL season, and that has come with rookie Kahlil Benson at left tackle in place of the injured Josh Simmons (Back). Last year’s starting right tackle at the University of Indiana has played every possible snap on the blind side so far, all 149 […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Kahlil Benson #70 of the Kansas City Chiefs looks on from the field during an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs are 2-0 through two weeks of the NFL season, and that has come with rookie Kahlil Benson at left tackle in place of the injured Josh Simmons (Back). Last year’s starting right tackle at the University of Indiana has played every possible snap on the blind side so far, all 149 per Pro Football Focus , and has filled in admirably. He has allowed four hurries and two quarterback hits through two games, but hasn’t been faulted for any of the four sacks quarterback Patrick Mahomes has taken against the Denver Broncos and Indianapolis Colts . Walk-on left tackle Khalil Benson has made quite the impression against the Colts. #NextGenStats powered by @awscloud . pic.twitter.com/z8XNMhDujy — Sunday Night Football on NBC (@SNFonNBC) September 21, 2026 He has held up on pass downs, with plenty of challenges to come if he stays in the lineup, but Benson’s run blocking has made him “one of the Chiefs’ five best linemen” right now, in the words of head coach Andy Reid before the season opener. During the preseason, Chiefs offensive line coach Andy Heck said the coaching staff “could see [Benson] had dominant physical traits.” He has shown that off on run plays early on. Chiefs talked about Kahlil Benson showing dominant traits during the summer It's the effortless power in his hands. Look how easily he puts 30 on the ground pic.twitter.com/pdjHra1b7q — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) September 21, 2026 Benson shows off effortless power with his hands after climbing to the second level to nonchalantly pancake a Colts safety. The power he brings to blocks has stood out throughout practice and game observations. Moves people off the line pic.twitter.com/OFV2cu3bp9 — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) September 21, 2026 He fires off the ball and uses that huge frame — 6 feet 6 inches tall with 34 1/2-inch arms — to create space for the Chiefs’ running backs. Running back Kenneth Walker had 10 carries to the left side of the line against Indianapolis; he totaled 69 rushing yards (6.9 yards per attempt) on those runs. After the game, head coach Andy Reid acknowledged the rookie’s efforts. “Yeah, there are a couple hiccups in there, but he was going against a good player,” Reid said to reporters. “And I thought he did a decent job… (General Manager Brett) Veach, great eyes, great eyes. I mean, to bring him in here, and then (Offensive Line Coach) Andy Heck believing in him and coaching him up, the kid believing in himself. “I think he’s winning over a lot of people,” Reid said. Is he winning over the coaching staff enough to keep him in the starting lineup? With Simmons’ return on the horizon, should we expect Benson to slide over to the right side? Or does Benson stay in Simmons’ place regardless of the injury report? Right tackle Jaylon Moore didn’t allow a pressure over 51 pass blocks against the Colts, per PFF . He had a rougher performance in Week 1, but either way, the Chiefs will soon have to make decisions about their starting five up front.

title: Chiefs’ Kenneth Walker is having a historic start to the season
summary: Two weeks into the NFL season, Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker has stayed atop the mountain as the star of the football world after earning last year’s Super Bowl MVP award. The NFL leader in yards from scrimmage (365) and rushing yards (290) has run rampant over the Denver Broncos and Indianapolis Colts […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Kenneth Walker III #9 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs the ball during the first quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Two weeks into the NFL season, Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker has stayed atop the mountain as the star of the football world after earning last year’s Super Bowl MVP award. The NFL leader in yards from scrimmage (365) and rushing yards (290) has run rampant over the Denver Broncos and Indianapolis Colts defenses in primetime. Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry is second in the NFL in rushing yards, with 72 fewer than Walker. As strong as the offensive line has looked, Walker has produced a lot of yards himself. On Sunday night, he forced a career-high 15 missed tackles, according to NFL Next Gen Stats . His previous high came last week against Denver (14). If those single-game totals sound like a lot, they are. The 29 forced missed tackles lead all NFL players (heading into “Monday Night Football”) this season and are five more than any player has registered in NFL Pro’s statistical database through two weeks of an NFL season since at least 2018. Players with 150+ scrimmage yards in each of their team's first 2 games of a season over the last decade: 🔸 Kenneth Walker III (2026) 🔸 Justin Jefferson (2023) Walker is the first Chiefs player to do so in franchise history. — NFL Researcher (@NFL_Researcher) September 21, 2026 Not only was Walker one of the only modern NFL players to surpass 150 scrimmage yards in each of the first weeks of the season, but he also joined memorable Oklahoma and Detroit Lions running back Billy Sims as the only NFL players to ever begin their careers with a team s urpassing 175 total yards in the first two games played there . Ken Walker is the first member of the Chiefs to rush for 100+ yards in back-to-back games since Clyde Edwards-Helaire did so in 2021. Through two weeks, Walker leads the NFL in rushing yards (290) and scrimmage yards (369). — Matt McMullen (@KCChiefs_Matt) September 21, 2026

title: 5 things we learned from the Chiefs’ Week 2 overtime victory over the Colts
summary: For the second straight week, the Kansas City Chiefs beat a team of horses. Unlike last week, the game never felt in hand. This game was back and forth — and although it wasn’t a perfect game by either team, it was quite entertaining and literally came down to the last possible second before the […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the second straight week, the Kansas City Chiefs beat a team of horses. Unlike last week, the game never felt in hand. This game was back and forth — and although it wasn’t a perfect game by either team, it was quite entertaining and literally came down to the last possible second before the Chiefs finally sealed their 33-30 victory in overtime over the Indianapolis Colts , via a walk-off field goal by Harrison Butker Here are five things we learned from Kansas City outlasting Indianapolis on Sunday evening: 1. The passing game isn’t dead. After a mostly quiet debut back from his injury last week, quarterback Patrick Mahomes — QB1 — was back to being that dude again, tossing the rock for 382 yards and three touchdowns. Patrick Mahomes famously did not complete a 10+ yard pass in Week 1. That changed tonight. On such throws: – 7/11 – 155 yards – 1 TD – 137.5 passer rating His 382 passing yards were his most in a game since 10/22/2023… and did so on an efficient 8.1 YPA pic.twitter.com/hObqfk4ue3 — Mike Kennedy (@MikeKennedyNFL) September 21, 2026 And while tight end Travis Kelce was the main beneficiary of Mahomes’ targets, the most encouraging part of this game was how many contributors Mahomes connected with to rack up nearly 400 passing yards. Mahomes completed passes to seven different receivers. Five of them had four or more receptions. It was also nice to see Jalen Royals get in the mix and score his first NFL touchdown. And as I mentioned, this was by no means Mahomes or the Chiefs’ best game, which should be even scarier for the rest of the league. The Chiefs had 523 yards of total offense, and it still felt like they left a few plays out on the field. 2. Kelce is still Kelce The Chiefs’ future Hall of Fame tight end proved tonight that he still has plenty left in the tank to play another season, and hopefully make another playoff run. Over two weeks, we’ve seen the explosive plays return to Kelce’s game. He’s not the player he once was, but he can still do the job. No matter his age, Travis Kelce remains one of the best big game players in the sport. Tonight was his first 100-yard game since 1/18/25… in the divisional playoffs Before that, he had 100 yards on MNF on 11/4/24 His last before that was the ‘23 AFC CG pic.twitter.com/QhzUUp9bjr — Mike Kennedy (@MikeKennedyNFL) September 21, 2026 After the game, former captain of the site and current Kansas City Star reporter Pete Sweeney asked Kelce about his touchdown. As the consummate team player he is, he credited wide receiver Xavier Worthy for laying the block on the Colts defender that allowed him to get into the end zone. Chiefs TE Travis Kelce’s postgame remarks in the locker room. Says the team is in a zone right now and feeding off each other. pic.twitter.com/BDzND5xxka — Matt Derrick (@mattderrick) September 21, 2026 Kelce may be Mrs. Swift’s husband, but he’s also still one of the best tight ends in the NFL. Taylor Swift points to the wedding ring after Travis Kelce scores a touchdown pic.twitter.com/RqU1GVaTcq — Bussin' With The Boys (@BussinWTB) September 21, 2026 3. Emmett Johnson will make Kenneth Walker better If you want to wear down an opposing defense, throw an absolute unit like Kenneth Walker at them 25 or more times a game and watch their will to make contact deteriorate. But if you want to absolutely obliterate them, then bring in another running back who is almost as talented as Walker. Johnson’s vision, lateral agility, and contact balance make him just as hard to bring down. Emmett Johnson DANCIN' out there INDvsKC on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/X7YXNw6QVs — NFL (@NFL) September 21, 2026 The one-two punch of Walker and Johnson is only going to get better as the year progresses, and we saw tonight what happens when an opposing defense has to respect the run first when Mahomes is on the field cooking. 4. Nohl Williams looks like a star For the second straight week, Chiefs’ second-year player Nohl Williams looked like one of the best cornerbacks in football. That matters, considering we don’t know when first-round draft pick Mansoor Delane will return to the lineup from injury. In the meantime, Williams is more than holding up his end of the bargain. He stayed in the opposing receiver’s hip pocket all night Sunday. He nearly single-handedly won the game for Kansas City, if the back of L’Jarius Sneed’s hand hadn’t grazed Colt’s receiver, Laquan Treadwell, on his way to the ground. LAQUON TREADWELL MAKES A GAME-DECIDING CATCH FOR THE COLTS, THEN ALMOST FUMBLES IT AWAY HE WAS TOUCHED pic.twitter.com/8l8uh1eVLt — NFL Drop (@TheNFLDrop) September 21, 2026 5. The ‘refs are in the Chiefs’ back pocket’ narrative is dead Listen, I’m not mad the refs overturned the call on the field in overtime to give the ball back to the Colts. I’m not angry, because the Chiefs still figured out a way to win. Now, if the game had been different. And the Chiefs hadn’t found a way to stop the Colts in the red zone, and they hadn’t figured out a way to drive down the field and win the game. I would have been fuming. But either way, this narrative is dead, or at least I don’t want to hear about it whatsoever anymore.
author: Rocky Magaña

title: Chiefs News: Travis Kelce sets all-time NFL record for yards after catch
summary: The ageless wonder that is Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce has been making the same plays he always has through the first two weeks of the 2026 NFL regular season. His team-leading performance in the 33-30 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts featured a lot of yards after the catch, a staple of […]
full_text: (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The ageless wonder that is Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce has been making the same plays he always has through the first two weeks of the 2026 NFL regular season. His team-leading performance in the 33-30 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts featured a lot of yards after the catch, a staple of his skill set throughout his prolific career. Less than a month from turning 37, Kelce moved up to the No. 1 spot on the career yards-after-catch list. Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device! For Apple devices, click here . For Android devices, click here . The latest Kansas City Chiefs news Travis Kelce sets NFL record for yards after catch | FOX 4 The 36-year-old set the NFL record for most yards after the catch against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday Night Football. Kelce surpassed Hall of Fame running back Marshall Faulk to supplant himself at the top of the list. He accomplished the feat in the first half of the game and also scored a touchdown. Other NFL records Kelce holds are career postseason games, postseason 100-yard games and career Super Bowl receptions. Five things that stood out about the Chiefs’ overtime win vs. the Colts on ‘SNF’ | The Kansas City Star The big play is back? Some 22 teams completed a downfield shot in the opening week of the NFL season. The Chiefs were not one of them. The years-long dilemma took a one-play reprieve in regulation and then another reprieve in overtime. On a pair of third-and-long throws – each bigger than the last — Mahomes hit Tyquan Thornton downfield on deep crossing patterns. Kansas City Does It Again In OT: 3 Takeaways From The Chiefs’ Win Over The Colts | FOX Sports The Chiefs Are So Good In OT It’s hard to find many situational stats where Kansas City doesn’t look good, but they’re a really good team once a game gets to overtime. When they pulled out an overtime win over the Colts on Sunday night, it was their sixth win in their last six overtime games. Their last overtime loss was to the Bengals in the 2021 AFC Championship Game. Even with that, they’re now 9-1 in overtime games since the start of the 2019 season. Patrick Mahomes heats up as Chiefs survive Colts in OT. How big of a threat is Kansas City? | The Athletic How big of a concern is the Chiefs defense after it struggled to stop the Colts? Pretty big. The Chiefs defense was never going to replicate a nearly flawless opener against the Broncos where it allowed just nine first downs in 11 non-kneeldown drives. The defense’s effort against the Colts, though, was a disaster for most of the night. In its first eight non-kneeldown possessions, Indianapolis scored six times. The Chiefs’ pass rush? Nearly non-existent. The secondary? Picked on repeatedly, starting with slot cornerback L’Jarius Sneed, whom the Colts saw as the weak link, targeting him 12 times for nine receptions, per SumerSports’ data. First-round rookie Mansoor Delane did not play because of a shoulder injury, and he certainly was missed on a night when the Chiefs defense disappointed. — Newell NFL Week 2: Takeaways, questions, fantasy spin for Sunday games | ESPN Did Patrick Mahomes’ performance demonstrate the Chiefs are back as contenders? That appears to be the case after two weeks. In overtime, Mahomes orchestrated the 25th winning drive of his 10-year career, which is tied with Kirk Cousins for second most in that span. Last season, the Chiefs were bad in one-score games, finishing with a 1-9 record. Mahomes, though, proved he’s capable of carrying the Chiefs yet again to another dramatic win. In just his second game after recovering from the torn ACL and LCL in his left knee, Mahomes finished with 382 passing yards and three touchdowns without committing a turnover. Around the NFL Bears QB Caleb Williams suffers hamstring injury in loss to Vikings | NFL.com “We’ll know more tomorrow,” Johnson said. Johnson added he had spoken with Williams prior to his postgame news conference and the third-year pro was “in good spirits.” “I’m actually happy it’s nothing with the knee,” Johnson told reporters. “That was my first inclination, but the hamstring could be pretty damaging as well. We’ll see how bad it is tomorrow, and we’ll go from there.” NFL intends to proceed with Ravens-Cowboys in Brazil, despite field concerns | Pro Football Talk Concerns exist regarding the quality of the playing surface in Rio de Janeiro for next Sunday’s game between the Ravens and Cowboys. The league, however, is undeterred. Via Mark Maske of Front Office Sports , a league spokesperson said Sunday that (quoting Maske not the spokesperson) “the league is looking forward to the game in Rio and, as with all international games, it has a plan in place to ensure a high-quality playing surface.” Separately, the NFL Players Association told Maske that it’s aware of the situation, and that it has been in touch with the league office about it. ‘F— that:’ Todd Monken fires back at Mike Tomlin’s ‘Browns is the Browns’ diss after win | CBS Sports Todd Monken initially brushed off former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin’s recent “Browns is the Browns” diss. He had a much different response, however, following the Browns’ Week 2 win over the Buccaneers, Monken’s first win as an NFL head coach. “Browns are gonna Browns. F–k that! The guys took that to heart,” Monken said. Harbaugh ‘not deterred’ as loss drops Chargers to unexpected 0-2 | ESPN It’s unclear whether Harbaugh, who often pauses at random times in his news conferences, was doing so because of the chant or whether he even heard it. Nonetheless, the moment was a cruel reminder of how quickly things have changed for the Chargers. “We’ll look at the tape. We’ll go back to work. That’s all I know how to do,” Harbaugh said as the chants continued. Coming into this season, ESPN’s Football Power Index gave the Chargers the fifth-highest odds to win the Super Bowl. And Sunday’s game was supposed to be a bounce-back opportunity for a team hoping to contend. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Rapid Reaction: 3 instant takeaways from Chiefs-Colts The Chiefs’ pass game is limited by its top wideouts However, the team’s top wideouts — Rice and Worthy — still lack the tough-catch ability crucial against modern pass coverages that rarely give receivers room to breathe. I mentioned Rice’s play late in the game earlier, but Worthy also mishandled a rifling throw from Mahomes that would’ve gotten the offense inside the five-yard line. In overtime, Thornton made his second downfield catch of the game, hanging on through a big hit by the oncoming safety to keep the drive alive on third and long. When it comes to catches in traffic, especially further downfield, Thornton has been much more reliable than the players who receive the top-2 most snaps in the receiving room. It probably shouldn’t have been this close, but Indy’s game plan featured a lot of running back Jonathan Taylor and quick passes from quarterback Daniel Jones to neutralize the Chiefs’ pass rush. It’s not a […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Travis Kelce #87 of the Kansas City Chiefs catches a pass during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts have caused more heart attacks for Kansas City Chiefs fans than Burnt Ends and Cheesy Corn combined. It probably shouldn’t have been this close, but Indy’s game plan featured a lot of running back Jonathan Taylor and quick passes from quarterback Daniel Jones to neutralize the Chiefs’ pass rush. It’s not a formula every team can execute, but the Colts were a couple of wild plays away from walking out of Arrowhead with a victory. Instead, quarterback Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs pulled out their eighth straight overtime victory with the most familiar playmakers and one that we’ve already grown to love. Here are a few who stood out on Sunday night. 6 Winners Quarterback Patrick Mahomes: Statistically, he was great— 382 yards, 3 touchdowns, and no turnovers. But it was the confidence, the deep ball, and the drive-extending run in overtime that were the most encouraging. The knee looks solid, the offense is putting drives together, and the MVP now has a big-play run game to lean on. Running back Kenneth Walker III: Two games into his Chiefs career, Walker has put up over 175 total yards both times. But, like Mahomes’s performance, Walker’s was about more than the numbers. When the Chiefs needed to move the ball in the fourth quarter and overtime, they went to Walker over and over again. K9 delivered. Cornerback Nohl Williams: The Chiefs were down a young corner, with Mansoor Delane watching from the sidelines after missing most of Week 1. Lucky for us, Nohl Williams is becoming a star. He broke up a pass and made a tackle in the backfield this week, along with his consistently blanket-like coverage. But the most impressive play almost ended the game. A hustling Williams flew in to force a fumble, and the game was a fraction of a second from being over. The ruling of down by contact kept the Colts alive for the moment, but that doesn’t take anything away from the hustle and punch play of #20. Cornerback Kristian Fulton: Speaking of cornerbacks, Fulton got the start on Sunday night and promptly stole the ball from Keenan Allen. Sure, there were some costly pass interference flags against him—but they could have gone either way. Fulton’s play has been a positive surprise this season, proving the Chiefs right for keeping him around while the previous starters moved to LA. Tight end Travis Kelce: Age is only a number, right? Kelce turned back the clock with nine catches, 101 yards, and a touchdown against the Colts. He became the NFL’s all-time leader in YAC (yards after catch), and showed that he’s still the man when the Chiefs need a big catch. The Mahomes/Kelce combination is back, Taylor Swift suite celebrations never stopped, and it feels like the dynasty could continue. Wide receiver Tyquan Thornton: The 45-yard catch downfield was incredible, but it was only Thornton’s second-best play of his 4-catch, 86-receiving-yard night. On third-and-long in overtime, Mahomes delivered a strike to Thornton—but it wasn’t an easy play. Tyquan had to go up and attack the football while taking a hit, and complete the catch to move the chains to keep the drive alive. It was a big-time play for a receiver who clearly has the quarterback’s trust. 3 Losers Defensive back L’Jarius Sneed: The Colts seemed to have a plan of attack that targeted L’Jarius Sneed. He gave up a few catches early, then was beaten deep on the aforementioned overtime play that nearly decided the game. His physicality and knowledge are assets for this defense, but Sneed may come with some limitations in his return. Tight end Noah Gray: Through two games, Gray has 5 yards on one catch. Meanwhile, Travis Kelce continues to be the team’s leading receiver in his age 35 season. The Chiefs paid Gray to be a serious number two tight end, if not a Kelce successor. He’s looked like just a guy ever since. Receiver/returner Nikko Remigio: The transition may have started this week— Brashard Smith and Emmett Johnson handled all of the kick returns. Both running backs show a level of explosion and ability to make people miss that Remigio seems to lack. We’ll see if Dave Toub decides to keep going with the safer option (Remigio) or if the Chiefs choose to roll with returners who have a better chance of delivering a big play. Note: Applying the labels “losers” is NOT a judgment on the talent or character of any of these individuals. It’s just a simple way to grade their job performance in a single game. No disrespect is intended.

title: Andy Reid says Mansoor Delane was available as ‘an extra guy’
summary: It took almost five quarters for the Kansas City Chiefs to defeat the Indianapolis Colts in overtime Sunday night. Fortunately, the team appears to have come out of the 33-30 victory relatively healthy. The Chiefs reported no injuries during the game. But for a strange situation, head coach Andy Reid had no injuries to discuss […]
full_text: Aug 15, 2026; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Kansas City Chiefs cornerback Mansoor Delane (5) arrives prior to a game against the Los Angeles Rams at at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jay Biggerstaff-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It took almost five quarters for the Kansas City Chiefs to defeat the Indianapolis Colts in overtime Sunday night. Fortunately, the team appears to have come out of the 33-30 victory relatively healthy. The Chiefs reported no injuries during the game. But for a strange situation, head coach Andy Reid had no injuries to discuss after the game. “Everyone who started the game finished the game,” said Reid to open his postgame comments. “There’s no real injuries to mention.” However, the most curious injury story coming out of Sunday involved a player who did not start the game. Rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane left Week 1’s contest with a shoulder injury after only three defensive plays. Delane participated in each practice prior to the Colts matchup and was declared active for Sunday’s contest despite drawing a questionable designation on the final injury report Friday. Despite being active, the rookie never took the field. Reid confirmed after the game that Delane was active in case needed in an emergency. However, the plan appeared to always have been that backup Kristian Fulton would play the game at Delane’s outside corner position. Reid believes Fulton played well despite drawing multiple costly pass interference flags. “It was as an extra guy,” Reid remarked. “I don’t want to take anything from Fulton either. He stepped in and did a heck of a job. A couple of those calls could go either way, I think. I’m glad [Delane] came out and was there in case we needed him.” The Chiefs will return to practice on Wednesday ahead of Sunday’s road contest with the Miami Dolphins. We will monitor Delane’s practice participation throughout the week.

title: Rapid Reaction: 3 instant takeaways from Chiefs-Colts
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs outlasted the Indianapolis Colts and won 33-30 in overtime on “Sunday Night Football.” Here are 3 rapidly written takeaways from the game: 1. Patrick Mahomes is getting stronger with each snap On Sunday evening, quarterback Patrick Mahomes looked much better than he did in the Week 1 win, whether it was […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs outlasted the Indianapolis Colts and won 33-30 in overtime on “Sunday Night Football.” Here are 3 rapidly written takeaways from the game: 1. Patrick Mahomes is getting stronger with each snap On Sunday evening, quarterback Patrick Mahomes looked much better than he did in the Week 1 win, whether it was his progression, his throws on the move, or his pinpoint deep pass to wide receiver Tyquan Thornton in the third quarter. Early on, old nemesis and Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo got the best of Mahomes on a third down. In man coverage, Indianapolis dropped into a zone blitz and was all over the pass attempt, which an oncoming defensive back knocked down at the line of scrimmage. He looked more comfortable than in the season opener as this game progressed. During the fourth possession of the game, a touchdown drive, Mahomes moved the chains four times before throwing one of his three touchdown passes. On a crucial drive in the fourth quarter, a pressured dropback was countered with an accurate pass to wide receiver Rashee Rice in tight coverage at the sticks; Rice was unable to muscle the pass in and allowed the rookie defender to strip it away, giving the Colts possession with less than four minutes to play. After getting the ball in overtime, Mahomes made some vintage plays that further showed he was shaking off the rust with each snap. He confidently settled and fired a throw downfield to Thornton on a third-and-long, then moved the chains with his legs by scrambling for 13 yards. He got one more chance to seal the victory, and he did it with style: on a third-and-one, he rolled out left, flicked his wrist over an oncoming defender, and into running back Kenneth Walker’s hands to set up the game-winning field goal by Harrison Butker. Mahomes completed 32 of 47 passes for 382 yards and posted a 114 passer rating. He threw for 19 first downs along with three touchdown passes. He led a 14-play touchdown drive and a 13-play field-goal drive coming out of halftime, putting the Chiefs up 27-20 in the fourth quarter. In overtime, he orchestrated an 11-play possession but failed to finish the job, with two incompletions that stalled inside the 15-yard line, but made the necessary plays to get Kansas City to 2-0. 2. The Chiefs’ defense gets humbled, then redeems itself One of the biggest takeaways from Week 1 was how ahead of schedule the Chiefs’ defense appeared to be. The unit came crashing back to earth against a Colts offense missing its top wideout for most of the game; Alec Pierce (Heel) left in the first half and did not return. Rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane (Shoulder) dressed but did not appear, leaving cornerback duties to Nohl Williams, L’Jarius Sneed, and Kristian Fulton. Early on, Fulton made a great play on a slant route, wrestling the ball away from the receiver for an interception that set up the first touchdown. In the slot, Sneed—and safety Christian Roland-Wallace, but mostly Sneed—struggled to handle the quick routes of wide receiver Joshua Downs. It led to multiple conversions late in the possession for Indianapolis. On the outside, Fulton struggled to match the physicality of the Colts’ run game, which is crucial at the position in defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s system. It led to some big runs to his side by running back Jonathan Taylor, but he wasn’t the only victim of the wall of strong blocks. Rookie defensive end R Mason Thomas got washed out on the first of Taylor’s two touchdown runs. The biggest flub of the game came in overtime, when quarterback Daniel Jones launched a 48-yard completion to wide receiver Laquon Treadwell running open from Sneed. Williams nearly made an all-time play with a punch-out, but it was still an ugly play for a secondary that looked much more competent in Week 1. For the game, Indianapolis moved the chains 24 times and converted 7/14 third- or fourth-down opportunities. The Chiefs’ defense would stuff some runs, then let others get into the second and third level. However, quarterback Daniel Jones’s efficiency (71% completion rate) put the Colts in position to keep chipping away all game. The pass rush made a defining play in the fourth quarter to keep the game tied, then linebackers Drue Tranquill and Nick Bolton stepped up in overtime to prevent a game-ending score. 3. The Chiefs’ pass game is limited by its top wideouts The Chiefs’ run game clearly helped open up the pass game against Indianapolis. An under-center, play-action pass clearly opened up the field, allowing wide receiver Rashee Rice to find plenty of space for a 30-yard catch-and-run over the middle. On the long ball to Thornton, attention on the run game created a one-high structure that let Thornton and wide receiver Xavier Worthy stretch thin with speed, giving the throw plenty of room deep for Thornton to make the play away from the deep safety. Light work for Worthy 😮‍💨 He was 5.2 yards away from the nearest defender when he caught this pass from Patrick Mahomes, per @NextGenStats INDvsKC on NBC/Peacock Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/xPar7wr1hb — NFL+ (@NFLPlus) September 21, 2026 On Worthy’s touchdown, attention on Walker created incredible separation. Second-year wideout Jalen Royals also stepped up with a strong catch, going up and getting a pass on the back line of the end zone on fourth-and-goal. However, the team’s top wideouts — Rice and Worthy — still lack the tough-catch ability crucial against modern pass coverages that rarely give receivers room to breathe. I mentioned Rice’s play late in the game earlier, but Worthy also mishandled a rifling throw from Mahomes that would’ve gotten the offense inside the five-yard line. In overtime, Thornton made his second downfield catch of the game, hanging on through a big hit by the oncoming safety to keep the drive alive on third and long. When it comes to catches in traffic, especially further downfield, Thornton has been much more reliable than the players who receive the top-2 most snaps in the receiving room. Soon-to-be 37-year-old tight end Travis Kelce is somehow still this team’s leading receiver, and that is not a positive review of the team’s receiving corps. He finished the night with a team-high nine catches and 101 yards; he also led the offense in yards after catch (66).

title: Final Score: Chiefs outlast Colts in overtime
summary: Patrick Mahomes completed 31 of 46 passes for 360 yards and three touchdowns without an interception, leading Kansas City to a 33-30 overtime victory. full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Jalen Royals #11 of the Kansas City Chiefs is tackled by Sauce Gardner #1 of the Indianapolis Colts during the second quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Patrick Mahomes completed 31 of 46 passes for 360 yards and three touchdowns without an interception, leading Kansas City to a 33-30 overtime victory. Travis Kelce paced the receivers with nine catches for 101 yards and a touchdown, while Tyquan Thornton added 86 yards and Rashee Rice finished with 83. Kenneth Walker III supplied 154 yards from scrimmage—115 rushing and 39 receiving—as the Chiefs amassed 499 total yards, 28 first downs and committed no turnovers. Indianapolis remained within striking distance behind Jonathan Taylor, who recorded 92 rushing yards, 40 receiving yards and two touchdowns. Daniel Jones completed 22 of 31 passes for 210 yards, one touchdown and one interception, while Josh Downs led the Colts with seven catches for 72 yards. After both teams exchanged field goals to begin overtime, Mahomes moved Kansas City into range one final time, and Harrison Butker made a 40-yard field goal with one second remaining to secure the win. Chiefs move to 2-0 on the season. Join Arrowhead Pride on game day! Stay on top of every Chiefs update and debate every snap with other members of Chiefs Kingdom. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . First Quarter Colts strike first Indianapolis opened the game with a methodical 13-play, 65-yard touchdown drive that consumed 6:33. Jonathan Taylor helped move the Colts into Kansas City territory, while Daniel Jones completed passes to Alec Pierce, Laquon Treadwell and Josh Downs. A roughing-the-passer penalty on Jaden Hicks moved Indianapolis to the 1-yard line, and Jones finished the drive with a one-yard touchdown pass to Tyler Warren. Spencer Shrader’s extra point gave the Colts a 7-0 lead. Kansas City answered with a six-play scoring drive. Kenneth Walker III gained 19 yards on the opening play, and Patrick Mahomes found Xavier Worthy for 16 yards to move the Chiefs to the Indianapolis 29. The drive stalled after Walker gained one yard and Mahomes threw consecutive incompletions. Harrison Butker made a 46-yard field goal, cutting the Colts’ lead to 7-3. Indianapolis’ second possession lasted only two plays. After Jonathan Taylor gained four yards, Daniel Jones’ pass intended for Keenan Allen was intercepted by Kristian Fulton at the Indianapolis 16. The takeaway gave Kansas City excellent field position with the Chiefs trailing 7-3. Fulton’s interception sets up Mahomes-to-Kelce touchdown Kansas City immediately converted Kristian Fulton’s interception into seven points. Kenneth Walker III gained three yards before Patrick Mahomes found Travis Kelce for a 13-yard touchdown. Harrison Butker made the extra point, giving the Chiefs a 10-7 lead. Indianapolis moved from its own 42 to the Kansas City 24 before the end of the first quarter. Jonathan Taylor converted fourth-and-1 and later broke an 11-yard run, while Daniel Jones connected with Josh Downs for 14 yards. Jack Cochrane dropped Taylor for a three-yard loss on the quarter’s final play. The Colts will begin the second quarter facing second-and-13 with Kansas City leading 10-7. Second Quarter Shrader’s field goal pulls Indianapolis even Kansas City’s defense prevented Indianapolis from advancing after the quarter break. Daniel Jones threw consecutive incompletions intended for Josh Downs and Keenan Allen, forcing the Colts to settle for a 42-yard Spencer Shrader field goal. The kick tied the game at 10-10 early in the second quarter. Butker misses go-ahead field goal After a penalty on the kickoff pushed Kansas City back to its own 30, Patrick Mahomes connected with Rashee Rice for a 30-yard gain into Indianapolis territory. The drive stalled at the Colts’ 33 after Mahomes’ third-down pass intended for Travis Kelce fell incomplete. Harrison Butker then missed a 51-yard field goal wide left, leaving the game tied at 10-10. A 26-yard defensive pass interference penalty on Kristian Fulton moved Indianapolis to the Kansas City 24, but the Chiefs’ defense kept the Colts out of the end zone. A delay-of-game penalty and a false start pushed Indianapolis into third-and-21 before Daniel Jones completed a four-yard screen pass to Jonathan Taylor. Spencer Shrader made the 49-yard field goal, giving the Colts a 13-10 lead. Mahomes finds Worthy to reclaim the lead Kansas City responded with a 15-play, 70-yard touchdown drive that consumed more than seven minutes. Patrick Mahomes overcame an offensive holding penalty by completing passes to Rashee Rice, Tyquan Thornton, Travis Kelce, Jalen Royals and Kenneth Walker III. Mahomes then connected with Xavier Worthy on consecutive plays, including a one-yard touchdown. Harrison Butker’s extra point gave the Chiefs a 17-13 lead. Taylor’s 24-yard touchdown puts Indianapolis back in front Indianapolis answered with a rapid 72-yard touchdown drive. Daniel Jones connected with Josh Downs twice, while a 23-yard defensive pass interference penalty on Kristian Fulton moved the Colts into Kansas City territory. Downs converted a third-and-6 before Jonathan Taylor broke a 24-yard touchdown run. Spencer Shrader’s extra point gave Indianapolis a 20-17 lead with 1:04 remaining in the first half. Kansas City went three-and-out after taking over with 59 seconds remaining. Patrick Mahomes found Emmett Johnson for eight yards, but an incompletion intended for Rashee Rice and an eight-yard sack by DeForest Buckner ended the possession. Matt Araiza’s 69-yard punt was downed by Jadon Canady at the Indianapolis 11 with the Colts leading 20-17. Third Quarter Royals converts fourth down for go-ahead touchdown Kansas City opened the second half with a 15-play, 80-yard touchdown drive that consumed nearly seven minutes. Kenneth Walker III gained 27 yards on three early carries before Khyiris Tonga converted fourth-and-1. Facing third-and-11 from the Indianapolis 46, Patrick Mahomes connected with Tyquan Thornton for 45 yards to the 1. The Colts stopped Walker on three consecutive carries, but Mahomes found Jalen Royals for a one-yard touchdown on fourth down. Harrison Butker’s extra point gave Kansas City a 24-20 lead. Indianapolis moved from its own 27 to the 48 behind Daniel Jones’ 15-yard completion to Jonathan Taylor, but the drive stalled. After a short completion to Laquon Treadwell on first down and a Taylor gained three yards on second down, Jones’ third-down pass intended for Treadwell fell incomplete. Rigoberto Sanchez punted 45 yards to the Kansas City 7, and Nikko Remigio returned it two yards to the 9. The Chiefs maintained a 24-20 lead. Kansas City drove from its own 9 to the Indianapolis 16 before the third quarter ended. Travis Kelce produced gains of 11, 16 and 18 yards, while Emmett Johnson added 27 yards on three touches. An offensive holding penalty on Kahlil Benson pushed the Chiefs into second-and-22, but Patrick Mahomes found Kenneth Walker III for 10 yards on the quarter’s final play. Kansas City will open the fourth quarter facing third-and-12 while leading 24-20. Fourth Quarter Butker extends Kansas City’s lead Patrick Mahomes found Rashee Rice for six yards on third-and-12, but the Chiefs remained short of the first down. Harrison Butker made the 28-yard field goal, completing a 15-play, 81-yard drive that consumed 6:21 and extended Kansas City’s lead to 27-20. Taylor’s second touchdown ties the game Indianapolis answered with a 15-play, 64-yard touchdown drive that consumed 8:37. Daniel Jones connected with Josh Downs for a 20-yard gain and later converted fourth-and-1 with a quarterback sneak after the Colts unsuccessfully challenged the previous spot. title: Is Chargers’ season over after 0-2 start at home?
summary: The Los Angeles Chargers are waking up in a bit of a pickle after losing to the Las Vegas Raiders at home in Week 2. The identical 26-14 final score that they suffered last week against the Arizona Cardinals. The Chargers were gifted the chance to start 2-0 by facing off against arguably the two […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Justin Herbert #10 of the Los Angeles Chargers calls to his team during the first quarter of the game against the Las Vegas Raiders at SoFi Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers are waking up in a bit of a pickle after losing to the Las Vegas Raiders at home in Week 2. The identical 26-14 final score that they suffered last week against the Arizona Cardinals. The Chargers were gifted the chance to start 2-0 by facing off against arguably the two “easiest” teams on their schedule to start the season. Both the Cardinals and Raiders picked in the top three of the 2026 NFL Draft and weren’t viewed as contenders for the playoffs coming into the season. However, they were both able to beat the Chargers with ease in their own building. Now the schedule is about to get a lot more difficult for the Chargers, which could spell the end of their season. Six of their next seven games on their schedule come against teams that were in the playoffs last season. The loan exception is the 2-0 Kansas City Chiefs, who were in the Super Bowl in Feb. 2025. The Chargers will face a two-game road trip, traveling to Highmark Stadium to take on the Buffalo Bills and Lumen Field to take on the defending champion Seattle Seahawks, both of whom are 2-0. They’ll return home for one game against the Denver Broncos before heading back out on the road to face the Chiefs and their crosstown rival, the Los Angeles Rams. They’re back at home for a date with the Houston Texans before visiting Jesse Mentor and the Baltimore Ravens on Monday Night Football. There’s a good chance the Chargers won’t be favored in any of these games, and if they were to lose all of them, it seals a losing season at 0-9. Simply put, the Chargers have to wake up. Otherwise, this season is going to be over by the middle of the year. BFTB community, feel free to air out your grievances in the comments below.

David Njoku Has Left The Game On The Cart, This Is Not A Good Sign For The Chargers. 😔❌ pic.twitter.com/fSUIl65aur — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) September 20, 2026 The Chargers are hoping Njoku can be a big part of the offense as a target for Justin Herbert. “I’ve been playing this game for a very long time, so at the very least I can add knowledge,” Njoku said about what he adds to the position via the team’s website . “I think my athletic ability speaks for itself, as well as the other tight ends. “I think we can push each other to be really good,” Njoku added. Njoku feels confident in what the position group can provide. “I feel like we can be destructive,” Njoku said. “We got the tools, we got the keys, we got the players to do it all. It’s up to us to put it all together.” The remainder of the Raiders vs. Chargers game can be watched on CBS or streamed on the Paramount Plus app.

title: Chargers vs. Raiders Game Recap: Self-inflicted wounds, lack of discipline lead Bolts to 0-2 start
summary: The Chargers were disastrous in Week Two, falling to the Raiders 26-14 at home to fall to 0-2 on the season ahead of what will be the league’s toughest schedule from Week Three on. Justin Herbert and the offense turned the ball over three times, including a pair of interceptions (although one was a David […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Justin Herbert #10 of the Los Angeles Chargers picks up a loose ball during the third quarter of the game against the Las Vegas Raiders at SoFi Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers were disastrous in Week Two, falling to the Raiders 26-14 at home to fall to 0-2 on the season ahead of what will be the league’s toughest schedule from Week Three on. Justin Herbert and the offense turned the ball over three times, including a pair of interceptions (although one was a David Njoku drop right in his hands). The other was a lost fumble by Omarion Hampton, the second of his in as many games this year. Defensively, the Chargers held the Raiders in check on most drives, but several broken coverages were the difference, including a 40-yard touchdown from Kirk Cousins to wideout Tre Tucker to break the opening tie where rookie Genesis Smith looked to play the wrong coverage. For the second consecutive game, the Chargers offense was frustratingly underwhelming and completely disconnected. But even when Herbert was hitting his receiver in their hands, they weren’t making catches. Rookie Brenen Thompson dropped a ball that his chest to kill the opening drive. Quentin Johnston also dropped a perfect pass up the left sideline between two defenders. Herbert finished with 15 completions on 27 attempts for 192 yards and one touchdown with the pair of picks. Hampton was one pace for a career-high in yardage, but his disaster second half brought that to a halt. He finished with 94 rushing yards (second most in a game) and a score to go with two catches for 21 yards. Ladd McConkey, broken rib and all, still led the team with three receptions. Tre’ Harris led the team with 53 receiving yards on a lone catch. Cornerback Cam Hart was unfortunately a main offender on defense. The young corner allowed several big plays to Tre Tucker, one of which was the 42-yarder near halftime that set the Raiders up with points before the break. Later on, he was called for hands to the face, giving the Raiders a first down despite the defense otherwise forcing a punt. Del’Shawn Phillips and Derwin James led the defense in tackles at seven each. Khalil Mack and Akheem Mesidor combined for the lone sack of Cousins. Cameron Dicker missed his only field goal attempt of the season thus far, a 58-yard kick that ricocheted off the right upright. I don’t think anyone knows where the Chargers are supposed to go from here, but right now, all signs are pointing to one of the worst seasons in recent franchise history. Deal with that accordingly. First Quarter The Chargers received the opening kickoff with Keaton Mitchell bringing the ball out to the 32-yard line. A three-yard rush by running back Omarion Hampton followed by a seven-yard pass to receiver Quentin Johnston combined to move the chains for the first time for the Chargers. A nine-yard reception by tight end David Njoku set up a short two-yard run by Hampton which moved the chains yet again. Cameron Dicker came out to attempt a 58-yard field goal following a third-down pass was dropped by rookie wideout Brenen Thompson on what would have otherwise been a big gain and another first down. Dicker pushed the ball just slightly right and it doinked off the lower right upright to keep the score 0-0. The Raiders looked like they had some early life on offense during their opening drive, but a pass intended for receiver Tre Tucker landed in the arms of cornerback Cam Hart after Tucker slipped at the top of the route. The Chargers couldn’t muster a drive after the turnover and punted away from their own 32-yard line. After forcing a three-and-out by the Raiders offense, the Chargers looked to grab some momentum back. On third down, Herbert lofted a pass to Njoku who broke free up the left sideline, but the pass wasn’t caught cleanly and it ricocheted off his hands into the arms of a Raiders cornerback who returned it all the way to the LA 23-yard line. Cousins found wideout Jack Bech for a 16-yard gain who fumbled it to himself to give the Raiders first-and-goal at the three-yard line. But the Chargers defense held on all four downs to force a turnover on down and gain possession at their one-yard line. Second Quarter Starting the quarter in the shadow of their own goal line, the Chargers needed to create space. Two runs by Hampton gained five yards, but that upcoming third-and-five was turned into third-and-nine after back-to-back false starts on right tackle Joe Alt. The Chargers would punt and give the Raiders possession at the Vegas 49. It took three plays in for Cousins to drop back and find wideout Tre Tucker for an easy 40-yard touchdown pass to break the tie via a deep post route. Rookie Genesis Smith was in at free safety alongside second-year safety R.J. Mickens and it looked like a big miscommunication as Smith let Tucker run right by him with no help on the other side. Needing points bad, the Chargers went to work, putting together a 10-play, 69-yard drive spurred on by a resurgent rushing attack led by Hampton. The second-year back had 27 yards rushing and 18 yards receiving on the drive, including a one-yard touchdown run to tie the game back at 7-7. Khalil Mack recorded his first sack of the season, beating the Raiders right tackle to bring down Cousins on third down and get the ball back to the offense in time for a two-minute drill ahead of the break. After platooning Trevor Penning in at right guard during their scoring drive, the Chargers put Cole Strange back in for the two-minute drill. The Bolts went 21 yards in four plays, but were forced to punt after Herbert and Johnston looked disconnected on a route that ended in an incompletion with nobody near where the ball fell. Cousins found Tucker again for a gain of 42 yards with 30 seconds left to get near field goal range. After several run stops by the Chargers for no gain, kicker Matt Gay connected from 59 yards out (a career long) to give the Raiders a 10-7 lead into halftime. Third Quarter The Chargers offense came out firing with a huge three-and-out forced that netted just one yard by the Raiders offense before they punted it away. Herbert and the offense responded in a massive way thanks to a huge 53-yard catch and run by Tre’ Harris to get the offense all the way down to the Las Vegas five-yard line. After a bobbled handoff exchange with Keaton Mitchell on first down, Herbert found Oronde Gadsden II in the back of the end zone after a nifty play-fake to take the lead 14-10 with 9:49 remaining the period. The Raiders responded to the Chargers touchdown with a score of their own which capped off a lengthy 11-play, 74-yard drive that ended in a Cousins pass to receiver Cody White who made a twisting catch over cornerback Rodney Shelley. The score put the Raiders back up on the Chargers 17-14 with 3:53 on the clock in the third. Herbert and the offense needed to once again meet the challenge and retaliate with a scoring drive of their own, but the inconsistent operation on offense reared its ugly head once more. On third-and-inches, Herbert motioned Harris from the right side of the formation to the left. However, center Jake Slaughter snapped the ball just as Harris passed behind him and the ball ricocheted off the receiver’s leg for a loss of four yards after Herbert managed to jump on it. Herbert was visibly enraged about the situation, yelling at his teammates during and after the debacle. Fourth Quarter On third-and-eight from the Chargers 46-yard line, Cousins luckily overthrew an open Malik Benson for what would have been a big gain early in the fourth quarter. The play forced another punt from the Raiders, but the Chargers could not do much with it on the other side. Herbert was nearly stripped inside his own 10-yard line but luckily the Chargers recovered at the two. A six-yard run by Hampton and a 12-yard pass to McConkey were just enough to move the…
