title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces seven active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks with the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook, heading into the season. 
 
 Garrett entered the season with 125.5 career sacks, which was tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald , who un-retired  to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald's 111 sacks currently sits two behind 30th.  
 
 As for Garrett, he entered his 10th season in the NFL averaging approximately 14 sacks per season. If he were to replicate that production, he would tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor, who currently sits at No. 7 all-time. If Garrett were to have another historic season, he would surpass Michael Strahan (No. 6) and approach top-five all-time territory. 
 
 
 
 Miller, who signed with the  Dallas Cowboys  in August, can also pass Strahan in his 15th season -- as he sits only three sacks behind him.   
 
 But Garrett's 125.5 career sacks were 10.5 more than any other player since his rookie season in 2017, according to ESPN Research, heading into the seaosn. The pass rusher recorded at least 14 sacks in each of the past five seasons, the longest such streak by any player since 1982. 
 
 If Garrett has 18.5 or more sacks this season, he will hold the record for the most over a two-season span since 1982, according to ESPN Research, and his current ascension up the all-time list ranks as the second-fastest pace among the top five all time behind only Reggie White.  
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape 
 We will update this file as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season. 
 

 

 Week 2 update 

 The second week of the season saw little movement near the top of the all-time list, but Watt's hot start continues, with the defensive end recording 1.5 sacks to now put him at 3.5 through two weeks and break a tie with Campbell to move to 25th. 

 Hunter (27th) and Mack (29th) also recorded 1 sack over the weekend to break ties and move up one spot on the list. 

 Donald (33rd) is set to make his season debut on "Monday Night Football" against the Giants.

 

 Week 1 update 

 Of all of the active sack leaders, Watt was the only one to record a sack, finishing the game with two to move to a tie with Campbell for 25th. 

 And while Donald was held out of the Rams' Week 1 game, Garrett will be out for at least the next four after failing to record a tackle in Australia and landing on injured reserve after having to have arthroscopic surgery on his knee.

 After the Rams' opening loss, Garrett said this was " the worst version of myself that I've put out there."

title: Who are the top 10 players without a Super Bowl ring?
summary: Introducing our Super Bowl Top 10s. First, we rank the best players who never won a championship, beginning with Dan Marino.
full_text:
Every NFL player has the same goal: win a Super Bowl ring.

 But football is the ultimate team sport, and with the exception of maybe someone such as  Tom Brady , it's hard for one player to will his team over the championship finish line. In the NFL today, active players such as Baltimore Ravens ' Calais Campbell (19th season) and New Orleans Saints ' Cameron Jordan (16th season) are still chasing a Super Bowl ring. Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (ninth season) has taken his team to the AFC Championship Game twice in eight tries and ran into Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs dynasty both times.

 

 How hard is it to win a Super Bowl? We ranked 10 of the best retired players who played at least half their careers in the Super Bowl era but never won a ring. Some of them made multiple appearances in the big game and came up just short, while others never made it beyond the conference championship. The methodology, which utilized Pro Football reference approximate values, included ESPN analyzing the statistics and intangibles of players in the Super Bowl era who didn't win a ring and put together a list ranking the best of the best.

 Here are 10 of the best players in NFL history who finished their careers without a Super Bowl win. Let's start with a Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback who spent his career with the Miami Dolphins .

 COUNTDOWN TO SUPER BOWL LXI: ESPN will televise the Super Bowl for the first time in February. We are counting down to the big game with a Super Bowl Top 10 series -- featuring rankings on everything from best catches and performances to biggest upsets -- that will run every other Sunday leading up to Super Bowl LXI on Feb. 14, 2027. 

 

 No. 1: Dan Marino, quarterback 
 Teams played for: Miami Dolphins (1983-99)

 What you might have forgotten: Marino's 1984 season was the gold standard for quarterbacks for years to come. Quarterbacks chased after Marino's single-season record of 5,084 passing yards for more than 20 years before Tom Brady and Drew Brees passed it in 2011. That 1984 season, Marino's second and his first full season as a starter, is still considered one of the best seasons by a quarterback. He led the NFL in passing attempts (564), completions (362), passing touchdowns (48), passing yards (5,084) and rating (108.9), among other records. 

 Number of Super Bowls Marino appeared in: 1 (Super Bowl XIX)

 Just how close did he come to winning a ring? Marino came into Super Bowl XIX with a 14-2 record as a starter that season and an MVP award. Unfortunately, he had to face the San Francisco 49ers ' Joe Montana in his prime. Both quarterbacks passed for more than 300 yards for the first time in the game's history, but Montana's 339 passing yards and 59 rushing yards were too much to overcome in a 38-16 win by the Niners.

 The Dolphins made it to two more AFC Championship Games, and Marino didn't play well in either of them, finishing with a 54.9 passer rating in a 31-14 loss to the New England Patriots in the 1985 AFC Championship Game and a 56.5 passer rating in a 29-10 loss to the Buffalo Bills in the 1993 AFC Championship Game.

 Marino retired with an 8-10 record in the playoffs after 17 seasons with the Dolphins.

 

 Marino said it: "That was the burning desire. That is what I played for," Marino said on the day he retired in March 2000. "That has been a dream of mine my whole career. I wanted to know -- as a player -- how it feels to win a Super Bowl."

 Why Marino is ranked No. 1: Though Marino's postseason play could be cause for debate, at his peak, he put up numbers that would still be respectable among quarterbacks today in a league that favors offenses. His 1984 season is among the greatest for a quarterback, but it ended without a ring due to the performance of another future HOF quarterback.

 

 No. 2: Barry Sanders, running back 
 Teams played for: Detroit Lions (1989-98)

 What you might have forgotten: The 5-foot-8 running back was picked third by the Lions in the 1989 draft, selected by a team whose last playoff win was 34 years before he got there. Sanders never had a Pro Bowl quarterback in his pro career, but he ran behind All-Pro left tackle Lomas Brown.

 Sanders, whose elusive running style gave defenses fits, abruptly retired on the eve of the 1999 season after making 10 All-Pro teams and winning two NFL Offensive Player of the Year honors and a shared MVP award with Brett Favre in 1997. Sanders retired with 15,269 rushing yards, the second most in NFL history at the time and still fourth all time. His 18,190 yards from scrimmage ranks seventh.

 Number of Super Bowls appeared in: 0

 

 Just how close did he come to winning a ring? Sanders' third season was his best chance for a Super Bowl appearance after the Lions made it to the NFC Championship Game, but the Lions were soundly defeated 41-10 by Washington. Sanders rushed only twice in the second half and finished with 11 carries for 44 yards. The Lions' 38-6 win against the Dallas Cowboys in the 1991 NFC divisional round was their last playoff win until the 2023 season.

 Sanders said it: "I had already achieved a level of success that gave me much satisfaction and pride. I didn't need to pass Walter [Payton and the career rushing record] to prove that to myself," Sanders wrote in his book : "Barry Sanders: Now You See Him ... His Story in His Own Words." 

 Why Sanders is ranked No. 2: Sanders left the game with the impression that he still had a lot more to give. His career is full of what-ifs -- what if he had played longer, or for a more successful team? While 30 is often considered an age in which running backs decline, Sanders had 1,780 all-purpose yards that final season. He never reached the physical point of no return -- he simply chose to walk away . 

 

 No. 3: Anthony Munoz, left tackle 
 Teams played for: Cincinnati Bengals (1980-92); Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1993 preseason)

 What you might have forgotten: When Munoz went into the Hall of Fame in 1998, he was described as "one of the most dominant offensive tackles in NFL history." Munoz was a big reason the Bengals had a run of sustained success in the 1980s. With Munoz paving the way for quarterback Ken Anderson, the Bengals' offense transformed from a bottom-two unit in his first season to a top-three group in Year 2.

 Number of Super Bowls appeared in: 2 (Super Bowl XVI, XXIII)

 Just how close did he come to winning a ring? The Bengals were one of many teams that lost to Montana and his Super Bowl successes with the Niners. Cincinnati turned the ball over four times in a 26-21 loss to San Francisco in Super Bowl XVI. The Bengals faced Montana again in Super Bowl XXIII, and he took the Niners on a 92-yard scoring drive late in the fourth quarter to win 20-16.

 

 Munoz said it: Last year on the "NFL Players Second Act Podcast," Munoz said all he wanted was a chance despite his injury history. The Bengals gave it to him, and three days into camp, the third pick in the 1980 draft realized he had greater ambition. "I told myself, I don't only want to compete, I want to be the best. I want to be a Pro Bowler every year," he recalled . 

 Why Munoz is ranked No. 3: How much impact can a left tackle have? The Bengals had seven top-10 offenses and four playoff appearances when he was there, and their 1990 win in the AFC wild-card round was their last playoff victory until the 2021 season. But Munoz, who earned 11 consecutive All-Pro and Pro Bowl nods, wasn't just a great tackle. He caught four touchdown passes and had a long career despite multiple knee surgeries before he turned pro. Munoz was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary team in 2019.

 

 No. 4: Dick Butkus, linebacker 
 Teams played for: Chicago Bears (1965-73)

 What you might have forgotten: Mean, tough and nasty are just some of the adjectives to describe the linebacker. He had the shortest career of anyone on this list, playing nine years and 119 games. Butkus retired in 1973 at 31…

title: Week 2 impact on the NFC: Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels hurt
summary: Caleb Williams and Jayden Daniels both got injured. The Packers nearly lost to the Jets. The Saints upset the Ravens. And three teams have a claim as the NFC's best.
full_text:
It's hard to say that any week of an NFL season can feel seismic, especially when it's the second week of the campaign. But I believe we're going to look back on Week 2 and say it was extraordinarily impactful in deciding and decoding the NFC.

 Injuries to young quarterbacks were the biggest stories of the day, but we also saw several of the conference's top contenders reaffirm themselves with big victories, a couple of teams we're still not sure about squeak by and a preseason contender narrowly save itself from the 0-2 cliff. We even saw the NFC South get on the board with a pair of victories.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Let's run through some of the results and events from Sunday that might really matter in the NFC's big picture and break down how they played out and how they impact the conference moving forward. I'll start with the game in Dallas, where the Commanders are facing serious short- and long-term questions about what's next.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 WSH and Daniels' injury 
 CHI and Williams' injury 
 NO and its big win 
 GB and its near loss 
 Three teams at the top 

 
 

 

 Washington Commanders (0-2) 
 Lost 37-20 to the Cowboys 

 Sunday showed why organizations were both transfixed and terrified by the idea of drafting Jayden Daniels as their quarterback of the future. For most of the first half, Daniels was single-handedly propelling the Commanders forward on offense. In addition to going 11-of-17 for 96 yards as a passer, he picked up five first downs with his legs, scrambling seven times for 69 yards. Having a QB capable of bailing the offense out and picking up explosive plays in the process gives the Commanders a floor that most other teams don't have on a weekly basis.

 And then, on the final play of the first half, we saw the other side of the coin. With the Commanders passing up a field goal attempt to try to score a touchdown with three seconds remaining, Daniels took the snap from under center and got caught up in the footwork of left guard Chris Paul . As Daniels fell to the ground, he tried to brace with his left elbow, only for it to visibly give way and dislocate. He somehow got up and threw an incomplete pass and then did not return after halftime in a game that got away from Washington after the break.

 

 The injury is likely to sideline Daniels for an extended period. He missed four games after dislocating the same elbow in Week 9 a year ago, then aggravated the injury in Week 14 and did not return over the remainder of the season. Missing a month would be a season-altering injury for the Commanders, who are already 0-2 and about to face the defending champion Seahawks in their home opener next week. Marcus Mariota is a capable backup, but the veteran doesn't offer the same sort of explosiveness and calmness under pressure that Daniels exhibited during his remarkable rookie season.

 The excuses that factored into Daniels' injury last season also don't apply. A year ago, coach Dan Quinn took the blame for having him on the field late in a lopsided game. Unless you want to be particularly pedantic about the idea that the Commanders should have taken the points on one play on the road against one of the best offenses in football, Daniels was on the field in a situation where he belonged. This wasn't a risky play or a product of taking too many hits as a runner. Even among those six scrambles I mentioned earlier, he ended the play by sliding or stepping out of bounds five times. This is early in the season without the sort of significant accumulation of hits that might wear Daniels down late in a campaign.

 In the past, it was easy to believe that he would stay healthy if he took fewer hits or if Quinn had him out of a noncompetitive game. The Commanders moved him out of the shotgun and the quarterback-read run game, putting him under center more often to try to keep him healthier. And yet, in a complete fluke, Daniels had his foot stepped on here.

 After a mostly healthy rookie season in 2024, Daniels will now have gone no more than three games without missing a start to injury since the beginning of the 2025 season. How do you rely on that QB as your franchise passer, even one as talented as Daniels? He'll be eligible for a contract extension after this season. Even if he returns after a month and stays healthy for the rest of the year, will the Commanders realistically be able to justify giving the face of their franchise the sort of contract his play deserves? Can you bet $60 million or more per year on that player if you can't count on him being on the field for most of the season, let alone all of it?

 The Commanders can pick up Daniels' fifth-year option and go year-to-year while holding on to the franchise tag, of course, but if there's any organization that knows the dangers of playing that game, it should be Washington. When it was under former owner Daniel Snyder, this same franchise picked up Robert Griffin 's fifth-year option, then sat him during his fourth season to avoid triggering the injury guarantee on that option year. (This was before all fifth-year options were fully guaranteed at the time of signing.) Washington franchised Kirk Cousins twice, lost him in free agency for nothing and then spent years cycling through quarterbacks before eventually landing on Daniels, who looked to be their QB of the future.

 What's more concerning is that Daniels isn't the only issue. Star left tackle Laremy Tunsil is out for most of the year with a torn triceps . Guard Sam Cosmi , who was excellent in the opening-week loss to the Eagles , was hit by his own teammate and needed help walking off the field after an extended time down. And 31-year-old wideout Terry McLaurin , coming off a contract extension and a disappointing 2025 season, has four catches on 13 targets through two games. Even a defense that looked solid in Week 1 allowed the Cowboys to score 37 points on eight drives Sunday.

 

 And yet, as with so many teams through two weeks, the Commanders could point to a couple of moments and feel like they were close to being 2-0. A fourth-quarter comeback against the Eagles was scuppered by a successful Jalen Hurts scramble on third-and-18 and Washington's failed 2-point try on a shovel pass to John Bates . Against the Cowboys, the Commanders narrowly missed on what should have been a pair of long touchdown passes to McLaurin and Treylon Burks  -- each on a drive that ended up producing zero points.

 Last season, a Commanders team with Super Bowl aspirations lost Daniels to an injury at the end of the game in Week 2 for a couple of weeks, kicking off what would be a wildly frustrating season. After an 0-2 start and another Daniels injury, it certainly feels like another one of those wasted years for Washington, if not something even more ominous.

 

 
 

 Chicago Bears (1-1) 
 Lost 9-3 to the Vikings 

 The Bears, meanwhile, might be facing a slightly better scenario than the one they feared Sunday afternoon. One week after he led the Bears to a 59-point performance against the Panthers , quarterback  Caleb Williams was struggling against a much more difficult opponent in Brian Flores' hyperaggressive Vikings defense. Battling the rain for most of the day, Williams and coach Ben Johnson finally found a way to create a big play against a Flores blitz look, faking a screen one way and slipping D'Andre Swift out the other for a 32-yard completion. After converting a fourth-and-1, the Bears were set up with a first-and-goal opportunity and a shot to take the lead midway through the final quarter.

 And then most of Chicago went silent. A scrambling Williams went down short of the goal line, clutched his hamstring and didn't get up. The 2024 first overall pick (taken one spot before Daniels) had to be helped off the field, was carted to the locker room with his face concealed by a towel and did not return . title: Who are the winningest NFL coaches of all time?
summary: From Belichick to Reid, there are many iconic coaches in NFL history. Who has the best career record? Check out the stat breakdown now.
full_text:
Only four head coaches in NFL history have won 300 career games across the regular season and postseason. Kansas City Chiefs  coach Andy Reid was the last to cross the 300-win plateau.

 Reid recorded his 300th career victory on Jan. 18, 2025, when his Chiefs defeated the Houston Texans 23-14 in the AFC divisional round.

 Reid, who signed a five-year, $100 million extension with the Chiefs in April 2024, entered the 2026 season looking to add to his career win total and close the gap between him and the NFL's all-time winningest head coach, Hall of Famer Don Shula.

 Let's take a look at which head coaches have the most career victories in NFL history (including both regular-season and postseason play):

 *Active NFL head coach 

 5. Tom Landry, 270 wins 

 Landry was the Dallas Cowboys' head coach for an NFL-record 29 years in a row and the team had 20 consecutive winning seasons, which is also a league record. Landry led Dallas to two Super Bowl wins, defeating the Miami Dolphins in Super Bowl VI and the Denver Broncos in Super Bowl XII. He was named the NFL's Coach of the Year in 1966 and the UPI NFL Coach of the Year in 1975. Landry was an innovator, with the 4-3 defense among his creations. He was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

 *4. Andy Reid, 309 wins 

 Reid is the only head coach in NFL history who has won 100 games with two franchises: the Philadelphia Eagles (coaching the team from 1999 through 2012) and the Chiefs (he has coached Kansas City since 2013). He led the Eagles on multiple deep playoff runs, including a Super Bowl in 2004 and three straight conference finals from 2001 to 2003. However, he wasn't able to hoist the Lombardi Trophy until he arrived in Kansas City. He has turned the Chiefs into a juggernaut, winning three Super Bowls. Reid is an offensive mastermind and quarterback whisperer. He'll likely continue to rack up wins moving forward with Patrick Mahomes , Travis Kelce & Co.

 

 3. George Halas, 324 wins 

 Halas was a co-founder of the NFL and creator of the Bears. For 10 years, he served as player-coach-executive for the Bears (which is how he earned the nickname "Mr. Everything"). In 1930, he retired as a player and focused on ownership, but he would later return to coach the Bears several times. Halas led the Bears to eight NFL championships, tying Belichick's number of titles. Halas coached the team for 40 years and had just six losing seasons. He helped create the T-formation system and used it to set an NFL record for the biggest blowout in league history: a 73-0 win over the Washington team in the 1940 NFL Championship Game. Halas was selected as the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 1963 and 1965, and he was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

 2. Bill Belichick, 333 wins 

 Belichick is considered by some as the greatest coach in all of professional sports, as he has won an NFL-record eight Super Bowls (six as a head coach with the Patriots and two as an assistant coach with the Giants). He also ranks first among all NFL coaches in playoff wins with 31. Belichick was named the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 2003, 2007 and 2010. Many franchises have hired away Belichick's assistants and tried to replicate his "Patriot Way," but it hasn't been the same without him. If Belichick returns to NFL coaching, he is just 26 regular-season wins from surpassing Don Shula as the winningest regular-season coach of all time. 

 1. Don Shula, 347 wins 

 After playing in the NFL as a defensive back for seven seasons, Shula decided to retire and become a coach. He got his first head-coaching opportunity in 1963 with the Baltimore Colts, whom he led to the NFL championship in 1968. From 1970 through 1995, Shula had a legendary run as head coach of the Dolphins. Shula led the Dolphins to a pair of Super Bowl victories (in Super Bowl VII and Super Bowl VIII). Miami had a perfect season in 1972, making Shula the only coach in NFL history to go undefeated. He was named the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 1964, 1967, 1968 and 1972. Whether you're just counting regular-season wins (328) or including playoff wins (347), Shula is the winningest coach in NFL history.

title: Judging the biggest overreactions to NFL Week 2 games
summary: Will Aaron Rodgers stay QB1 all season? Is anything different for the Eagles' offense? And could the Lions miss the postseason again? We're judging Week 2 overreactions.
full_text:
OK, so we all know we aren't supposed to overreact to Week 1 of the NFL season . But what about Week 2 ???

 Is this enough data yet? Are we ready to crown the Bills as the team to beat? Are the Panthers truly an offensive juggernaut? Are teams out of their minds to not be hiring Brian Flores as a head coach? Is the Bengals' defense suddenly really good?

 Yes, of course it's still too soon. And of course we still don't know anything. But we have twice as much information as we had a week ago, so why not dive in? It's our Week 2 overreactions column, where we look at five potential takeaways and judge them as legitimate stances or irrational overreactions. Plus, we hit a few fantasy football overreactions at the bottom.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Rodgers on thin ice? 
 Same Eagles offense? 
 Huge QB problems for Atlanta? 
 Flores should be a head coach? 
 Lions missing the playoffs? 
 Fantasy overreactions 

 
 

 

 Aaron Rodgers will get benched at some point this season 
 Rodgers came back for one more season with the Steelers and reunited with his old Packers coach Mike McCarthy. Neat story ... not such a neat offense so far.

 The Steelers were sluggish in their Week 1 victory over the Falcons , and they were putrid Sunday in a 20-3 loss to the Patriots in Foxborough, Massachusetts. The Patriots sacked Rodgers four times. One of those resulted in a fumble that New England ran back for a touchdown to effectively ice the game early in the fourth quarter.

 

 Rodgers had no answer for New England's pressure, whether the Patriots were blitzing or not. He was 5-of-12 for 34 yards and four sacks when pressured Sunday. The Patriots blitzed him on 19 of 44 dropbacks, and Rodgers was 8-for-17 for 42 yards, two sacks and an interception on those. Through two games this season, Rodgers is completing 33% of his passes for an average of 3.5 yards per attempt when pressured. This is not sustainable, and the fact that Rodgers is 42 years old makes the extent to which he's getting pressured and hit all the more worrisome.

 Verdict: OVERREACTION 

 I simply do not believe that McCarthy would bench Rodgers in his final season for Mason Rudolph , Will Howard or Drew Allar  -- at least not until the Steelers are eliminated from postseason contention. These two guys reunited in Pittsburgh this year to pursue a championship together, and no matter what the rest of us think, they believe it's possible and won't give up the ghost until they have to.

 Plus, you really can't lay Sunday's performance entirely at Rodgers' feet. The Steelers need to figure out a run game and some better protection schemes if they're going to keep Rodgers upright and have a chance this season. It's just too early to sit here and predict that they won't.

 

 
 

 The Eagles' offense isn't any better than it was last season 
 Yes, they won. They almost always do. The Eagles came back to beat the Titans 24-20 on Sunday in oppressive September Nashville heat. But still ... they had 2.8 yards per rush, 4.7 yards per play overall and two turnovers. It just felt like everything was difficult, which was a 2025 characteristic of the Eagles' offense -- one they were hoping to improve with another coordinator change.

 Quarterback Jalen Hurts was pressured on 24 of 42 dropbacks, which is the highest percentage (57%) the Eagles have allowed since ESPN began tracking pressure metrics in 2009 and raises concerns about the effectiveness of a banged-up offensive line that's playing without star guard Landon Dickerson . Two years ago, when the Eagles steamrolled their way to their second Super Bowl title, their offensive line was straight-up dominant . It has not been thus since the 2024 season.

 Verdict: OVERREACTION 

 Sure, Hurts was pressured a lot, but he was awesome Sunday when pressured. He was 11-for-20 for 137 yards and two touchdowns, including the winning TD in the final seconds. Saquon Barkley left this game early with an injury, and although he came back briefly in the second half, he wasn't able to finish the contest. That surely emboldened the Titans' pressure plan.

 I get that it doesn't look great or smooth. But it's Week 2, and the Eagles are 2-0 while they're putting things together. Two of the big questions coming into this season were whether Hurts could thrive with all the change that was made around him and whether  DeVonta Smith  could fill the No. 1 receiver role with A.J. Brown traded to New England. Well, Hurts was heroic in leading the comeback, and Smith caught 10 passes for 117 yards and a touchdown.

 There are a lot of offenses with a lot less hope than the Eagles deserve to have in theirs right now.

 

 

 
 

 Matt Ryan needs to find his shoulder pads and helmet because the Falcons might need him at QB 
 Ryan is in his first season as the Falcons' president of football. And the greatest quarterback in franchise history cannot like what he's seeing right now out of his team's QB situation.

 Michael Penix Jr . has missed the first two games while still recovering from last season's ACL tear . Tua Tagovailoa has missed both games with a back injury . Cooper Rush has been awful in both games as the fill-in starter, and rookie Jack Strand clearly isn't ready. The Falcons' quarterback situation is a complete mess. Head coach Kevin Stefanski has to be wondering how he could possibly have left Cleveland's QB situation for one that isn't demonstrably better.

 Verdict: OVERREACTION 

 It sounds like there's at least a chance that Penix can start this Thursday's game in Green Bay . And while Penix's past performance isn't any kind of guarantee that he'll play well, he's surely going to be a better option than Rush has been.

 Moreover, the Falcons need to get a long look at Penix at some point this season before they decide whether the No. 8 pick of the 2024 draft is part of their long-term QB solution or they need to look for one in next year's draft. This is a brand-new coaching staff and a brand-new front office with no built-in loyalty to Penix and a mandate to fix the quarterback situation once and for all. Ryan can leave his shoulder pads in the closet for now, as there are still likely plenty of twists and turns to come in this saga as the season moves along.

 

 
 

 Brian Flores deserves another chance to be a head coach 
 The Vikings' defensive coordinator is as locked in right now as any playcaller on either side of the ball. A week after the Bears scored a stunning 59 points against Carolina , the Vikings held Chicago to just three points in a 9-3 victory that should never be replayed on any television or internet-connected device for the remainder of time.

 Flores' defense blitzed Packers QB Jordan Love on 72% of his dropbacks in Week 1 and then turned it up even further Sunday, blitzing Bears QB Caleb Williams on 78% of his dropbacks. That's the highest blitz percentage any NFL quarterback has faced since Detroit's Jared Goff was blitzed on 79% of his dropbacks in Week 18 of the 2023 season by ... yep, the Vikings. What's remarkable about what Flores is doing right now isn't just that he's blitzing at such an extreme rate -- it's that his players are so bought into what he's calling, and so practiced at executing it, that it feels like Flores could call anything he wants right now and count on it to work.

 

 This is his fourth season as Minnesota's defensive coordinator, and the former Dolphins head coach has established himself as possibly the scariest playcaller in the league.

 Verdict: NOT AN OVERREACTION 

 I understand this issue is complicated by what we've learned about Flores' time as Miami's head coach and the fact that he still has a pending lawsuit against the league alleging racial discrimination in NFL hiring practices. It's not a stretch at all to believe that team owners might be reluctant to hire Flores as a head coach while he's suing the league, and it's possible he won't get another crack at the big job until that suit is dropped or settled. And…

title: Van Ness' breakout game saves Packers in OT win vs. Jets
summary: Packers hope it's a sign of things to come as Micah Parsons nears his return from a torn ACL.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- No one was more excited about what Lukas Van Ness did in Sunday's 20-17 overtime win against the New York Jets than Micah Parsons -- to the point that Parsons was telling some of his fellow Green Bay Packers defensive players that Van Ness was so dominant at the line of scrimmage that he should never, ever drop into coverage.

 And the more Parsons talked in the back corner of the locker room, the louder he got.

 After all, Parsons has been touting the underachieving Van Ness ever since Parsons arrived in Green Bay last year. This offseason, he predicted the defensive end would break out and said Van Ness' popularity might rival his own.

 

 Parsons, who has at least two more weeks on the physically unable to perform list before he can come back from last year's torn ACL, might have some catching up to do after a game like this from Van Ness: nine tackles (three for a loss), 1.5 sacks and four quarterback hits.

 The Packers needed every bit of it to come back from a 10-point fourth-quarter deficit and beat the Jets in overtime at MetLife Stadium on a day when injuries piled up , especially on offense.

 While Parsons slipped out the back door without talking to reporters, there were plenty of others left to sing Van Ness' praises.

 "He was all over the place," coach Matt LaFleur said.

 "It seemed like he was everywhere," Packers safety Evan Williams said.

 "He was flying around making a lot of plays, especially at the end," quarterback Jordan Love said.

 

 The end was when they needed it the most.

 How about a fourth-and-1 stuff of running back Braelon Allen at midfield with the game tied and 1:15 left in regulation? It got the Packers to overtime.

 And what about a shared sack with rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton on the Jets' second play of overtime right after Barryn Sorrell and Brandon Cisse sacked Geno Smith on the first play? Next thing you know, the Jets were in third-and-30 and punting the ball away to set up Trey Smack 's game-winning field goal.

 "I was just focused on dominating," said Van Ness, whose status for the game was unclear until Saturday when he passed the concussion protocol.

 To be sure, there were other standout defensive plays by other players. There was Williams' breakup of a deep pass intended for receiver  Adonai Mitchell right before the 2-minute warning in the fourth quarter. There was safety  Xavier McKinney 's tackle on third down to stop a drive and force a punt that Skyy Moore returned 63 yards to set up the game-tying field goal with 2:59 left in regulation. And there was coordinator Jonathan Gannon seemingly knowing exactly when to send pressure.

 "I can't give enough credit to our defense, our defensive staff, Jonathan Gannon, just calling a very aggressive game," LaFleur said. "I'm sure glad we got him because I think he's an elite defensive coordinator, football coach and just a great leader."

 

 But it kept coming back to Van Ness, the 2023 first-round pick who in two games this season has 2.5 sacks, which is one more than he had all of last season.

 "Barring injury last year, he would've been doing the same stuff," Packers tight end Tucker Kraft said. "He was already doing the same stuff that he's doing right now, so with a guy like Lukas Van Ness, you hate to say the sky's the limit because I think that he can be even better than that. He's a dog. He's a physical specimen, and I'd hate to have to play against him when the lights are actually on."

 The Packers were banking on this kind of production from Van Ness when they made him the No. 13 pick of the 2023 draft. That was the pick they got via the Jets as part of the Aaron Rodgers trade.

 Now, they can't wait to see what Van Ness and Parsons can do together whenever Parsons returns from his knee injury. PUP rules say Parsons can actually begin practicing this coming week even though he's not allowed to play before Week 5 against the Bears.

 "It's gonna be fun," Van Ness said of playing with Parsons. "I'm excited about it, and that's what's been so important with him continuing to be involved in meetings and the film room, and just how we're gonna communicate on the football field and align our rushes and work together. I can't wait for the day he gets back, and we're gonna have a lot of fun together."

title: How to bet Giants-Rams on MNF: Analysis, tips and favorite plays
summary: Odds, bets and analysis to help you bet Giants-Rams on "Monday Night Football."
full_text:
The New York Giants ' offense hummed in its opener and will look to prove it isn't a pretender as the team travels to Los Angeles for another primetime affair.

 The revamped Giants regime put together a triumphant debut, besting the division rival Dallas Cowboys by a score of 28-20 in Week 1. Big Blue controlled much of the contest, despite the single-digit differential. Jaxson Dart picked apart Dallas' secondary, managing a career-best completion percentage of 70.3% while throwing for 230 yards and three scores. In addition to his arm, Dart successfully flustered the Cowboys' defensive front with his legs, closing out the contest with 54 rushing yards on 11 attempts (4.9 yards per carry). In classic John Harbaugh-ian fashion, the ground attack remained physical and efficient, with Cam Skattebo leading the charge with 81 rushing yards, a score and an accompanying end zone backflip.

 

 In stark contrast, the Los Angeles Rams repeatedly tripped up, eventually stalling out against a resurgent San Francisco 49ers squad. Snapping a 17-game TD streak, Matthew Stafford appeared particularly disjointed, finishing with a meager 155 passing yards and a dismal 61.2 quarterback rating. The ground game proved more effective, as the tandem of Kyren Williams and Blake Corum combined for 95 rushing yards and the team's lone score before being scripted out of the contest. The duo will look to establish pace against Giants DC Dennard Wilson's rejuvenated unit.

 Back on home soil and with 10 days to prepare, the Rams have a distinct advantage over the traveling G-Men. Still, with Myles Garrett on IR (knee) and questions swirling around Aaron Donald 's return to action and Puka Nacua 's health ( questionable, groin ), the Giants shouldn't be overlooked. Expect Harbaugh to build on the suffocating approach he took in Week 1, focusing on winning the time-of-possession battle via long drives and efficient passing. Meanwhile, Sean McVay should counter by establishing an up-tempo rhythm early, aggressively dispatching Davante Adams  and his other available pass catchers downfield.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 

 Even with Nacua potentialy sitting, both teams have the adequate firepower to put up points. That's why I'm eyeing the total in this clash . Despite a lackluster Week 1, the Rams' dynamic aerial attack should improve, particularly given key injuries to the Giants' secondary. If Los Angeles gets up early, Dart won't hesitate to push the offense while leaning on a healthy-enough Malik Nabers . With Garrett sidelined and Donald likely on a snap count, the sophomore signal-caller figures to be gifted sufficient time to convert, ultimately boosting the combined score toward 50 points.

 

 The market is anticipating a bounce-back effort from the Super Bowl favorites in their first home game of the season. I liked the Giants' potential to cover when the spread opened at the beginning of the week, featuring the Rams as 8.5-point favorites. However, that number has since shrunk. With so many variables still in question and so little data yet at our avail, a wager on the spread seems like a dicey endeavor.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Matthew Stafford passing yards OVER 238.5 (-113) 

 Eric Moody: Stafford was unusually inaccurate and out of sync with his receivers in Week 1 against the 49ers in Australia. With Nacua, if he can play, and Davante Adams forming one of the league's top wide receiver duos, I expect Stafford to bounce back and remind everyone he's an MVP-caliber quarterback. He cleared this line in 15 of 20 games last season, including the postseason.

 

 Jaxson Dart rushing attempts OVER 6.5 (+102) 

 Loza: Dart managed seven or more carries in six of 12 starts last season. He took off 11 times in Week 1. Notably, five of those attempts were designed runs, indicating OC Matt Nagy's intention to lean on Dart's mobility. With the Rams sending regular pressure, it also makes sense that a dual-threat talent like Dart might attempt to utilize his legs. To what success remains to be seen. Still, with the Giants likely to employ a heavy ground approach, expect Dart to tally seven or more totes on Monday night.

 Dart rushing yards OVER 33.5 (-108) 

 Pamela Maldonado: Dart's legs are part of what makes him difficult to defend. He showed that right away in Week 1. And his involvement in the run game goes back to his rookie season. Donald's return makes attacking the Rams straight up the middle more difficult, but the Giants' offense can create opportunities for Dart when the pocket collapses or the play calls for moving him outside. With Garrett out, the Rams also lose their best edge presence. Whether through designed runs or scrambles, Dart should have enough chances to threaten this total without needing another huge rushing performance.

title: Donald in, Garrett out: How will Rams defense look with huge addition (and subtraction)?
summary: Despite the defensive tackle returning from retirement, L.A. has never doubted that he could still make an impact.
full_text:
LOS ANGELES -- When Aaron Donald runs onto the field at SoFi Stadium on Monday night, it will have been 981 days since he last played in an NFL game.

 Though the future Pro Football Hall of Fame defensive tackle said he knows it has been two full seasons since he walked off the field after the season-ending loss to the Detroit Lions , in a way, it feels like he never left.

 "[After] being back around, I feel like I was just here last year," Donald said. "Time flies by so fast, and I forget that I haven't play[ed] football for two years. I feel like I'm just back to my normal self."

 Donald did not play in -- or even travel to -- the Rams' season-opening loss to the  San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne, Australia, as he worked to get up to speed after coming out of retirement Aug. 30.

 He began thinking about rejoining the Rams after hearing from coach Sean McVay in late May that Los Angeles was considering trading for reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett . In the past three years, the Rams had built "a stacked" defensive line, Donald said, but when the Rams traded for Garrett on June 1, Donald started to think about how much fun he might have playing with the group.

 

 Donald's return to the field Monday night against the New York Giants ( 8:15 ET, ESPN ) will look slightly different than he and the team expected. A week ago, Garrett had arthroscopic surgery on his knee, requiring a trip to the injured reserve list that will keep the pass rusher sidelined for at least the next four games. Though McVay said Garrett's absence is unrelated to how the Rams will handle Donald's return, there's no doubt not having the pass rusher on the field -- despite the outstanding pass-rush group around him -- impacts Donald.

 Instead of the chance to play with a player who might be double-teamed, giving him the chance to face more single coverage than he did throughout his career, Donald will likely be getting the extra attention from teams, even if he hasn't played in two seasons.

 Despite Donald not playing in 2024 or '25, he ranks second in pass rush wins since 2017, according to ESPN Analytics/NFL Next Gen Stats. He had that success even though he was double-teamed on the fourth-most pass rush plays in the NFL over that span. His 276 pass rush wins against double-teams are still by far the most in the league since 2017, when pass rush win rate was first tracked.

 Though Donald laughed off the idea of being double- or triple-teamed after coming out of retirement -- "They ain't worried about me, man!" -- McVay said he believes the Rams will see Donald playing at the same level he did before he retired.

 In early September, 49ers left tackle Trent Williams described going against Donald as "trying to catch a fish in water with your bare hands."

 "I expect him to be the same [No.] 99 that the league grew to fear," Williams said.

 
 

 AFTER DONALD ANNOUNCED his return, McVay made it clear that the team would not rush him back into a game.

 Although Donald stayed in shape after retirement, he has acknowledged that at 35, his ramp-up to practicing and playing again looked different than his first stint in the NFL. Though Donald did individual drills the day he signed his one-year deal with the Rams, he did not take part in 11-on-11 drills until Sept. 6.

 "I'm 35, I didn't play football in two years, so you have to be smart," Donald said as he worked his way back. "Even if I feel good, you still have to be smart."

 As the Rams and Donald decided whether the defensive tackle would play against the Giants, they wanted to see how he felt after practicing in full on back-to-back days. Because the Rams traveled to Melbourne for Week 1, there hadn't been as many opportunities for Donald to take part in team drills. But on Friday, Donald said he was feeling like himself.

 "I feel a lot better now that I got more practice under my belt instead of one," Donald said. "I'm getting in the groove of things, understanding everything a lot better out there, playing a lot more free, a lot more loose, and looking more like myself to me."

 Donald has been clear that it was important to him that if he were going to return to the Rams, he wanted to do it at the same level he played at before he first retired. Though Los Angeles believes it is getting back the version of Donald who was a three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and an eight-time first-team All-Pro, the Rams also know the success will come with him playing in a different role than he did when he played 76.46% of defensive snaps during his final season before he retired.

 Despite the success Donald has had during his career, Rams defensive coordinator Chris Shula said Donald hasn't wanted "any type of special treatment" in his return and "just loves being one of the guys."

 "Not that we expected anything different," Shula said, "but it is really cool to see when future Hall of Famers act like that."

 Though it will be different than Donald is used to, the Rams don't need him in that role, even with Garrett on IR. Donald said he has embraced his responsibility, whatever that looks like. The defensive tackle said he thinks the reduced usage will help him feel "a lot more fresh" during a long season.

 "We have a lot of good football players out here," Donald said. "My game plan is, however it's going to be, I'm going to go out there and play hard. And when I need a break, tap out, let the next guy go out there and eat, and I'll be right back. I think we have a good game plan to get myself going and get this team going.

 "Whatever that role is, I'm ready for it."

 

 DESPITE THE FACT  that Donald will be on the field without Garrett on Monday night, the defensive tackle says he doesn't feel added pressure.

 "We still have a lot of good players around us, around me at least, to be comfortable," Donald said. "I'm just one guy. I'm just one guy. There are a lot of good football players out there that have been here for the last two years when I wasn't even playing football, so we're going to be good, and when he gets back, we'll be even better."

 

 Though Garrett will miss at least the next four games on IR, McVay said the team will not rush him back before he can play at the level he is accustomed to. The loss to the 49ers was Garrett's first game without a tackle since Week 11 of the 2024 season and just the fourth of his career, according to ESPN Research.

 "I've got to find a way to recover and get back to the player I know I can be and I've shown that I've been before," Garrett said after that game.

 McVay said he doesn't think Donald puts pressure on himself, but that "the standards that he has for himself are different than I think anyone could place on him."

 "There's an intrinsic motivation," McVay said. "There's a rage to master your craft. There's an ability to pick things up quickly in your domain. He's checking all those boxes. This guy is as driven as anybody as I've been around, the work capacity, the competitive stamina. I love everything this guy is about."

 Donald has a pre-practice routine that goes back to when he played at the University of Pittsburgh. Donald walks onto the practice field early and finds one of the large red medicine balls, somewhere else to sit and lets himself relax and appreciate where he is. Donald is aware that not many players have the chance to walk away from the NFL on their terms and have the chance to come back.

 By playing in a game Monday, Donald will join Deion Sanders as the only players in NFL history to be a five-time first-team All-Pro, have a 750-day layoff and return to the NFL, per ESPN Research.

 "I'm just taking it all in," Donald said. "This is a blessing to be out here playing this game. I still remember as a kid dreaming about and wishing to get to the NFL. As a guy that played 10 years, retired and got to come back and do it again, I'm taking this moment in, taking it all in, and just enjoying my blessing."

title: NFL betting buzz: Most popular survivor pick loses for second week in a row with Bucs' defeat
summary: With 27% of ESPN survivor picks and 6,601 entries in Circa Survivor, the Bucs lost at home to the Browns.
full_text:
Everything that happens in sports has additional context when viewed from a sports betting perspective. From season-changing injuries to record-setting moments and so much more, the sports news cycle will constantly and significantly affect the sports betting industry. 

 Our NFL betting buzz file, with contributions from David Purdum, Doug Greenberg and others, aims to provide fans a look at the sports betting stories that are driving the conversation throughout each week of the season.  

 Key links: NFL futures | Awards odds |  Sports betting home  |  DraftKings   

 

 Sept. 20: Most popular survivor pick loses for second week in a row 

 By David Purdum 

 The most popular pick in ESPN survivor contests lost for a second straight week.

 In Week 1, it was the Los Angeles Chargers , who were upended by the Arizona Cardinals . On Sunday, it was the Tampa Bay Buccaneers as they fell to the Cleveland Browns .

 The Chargers were picked in 21% of ESPN entries last week. The Bucs were backed by 27% this week.

 In the high-stakes Circa Survivor contest ($1,000 buy-in, $25 million prize pool), 6,601 entries backed the Bucs in Week 2. Only the San Francisco 49ers (versus the Miami Dolphins ) were more popular.

 The 49ers took care of their business, but the Buccaneers did not and lost to the Browns 24-19 at home in a game that featured a lengthy weather delay.

 If it provides any solace for Tampa Bay supporters, 42 entries in the Circa contest failed to submit their picks by the deadline. Those entries are now worth the same as the 6,601 that had the Buccaneers.

 Tampa Bay, an 8.5-point favorite, failed to cover the spread in its 11th straight game, tied for the longest such streak in the Super Bowl era, according to ESPN Research.

 Ahead of the primetime game, Tampa Bay was one of five favorites that lost outright Sunday, joining the Baltimore Ravens ,  Chicago Bears ,  Houston Texans  and Chargers.

 

 Sept. 13: Circa Survivor kicks off with $25 million grand prize, Jaguars lead Week 1 picks 
 

 By Doug Greenberg 

 The Circa Sports pro football contests are locked in for the 2026 season with a total of $38.7 million on the line. 

 Circa Survivor will begin the season with a record 25,017 entries, making a winner-take-all $25,017,000 prize pool. The contest exceeded its guarantee of $20 million with four days remaining before registration closed.

 Grandissimo, Circa's $100,000-per-entry survivor contest, also easily met its $4 million guarantee and ended up with a record 77 entries vying for a $7.7 million prize pool. The casino's traditional $100,000-per-entry handicapping contest, Circa Million, did not meet its $6 million guarantee and ended up with 5,790 entries, creating an overlay of $210,000.

 Circa Survivor is the largest legal pro football contest in the country. Contestants pick one NFL team to win outright each week, with the caveat that they cannot use that team again the rest of the season. The entries must survive all 18 weeks of the regular season, plus two "mini weeks" for the Thanksgiving and Christmas slates.

 The Jacksonville Jaguars are the most popular pick in the contest for Week 1, with 8,121 entries (32.5% of the pool) selecting them to defeat the Cleveland Browns . The Los Angeles Chargers come in next at 7,585 entries (30.3%) and the Pittsburgh Steelers round out the top three at 4,013 entries (16.1%). 

 Some entries opted to pick from the first two games of the season, with 174 (0.7%) getting through with the Seattle Seahawks and 10 (~0.0%) surviving with the San Francisco 49ers . On the flip side, 49 entries (0.2%) backed the Los Angeles Rams and 25 (0.1%) were on the New England Patriots , leading to their immediate elimination.

 There were also 18 (0.1%) immediate eliminations via the dreaded No Pick designation.

 

 Sept. 11: Rams suffer worst opening loss by preseason Super Bowl favorite in 50 years 
 

 by David Purdum 

 Preseason Super Bowl favorites have lost before, just not as badly as the Los Angeles Rams did Thursday in Melbourne, Australia.

 The Rams lost 27-7 to the San Francisco 49ers , becoming the first preseason Super Bowl favorite to lose its opener by 20 or more in the past 50 seasons, according to SportsOddHistory.com. The 1993 Dallas Cowboys lost by 19, and the 2017 New England Patriots and 1987 New York Giants each lost by 15 in their season openers. Both the Cowboys and Patriots would play in the Super Bowl in those seasons, with the Cowboys winning and the Patriots losing, but the Giants failed to make the playoffs.

 Los Angeles closed as a 3.5-point favorite over the 49ers and attracted the bulk of the bets and money from bettors. BetMGM reported that 60% of the money bet on the point spread was on the Rams.

 The Rams have attracted more than twice as many bets to win the Super Bowl as any other team at DraftKings Sportsbook. They remain the favorites to win the Super Bowl, NFC and NFC West, but their odds dipped from 5-1 to 6-1 after Thursday's loss, and their odds to win the NFC West shifted from -105 to +164.

 The 49ers, in turn, improved from +300 to +180 to win the division. The defending-champion Seattle Seahawks moved from +215 to +184 in the tightly contested NFC West. San Francisco improved from 19-1 to 14-1 to win the Super Bowl at DraftKings.

title: Miami Dolphins end road trip with more lessons than wins
summary: Miami's players, coaches say takeaways from 49ers blowout will be building blocks for the rest of the season.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- Just before the final two-minute warning of the Miami Dolphins ' 35-13 loss to the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday, quarterback Malik Willis found receiver Ryan Miller for a 77-yard touchdown -- his first touchdown pass of the season and the team's longest passing touchdown since Week 1 of the 2024 season.

 Willis wasn't impressed.

 "I felt good for Ryan, I didn't feel good for the Miami Dolphins," he said. "That didn't help us. I mean, obviously it helped on the stat sheet, but it didn't help us as a team."

 The Dolphins spent the past week in northern California in preparation for what offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik called "a really good challenge" against the 49ers, and will return home from this two-game road trip, after losing to the  Las Vegas Raiders  in Week 1, with more lessons than victories.

 

 San Francisco scored touchdowns on each of its first five possessions, including both of their two offensive drives in the first half. Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley called the game "a tale of two halves" after Miami watched a 14-6 halftime deficit balloon to a 29-point hole within minutes.

 Hafley said his team began the game strongly, but 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy found a wide-open George Kittle for a 40-yard completion on the first play of the second half, ultimately setting up a Kittle touchdown three plays later.

 The 49ers went on to score two more touchdowns in their next 10 plays to put the game out of reach.

 "We did something extremely uncharacteristic on the first play of the half that went for an explosive," Hafley said. "And we had another huge mistake that went for a touchdown. So quickly, it hit us in the face really hard in the second half. And we didn't coach well enough in the second half, we didn't play well enough. So really disappointing.

 "Thought we had a great week of preparation and I felt like we were ready to play better. And the first half we did -- the second half was just not good enough in any phase."

 The discrepancy in overall experience between the Dolphins and 49ers was clear in a game between the youngest and second-oldest teams in the NFL respectively. Seven of Miami's top 10 leaders in defensive snaps Sunday have played in the league for fewer than two seasons.

 The veteran Purdy had more total touchdowns (3) than incompletions (2), and San Francisco's offense averaged 7.8 yards per play as 49ers receivers consistently found open field. According to NextGen Stats, Purdy's targets created 4.8 yards of separation on average, the most in the NFL this week.

 "You've got guys who's [in] the second game ever in the league and they're playing a championship team," linebacker Jordyn Brooks said. "So it's like you don't want those things to happen, but I always look at things from the positive side and I'd rather them happen now, where we can learn from them and build later. As the season progresses, we get better and better.

 

 "We get these mistakes out the way and we try to close the gap and get better as the season goes on."

 Hafley said he "didn't see that coming" when asked about the start to the second half, and said his players needed to learn from it -- although he admitted that any struggles "start with me."

 Miami closed the game with a pair of forced punts on consecutive drives before scoring on the pass to Miller. Brooks said games like Sunday's teach players who their teammates are. It's easy to be upbeat after a win, he said, but losses are when players' true character comes out.

 "When you get beat the way that we got beat today, you start to see who's who," Brooks said. "And so you can see the character of men. Are we going to still play hard even though there's no way to win this game? We down, we getting hit here, we getting hit there. Are we still going to play hard?

 "So I think that was the cool part to see is that we didn't execute, we didn't win, we didn't play the way that we wanted to play ... but we still fought. So we could work with that. You know what I mean? That's something that we take and we keep building as the season goes on. So at least we got the 'want to,' and if we got the 'want to,' we've got a chance."

 The Dolphins host Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 3, their first home game of the season and another matchup against a veteran-led team that can punish a young team for its mistakes.

 Brooks said Miami has the "right guys" in the locker room and things will not "unravel" as the season progresses. Defensive tackle Zach Sieler said the team can use the positive moments from its 0-2 start as building blocks for the remainder of the season.

 "The first thing I'm going to turn on is those last two minutes, see how we play and then we'll go back to the start," Sieler said. "That first half, I feel like we had them. We were doing good, we've just got to finish. There are some little things here and there that we let up and we gave them and I feel we gave them a lot of stuff. It's a good team. It's a good ball club. And that's how you win, is you make their guys make the mistakes. And we (made the mistakes). So we've got to make those corrections and just accelerate that growth."

title: NFL Week 2 eye-popping stats from Eagles, Pats, Jets, Bears
summary: We found six of the coolest advanced stats to come out of Sunday's games -- from third-down completions to matchup route stats.
full_text:
Week 2 is in the books! A little less exciting than Week 1 if you're a fan of offense; only 440 points had been scored through Sunday afternoon's games , whereas 702 had been posted by this time last week. If you're a fan of fumbles, be sure to tune in; there have been 82 fumbles through the first two weeks of the NFL season so far. Though, if you are a fan of fumbles, consider becoming a fan of something else.

 Every Sunday, I'll find several of the coolest advanced stats from the day's NFL action to share with you. Some call them NFL Next Gen Stats. I call them Next Ben Stats: the data that might not make it on the broadcast but will make you a smarter fan (and laugh a little bit, probably).

 Let's start with the statement day from Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts .

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Hurts' long conversions   
 Bears' scoring regression 
 Jets like Mitchell on third down   
 Gonzalez vs. Metcalf 
 Saints' bad first-half offense   
 Less pressure on Nix 

 

 

 
 

 3: How many third-down conversions Jalen Hurts had on third-and-11 or longer in the Eagles' win  -- the first such game of his career. 
 Hurts had nine total third-down conversions -- the most he has had in any game, regular season or postseason.

 Hurts' best trait has always been his poise and confidence.  Never has that been more clearly on display than against the Titans when things at times did not go the Eagles' way. Philadelphia's methodical opening drive ended in a 90-yard interception return after Hurts was duped on a quality play from safety Amani Hooker . Eagles running back Saquon Barkley and tight end Dallas Goedert both went down with injuries for an offense already missing guard Landon Dickerson . The defense started struggling mightily in the second half.

 

 Hurts, armed with as bad of a run game as he has ever had to endure, still lined up on third down and diced 'em up. The Titans' wanted to be a zone team to keep eyes on Hurts. (Think Jeffery Simmons ' pregame comment of "making Hurts play quarterback.") And Hurts did. His comfort with new wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks (five catches, 74 yards) is notable, and DeVonta Smith 's rise to WR1 was punctuated by an unbelievable catch against the sideline to set up the go-ahead score.

 

 The Eagles are 2-0. It has been far from pretty, but Hurts is willing this team to tough wins in September.

 
 

 4: How many third-down conversions WR Adonai Mitchell had for the Jets -- after having just 10 in his career (34 games) previously. 
 Mitchell fell out of trust in Indianapolis after his errors cost the Colts' a tight Rams contest in 2025, hence the trade to New York shortly thereafter. The Jets have been nothing but enthusiastic about Mitchell's maturity and focus, and you saw the fruits of that labor in a strong if ultimately disappointing showing against the Packers.

 The third-year wideout ended his day with six catches on 11 targets for 63 yards. In four of his past eight games with the Jets, Mitchell had at least nine targets -- more than he had in a single game as a Colt. Mitchell got schemed-up targets in this game, he got high-value looks off of motion, he made himself available on the scramble drill, he had yards after catch opportunities and he had two deep looks that were close but not connected.

 

 It was a complete WR game. The Jets are telling you they really like what they have in this young player. And Geno Smith is one of the best quarterbacks to keep hammering a young receiver, even through mistakes and drops (which Mitchell had one of in this contest). Mitchell's stock is rising.

 

 

 56: The difference in the Bears' point total from Week 1 to Week 2 -- the fourth-largest week-over-week point difference in NFL history. 
 According to ESPN Research, it was the biggest swing since the 1973 Falcons, who had a 62-point falloff. Before them? The 1934 Eagles and the 1920 Rochester Jeffersons -- a real team, apparently!

 (Incidentally, 56 is also the difference in the Panthers' defensive outing, with 59 points allowed in Week 1  and only 3 in Week 2 . That is the second-biggest such swing in league history.)

 

 Everything went right for the Bears' offense in Week 1; everything went wrong in Week 2. Chicago had multiple drops on the day. D'Andre Swift fumbled at Minnesota's 1-yard line. A penalty wiped out a completion to the Vikings' 16; that drive ended in a punt. And of course, the Bears had a field goal blocked inside the Vikings' 10 -- after QB  Caleb Williams came up lame on what would have been a walk-in touchdown, screaming and holding his right hamstring.

 

 The rain had an enormous impact on the Bears' offense, but coordinator Brian Flores and the Vikings' defense deserve worlds of credit for finding solutions against Ben Johnson's offense. The play of defensive tackle Jalen Redmond stood out, but rookies Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange  contributed, as well. And the breakout season of edge rusher Dallas Turner is well upon us. The Vikings' defense is as legit as it gets.

 We await news on Williams' injury with bated breath. Even in a bad game, he was making some special plays. The league is more fun when he's healthy.

 

 

 34: How many routes Christian Gonzalez was opposite DK Metcalf -- the most shadow snaps Gonzalez has taken in a single game, per NFL Next Gen Stats. 
 What was the result of that coverage in Patriots' 20-3 win over Steelers? Three receptions for 11 yards, and two were on throws behind the line of scrimmage.

 

 The Steelers did their usual with Metcalf by running him on shallow crossers and quick slants, using his superior speed and size to outclass man cover corners. But that's the thing about Gonzalez: Even among the league's premiere corners, he's noticeably big and fast. He can play these heavy man coverage days against bigger receivers -- such as Metcalf or Atlanta's Drake London  -- when other corners can't.

 

 

 32.9%: The Saints' offensive success rate in the first half, which is 29th leaguewide. They're 27th in EPA per play and in yards per play, as well. 
 And what about the second half? Great question. Including overtime, they are eighth in success rate (50%), sixth in EPA per play and 11th in yards per play.

 It's too early yet to say what exactly is happening. Is Kellen Moore and his offensive staff cooking up excellent second-half adjustments? That's part of it. Is quarterback Tyler Shough settling down once defenses capitulate into softer coverages when protecting second-half leads? That is absolutely part of it. How about getting to use all four downs to string together a series? Yep. The Saints are 4-for-4 on fourth down, and all of them have come in the fourth quarter or later.

 

 The Saints are now 1-1 with two second-half comebacks under their belts. Those are great experiences for a young team, which will never count itself out of a game for the rest of the season. But the Saints need to find a way to get early offense. The offseason investments in the running game (RB  Travis Etienne Jr.  and G David Edwards ) have yet to show up. The heavy reliance on WR  Chris Olave (second in the league in receiving yards with 268) feels fragile, as he doesn't have a great injury history.

 

 Still, I like what I've seen from Moore. Shough is stringing together enough plays -- though he does have to cut down on the sacks -- and the Saints are cooking something on offense.

 

 

 19.4%: How often Bo Nix was pressured in a win versus the Jaguars, per Next Gen Stats. It was less than half his pressure rate (45.5%) from Week 1. 
 The Broncos'  31-10 loss to the Chiefs in Week 1 was uncharacteristically riddled with pressures and sacks from the usually sack-averse Nix. I'm impressed with how quickly Denver offensive coordinator Davis Webb cleared things up. Nix was pressured on only six dropbacks against Jacksonville after enduring 15 pressures (and taking four sacks) a week ago. The Broncos' 17 unanswered points and seven-point victory feel sweet, but…

title: Jaxson Dart's coming at you from all angles
summary: Dart's ability to throw from different angles gives him a chance to be not just a quarterback who makes special throws but a special quarterback.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- The New York Giants were in the midst of their final training camp practice. It was their 20th camp practice in 29 days stretching across three states and much of the East Coast.  

 It would have been easy for quarterback Jaxson Dart & Co. to be going through the motions on this sunny Wednesday afternoon back at the under-construction Quest Diagnostics Training Center. The third and final preseason game was just days away, with the 2026 regular season and real games on the horizon. 

 But those who were around the Giants this summer know that going through the motions is not how they operated under new coach John Harbaugh, for whom it's all football, all the time. Just how Harbaugh and Dart like it. 

 On the 37th of 87 live reps that day, Dart went back to pass and was pressured off the edge by Abdul Carter . He sprinted right, running as fast as he could to elude the speedy linebacker. Rather than hit the brakes and establish a strong base to throw, the quarterback remained at top speed as he spotted wide receiver Darnell Mooney downfield. To make the play on the move, Dart heaved the ball 50 yards using the most unconventional motion. He threw the football submarine-style with his knuckles coming just inches from the ground. After the ball was released, Dart's momentum flung him to the ground, where he rolled over twice. His body had no other option.

 The ball sailed into the bright blue sky, covering half the field in air yards before dropping perfectly on his receiver. Mooney made the catch for a 40-yard gain. Dart peeled himself off the grass as if nothing had happened and jogged back to the huddle.

 This is what the young, dynamic quarterback brings to the table: the ability to make special plays and throws from unique angles. It's part of what convinced the Giants to trade up for Dart last year in the first round of the NFL draft and what persuaded Harbaugh to choose the Giants over the Tennessee Titans and Atlanta Falcons . They think with some refinement, Dart can become one of the league's best quarterbacks, in large part because of the special throws he can make.

 His ability almost defies logic and physics. It certainly goes against old-school principles. 

 "I was a baseball player my whole life. Played middle infield and thought that I was pretty good," Dart said. "So, being able to have the arm talent to do those [throws], I think, is something that I feel confident translating over into this game."

 

 The training camp throw was Ozzie Smith-esque. It's what we've become accustomed to seeing each week from some of the league's best quarterbacks, as well. Kansas City Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes  normalized unorthodox arm angles and sidearm throws even though quarterbacks have been doing it for years. 

 "Mahomes didn't take it to the next level. People were capable of doing that, too," former NFL quarterback and QB coach/mentor Matt Simms said. "But he was the person that allowed people to be more accepting of it."

 Dart's opposing quarterback this week, Matthew Stafford of the Los Angeles Rams (Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN), is currently one of the best in the league at altering his arm angles to manipulate throwing windows. Like Dart, he's a flip-of-the-wrist thrower, which helps on screens, touch passes and fitting the ball into tight windows. 

 The arm-angle variety has suited Stafford well, even if it's not necessarily for eye-popping throws. He has three Pro Bowl selections, an NFL MVP award and a Super Bowl win on his résumé heading into the Week 2 game against the visiting Giants. 

 "Those are the little throws where the average fan probably watches and just goes, 'There's a checkdown for 4 yards to the running back,'" Stafford said last week. "But maybe that ball gets batted or you don't even throw it with that defensive lineman in your face or something like that. That's where I feel they come.

 "It's not the launches down the field where I'm like, 'I got a great clean pocket, let me just drop it down for no reason.' It's just the instinctual plays."

   

 Dart is an instinctual quarterback. It was on display in the preseason when he whipped the ball sidearm against his body to rookie Malachi Fields for a touchdown. It worked in Week 1 when he threw several balls around defenders to find tight end Isaiah Likely in the middle of the field during a 28-20 win against the Dallas Cowboys . 

 It gives Dart a chance not just to be a quarterback who makes special throws, but to be a special quarterback. 

 "[Dart's] very talented," Harbaugh said this summer. "He's got exceptional arm talent. He can throw off different platforms. The quarterback coaches will talk to you about throwing off-platform and things like that, off-balance throws, arm angles. I think he's really good at that."

  
 

 DART'S WARMUPS THROUGHOUT his rookie season included practicing all kinds of throws -- over the top, sidearm, three-quarters and submarine. The routine consisted of approximately 15 minutes of delivering balls to equipment managers turned wide receivers during the early pregame warmups. It's part of a program Jaxson developed through his work at 3DQB, a quarterback training company he has worked with since he was a teenager and still employs in the offseason. 

 It was only natural after he spent a large chunk of his childhood in Kaysville, Utah, playing travel baseball.  

 Naturally, the skills transferred to the football field. 

 "As a kid, he would do that funky stuff too, and you'd just be like, 'What the hell?'" Brandon Dart, Jaxson's father, said. "But then it would be like, 'Damn, that's pretty good.'"

 Brandon said one of the happiest days of his son's childhood was when Rivals, a media company that focuses on recruiting and high school player rankings, changed his profile from dropback quarterback to dual threat. Jaxson Dart didn't want his ability to throw and run minimized. The change was validation of the quarterback he envisioned himself to be and wanted to become.  

 Naturally, his running and unique throws met with some resistance. Dart had a personal quarterbacks coach who showed Dart film and wanted him to throw like Peyton Manning. Some of his high school coaches would get frustrated with the things he did. During his college recruitment, he eliminated the University of Oklahoma because the Sooners were too rigid with their quarterbacks for his liking at the time, and even coach Lane Kiffin at Ole Miss was resistant to some of the unconventional things Dart did.

 But Dart knew from a young age he wasn't going to be put into a box. 

 "I just remember laughing when he was a freshman and he had this quarterback coach that was in his mid-to-late 60s, and Jaxson drove him crazy just because he was the in-the-box robotic quarterback coach and Jaxson would just like, 'Nah, that's not what we're doing. We're not going to do it like that,'" Brandon said. "I just remember them arguing all the time about just ways that he wanted to do it versus the way that Jaxson was being coached how to do it." 

 Dart's work with 3DQB and his coaches in high school, college and now the NFL has paid dividends. Dart is already one of the NFL's best passers on the run. 

 He completed 52% of his passes outside the pocket as a rookie despite averaging the fifth-most air yards per attempt (9.8) last season. That's comparable to two-time MVP Lamar Jackson in 2025.

 It's not an accident. 

 "[Dart's] throwing mechanics on the run are as good as anybody in the NFL," said Simms, son of former NFL star and Giants legend Phil Simms, who was ahead of the curve in teaching his kids off-platform throws.  

 Dart has also been developing and refining these throws for years. It began in the backyard and has been perfected in the lab. 

 It was done with a vision in mind: becoming a new-age quarterback who can thrive off-platform.

 "You really need to be able to play in that style to be successful in the NFL," Simms said.
